pages.body:
# Water

**What this section holds.** 10 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 03-01 **How much water we need (household math)**: Water is the fastest survival clock in the house: you can go weeks without food but only days without water.
- → 03-02 **Storing water safely**: How to store drinking water so it is still safe when you need it: which containers, how to clean them, where to keep them, and how to get the water already i…
- → 03-03 **Pool and hot tub water: utility water, and distilling it to drink**: A swimming pool or hot tub is a large store of water already at your house.
- → 03-04 **Purifying water: boil, chemical, filter**: How to make fresh water (rain, snow, rivers, ponds, wells, doubtful tap water) safe to drink, with or without fuel.
- → 03-05 **Rain catchment and melting snow and ice**: Rain and snow are the cheapest water you can get in fuel terms: they need disinfecting, not distilling.
- → 03-06 **Water when everything is frozen**: Winter brings two separate water problems: **your plumbing freezing and bursting** (which can flood the house and destroy the water you have), and **every ou…
- → 03-07 **Judging and testing water quality**: How to rank water sources from bad to worse, what a real test can tell you, and which tests to buy now while labs and shops are open.
- → 03-08 **Keeping stored and pool water from going bad (algae, bacteria, mosquitoes)**: Standing water left alone goes bad: green, slimy, smelly, and full of mosquito larvae.
- → 03-09 **Filter care: straws, bottles, squeeze and gravity filters**: How to choose, use, clean, store and retire the portable water filters most households buy.
- → 03-10 **Well water without power**: Getting water out of a drilled well when the grid is down, at your own home or at any place you might go that has one.

pages.title: How much water we need (household math)
pages.body:
# How much water we need (household math)

**What this page is for.** Water is the fastest survival clock in the house: you can go weeks
without food but only days without water. This page turns the CDC planning figure into your
household's numbers: how much to store, and how many days the water you already have will
last. Every other water page uses the numbers printed here.

> **CAUTION.** The numbers below are planning minimums from the CDC, not comfort levels. Heat,
> hard work, illness, pregnancy and nursing all push real need higher. Plan above the
> minimum, never below it.

## Do this now

1. **Know your two numbers.**
   - **Floor:** {{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }} gallons a day for the whole household. This
     is the bare minimum. It is the number you fall back to in a crisis, never the plan.
   - **Plan:** {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} gallons a day. Store to this number.
2. **Three days is the minimum store. Two weeks is the goal.** For your household, two weeks
   at the plan rate is **{{ derived.water.two_weeks_gal }} gallons**.
3. **Know your runway.** You have {{ gear.water.stored_gal }} gallons stored. At the floor
   rate that is about **{{ derived.water.stored_days }} days**. At the plan rate it is
   shorter. Recount every week during an emergency.
4. **Store more if** anyone is sick, pregnant or nursing, if it is hot, or if people are
   doing hard physical work.
5. **Never ration drinking water to the point of thirst.** Drink what you need today and put
   your effort into finding more (→ 03-05 rain and snow{{#if has.pool}}, → 03-03 your pool{{/if}}{{#if has.well}}, → 03-10 your well{{/if}}).

## Why these numbers

The CDC planning figure is **1 gallon per person per day**, with **at least a 3-day supply**
at home and a **2-week supply** if you can manage it (CDC, How to Create and Store an
Emergency Water Supply). That gallon is not all for drinking. Roughly half is drinking water
and half covers cooking, dishes, brushing teeth and basic washing.

**Needs go up**, says the CDC, for children, nursing mothers and sick people, in hot weather
(heat can double the need), and during hard physical work. A grid-down summer with laundry by
hand and wood to haul is not a quiet day on the couch.

### How your numbers are worked out

The binder builds your **floor** from your household profile on the CDC basis:

| Who | Added to the daily floor |
|---|---|
| Each person | 1 gallon |
| Each pregnant or nursing member | 0.5 gallon more |
| Each infant (formula mixing and washing) | 0.5 gallon more |
| Each pet | 0.25 gallon (about a cup for a cat; dogs drink more, check yours) |

Your household: **{{ household.size }} people**, floor **{{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }}
gallons a day**.

The **plan** figure is the floor plus a 30 percent margin ({{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }}
gallons a day). The margin covers heat, sickness, spills and the water that cooking eats.
If your food store leans on freeze-dried or dehydrated meals, those meals are rehydrated with
water that counts against the day, so treat the plan number as the least you need
(→ 07-07).

| | Per day | Two weeks |
|---|---|---|
| Floor (crisis ration) | {{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }} gal | floor x 14 |
| Plan (store to this) | {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} gal | {{ derived.water.two_weeks_gal }} gal |

### People who need extra care

{{#if has.infant}}- **Your infant.** Any water used for bottles, formula, cups or feeding must
  be safe water: boiled or treated, never raw pool or surface water. Infants are the least
  able to survive a stomach illness from bad water (→ 20-05).
{{else}}- **Infants.** Any water used for bottles, formula, cups or feeding must be safe water:
  boiled or treated, never raw pool or surface water. Infants are the least able to survive a
  stomach illness from bad water (→ 20-05).
{{/if}}
{{#if has.nursing}}- **The nursing member.** The CDC says needs rise while nursing. The margin
  in your plan number exists for her. Hers is never the line to ration.
{{else}}- **Anyone nursing** needs more water, says the CDC. Never ration a nursing mother's
  share.
{{/if}}
- **Diabetes.** Dehydration and high blood sugar feed each other: high sugar makes the body
  pass more urine, which concentrates the sugar further. Keep drinking water within reach of
  a person with diabetes, day and night, and give them a larger share
  {{#if has.condition.CL-01}}(→ 02-01){{else}}(→ 02-05){{/if}}. Some households agree in
  advance that this person gets water first if supply runs short. That is a conversation to
  have now, not during the shortage.
- **Children** get a full share. Do not shortchange them.
{{#if has.pets}}- **Your pets drink treated water too.** Raw pool or pond water can make an
  animal sick, and there may be no vet. Keep pets away from the pool and pour their water from
  the treated supply (→ 20-09).
{{else}}- **Pets** drink treated water, the same as people (→ 20-09).
{{/if}}

### Water that is not drinking water

Flushing a toilet uses gallons each time. Laundry and bathing use more. **Do not spend stored
drinking water on these.**
{{#if has.pool}}Your pool is for that: raw pool water flushes toilets, washes floors and
fights fires perfectly well (→ 03-03).{{else}}Use rain barrels, a pool or pond, or other
untreated water for flushing and washing floors (→ 03-05, → 13-01).{{/if}}

### The runway

**Runway = stored gallons ÷ gallons used per day.** That is how many days you have before you
*must* be producing water. Divide by the plan figure while things are normal; divide by the
floor only after you have already cut back to the floor. Write the number on the consumables
table (→ 23-02). For most households the honest answer is under two weeks, which is why rain,
snow{{#if has.pool}}, the pool{{/if}}{{#if has.well}}, the well{{/if}} and a way to treat
water matter so much.

## Gear and supplies

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Food-grade water containers (5 to 7 gal jugs, or a 55-gal drum) | The bulk of the store | Jugs can be moved. A full 55-gal drum weighs about 460 lb and never moves again |
| Bottled water by the case | Safest water with no preparation | The CDC calls it the safest reliable emergency source |
| Bathtub water bladder | Fills a tub cleanly before the water stops | About 100 gal; only useful if filled *before* pressure is lost (→ 03-02) |
| Labels and a marker | Track what is left | Date each container; mark drums in gallons |
| A runway card | Know the number without doing maths under stress | Write "stored gallons ÷ {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }}" on the container |

**If you don't have it, use what is in the house:**

{{#if has.water_heater_tank}}- **Your water heater** holds about {{ dwelling.water_heater_gallons }} gallons. It can be
  scalding hot, and gas heaters keep heating while gas flows. Never drain it from memory: use
  the step-by-step procedure on → 03-02.
{{else}}- **A tank water heater**, if you have one or find one, holds 30 to 80 gallons. It can
  be scalding hot; use the step-by-step procedure on → 03-02.
{{/if}}
- Toilet **tanks** (the box behind the seat, not the bowl), if no cleaning tablets are in
  them, and ice in the freezer.
- Any clean food-grade container: soda bottles, juice jugs. **Not** milk jugs (milk protein
  is hard to clean out and the water spoils), and never containers that held chemicals.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** stored gallons ÷ {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} a day (÷ {{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }}
  only once you have already cut back to the floor). Recount weekly.
- **Ration:** cut washing and cooking water first, never drinking water. Move washing and
  flushing to untreated water at once; that alone can halve how fast stored water goes.
- **Resupply:** rain and snowmelt first, because they cost the least fuel to make safe
  (→ 03-05). In winter, snow is often the easiest large source (→ 03-06).{{#if has.pool}}
  Distilling pool water works but burns a lot of fuel (→ 03-03).{{/if}}{{#if has.well}} Your
  well can still give water without power (→ 03-10).{{/if}}

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** build the two-week store now, while it is a shopping trip.
- **B (moving):** water weighs 8.34 lb per gallon, so you can carry very little. Carry one
  to two days per person and a way to treat more (→ 03-04), and plan the route around water.
  For {{ household.size }} people that is roughly {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} to twice
  that in gallons. Load it low in the vehicle, over the rear axle, strapped down; never in a
  roof box and never loose in the passenger area (→ 22-05). Fill containers from the tap on
  the way out if there is time.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** find out before you go where the water comes from.
  On **town or district water**, pressure dies when the grid's pumps stop, so the first job
  on arrival is to **fill every container and tub at once**, then set up rain catchment
  (→ 03-05). On a **private well**, the pump needs power; → 03-10 explains how to get water out
  without it. Either way the daily maths becomes a hauling and treating problem, not a storage
  problem.
{{#if has.destinations}}
  Your destinations:
{{#each destinations as d}}  - **{{ d.name }}** ({{ d.county }}, {{ d.state_name }}). Write its water source here: __________
{{/each}}
{{/if}}

## Cross-references

→ 03-02 storing water · → 03-03 pool water · → 03-04 purifying water · → 03-05 rain and snow ·
→ 03-06 winter water · → 03-10 well water without power · → 23-02 consumables table ·
→ 22-05 vehicle loading

pages.body:
# Storing water safely

**What this page is for.** How to store drinking water so it is still safe when you need it:
which containers, how to clean them, where to keep them, and how to get the water already in
your house (including the water heater) out safely.

> **CAUTION.** Stored water goes bad because of **what you put it in** and **what you touch it
> with**, far more often than because of age. A contaminated 55-gallon drum is not a water
> supply; it is 55 gallons of disease. Follow the container and handling rules exactly.
>
> **Floor:** bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners. The
> mix gives off chlorine gas. (→ 30-01)

## Do this now

1. **Fill everything when the forecast turns bad, not when the power fails.** Ice storm
   warning, blizzard warning, hurricane watch, severe thunderstorm watch: fill the bathtub
   bladder and every container then. City water pressure often holds for **12 to 48 hours**
   after a grid failure, but it **fades before it stops**: weak flow upstairs first, then
   sputtering and air. **By the time you notice, you are at the end of the buffer, not the
   start.** A bathtub bladder takes 20 to 30 minutes at full pressure and much longer at low
   pressure. This is the only water job with a hard deadline.
2. **When pressure comes back after an outage, assume the water is contaminated.** Empty
   pipes suck in dirty water at leaks and joints. Filter and chlorinate (→ 03-04) until the
   water utility says it is safe.
   {{#if has.municipal_water}}Your water utility: {{ contacts.utility.water.provider }},
   phone {{ contacts.utility.water.phone }} (check it against a current bill).{{/if}}
3. **Use food-grade containers** with tight lids: water jugs and drums made for drinking
   water, or clean 2-liter soda bottles. **Never** reuse containers that held chemicals, and
   do not use milk jugs.
4. **Sanitize before filling:** wash with soap, rinse, then swirl **1 teaspoon of unscented
   5 to 9 percent household bleach in 1 quart of water** over the whole inside. Wait
   **30 seconds**, pour it out, let it air dry (CDC). Bleach basics: → 29-05.
5. **Label** every container **"DRINKING WATER"** with the **date filled**.
6. **Store at 50 to 70 °F, in the dark, off bare concrete**, away from gasoline, pesticides
   and solvents (fumes pass through plastic).
7. **Replace home-filled water every 6 months.** Store-bought sealed bottles: use the printed
   date.
8. **Never put hands or a dirty cup into stored water.** Pour it, or use a clean scoop kept
   only for that.

## Why it works this way

Tap water from a city system leaves the plant with a little chlorine in it. That chlorine
fades in storage. Once it is gone, whatever got in (from the container, the air or a hand)
can multiply. That is why the CDC's rules are mostly about **clean containers, sealed lids
and clean handling**, not about water "expiring" (CDC, How to Create and Store an Emergency
Water Supply).

{{#if has.well}}Well water usually has no chlorine in it to begin with, so clean handling
matters even more. Many households add the CDC bleach dose (→ 03-04) to well water before
long storage.{{/if}}

### Container choices

| Option | Gallons | Good | Bad |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bottled water, sealed | varies | Safest, no preparation, portable | Costs most per gallon; bulky |
| 5 to 7 gal jugs | 5 to 7 | Can be moved when full, stack, good for leaving home | Modest volume; about 50 lb each |
| 55-gal food-grade drum | 55 | Cheapest per gallon; two weeks in one container | About 460 lb full: it never moves again; needs a pump |
| Bathtub bladder | about 100 | Huge and cheap | Only works if filled **before** the water stops |
| Clean 2-liter soda bottles | 0.5 | Free, tough, good for freezing and for children to carry | Work to fill and rotate |

### Where to put it

A basement or an inside room is best: dark, cool, steady temperature. {{#if has.basement}}Your
basement is the right place.{{/if}} {{#if has.garage}}**An attached garage is the wrong place
for winter.** In a grid-down cold spell the garage drops below freezing and bottles split.
Move any water stored there inside before winter, or on the first day of an outage at the
latest (→ 03-06).{{/if}} Water expands when it freezes: leave a little air space at the top of
any container that might get cold, and never use glass for cold storage.

**Write down where your water is** so anyone in the house can find it (→ 22-04).

{{photo stored-water-location}}

### Handling

One person's dirty hands can spoil a whole drum. Use a spigot, pump or pour spout kept only
for water; keep it capped; never pour unused water back into the container.

**If stored water tastes flat,** pour it back and forth between two clean containers to put
air back in it, or add a pinch of salt per quart. The CDC suggests this for boiled water and it
works the same here.

## The water heater: the biggest store already in your house

{{#if has.water_heater_tank}}Your tank water heater holds about {{ dwelling.water_heater_gallons }}
gallons.{{else}}A tank water heater holds 30 to 80 gallons. If you have one, or reach a house
that does, this applies.{{/if}} It is also the most dangerous water in the house to get at
carelessly.

- **It is hot.** Water heaters are usually set at 120 to 140 °F. At 140 °F, water scalds a
  child's skin in seconds (US Consumer Product Safety Commission, Tap Water Scalds).
- **A gas heater keeps heating** while gas flows, grid or no grid. An electric one stops when
  the power stops, but stays hot for many hours.
- **Until you drain it, it is your only safe hot washing water.** Use it for the first days'
  hand washing and dishes before you drain it for drinking (→ 13-02, → 13-10).

{{photo water-heater-drain-valve}}

**Draining the water heater: six steps, in this order.**

1. **Turn the heat off.** On a gas heater, turn the gas control to **OFF** (not "pilot"). On an
   electric heater, switch its breaker off. Draining with the burner or elements live will
   fire them on an emptying tank and ruin it.
2. **Close the cold-water inlet valve** on the pipe at the top of the tank.
3. **Open a hot tap** somewhere higher in the house (a bathroom sink) and leave it open. This
   lets air in so the tank will drain.
4. **Put a hose or bucket on the drain valve at the base, then open it slowly. THE WATER CAN BE
   SCALDING.** Wear gloves and long sleeves and keep children out of the room. If you can, let
   the tank cool for hours first, or run the first water into a lidded bucket and walk away
   from it.
5. **The first gallon or two carries sediment** (sand and scale from the bottom of the tank).
   Let it settle, pour off the clear water and throw away the sludge. If the tank has sat for
   weeks, treat the water before drinking (→ 03-04).
6. **Do not turn the heat back on until the tank is full again:** inlet valve open, hot tap
   running steadily with no air. A heater fired empty burns out.

Every other page that says "drain the water heater" means this procedure.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Food-grade water jugs, 5 to 7 gal | Water you can move; for leaving home | Rigid, with a spigot or cap you trust |
| 55-gal food-grade drum, bung wrench and pump | Bulk storage | Put it where it will live for ever before you fill it |
| Bottled water by the case | Safest, no preparation | Use by the printed date |
| Unscented household bleach, 5 to 9 percent | Cleaning containers **and** treating water | Buy fresh; it weakens within months (→ 29-05) |
| A scoop, pour spout or pump kept only for water | Keeps hands out of the supply | Store it capped and clean |
| Waterproof labels and a marker | Date and name every container | "DRINKING" or "UTILITY" |
| Bathtub bladder | Large cheap volume at the warning stage | Practice putting it in the tub once |

**If you don't have it:**

- Clean 2-liter soda bottles are good containers: free and strong.
- Food-grade buckets from bakeries or restaurants. Ask what was in them; avoid anything oily.
- The water heater (above), toilet tanks (not bowls) and ice in the freezer.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** stored gallons ÷ {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} gallons a day, your plan rate
  from → 03-01. The floor rate ({{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }}) is a crisis ration, not the
  number to divide by.
- **Ration:** the moment the tap is in doubt, stop using stored water for anything but
  drinking, cooking, infant feeding and medical needs. Everything else uses rain or untreated
  water.
- **Resupply:** refill containers with treated rain, snowmelt or other treated water
  (→ 03-04, → 03-05, → 03-06). **Clean the container again** before each refill.
- **Rotation is the quiet failure.** Water you stored and forgot is water you will not trust
  when it matters. Put the six-month swap on the calendar with the smoke-alarm batteries.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** fill the bladder and every container the moment a warning is
  issued, before pressure is lost.
- **B (moving):** only jugs and bottles travel. Water weighs 8.3 lb a gallon; carry one to two
  days and a way to treat more, not a week.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** set up storage at once (a cistern, drums or barrels) so
  you are not hauling water every day. The same cleaning rules apply to anything you press
  into service.

## Cross-references

→ 03-01 daily water needs · → 03-04 purifying water · → 03-05 rain barrels ·
→ 03-06 winter water · → 03-08 keeping water from going bad · → 22-04 where everything is ·
→ 29-05 chlorine products

pages.body:
# Pool and hot tub water: utility water, and distilling it to drink

**What this page is for.** A swimming pool or hot tub is a large store of water already at
your house. This page explains what that water is good for, why you cannot simply drink it,
and how to distil it (boil it and collect the steam) when you must.
{{#if has.pool}}Your pool holds about {{ dwelling.pool_gallons }} gallons.{{else}}{{#if has.hot_tub}}Your hot tub holds about {{ dwelling.pool_gallons }} gallons.{{/if}}{{/if}}

> **SAFETY.**
> - **A saltwater pool cannot be made drinkable by boiling, bleach or an ordinary filter.**
>   None of them removes salt, and drinking salt water makes dehydration worse. Only
>   **distillation** removes salt.
> - **Pool and hot tub water also holds chemicals:** chlorine or bromine, stabilizer
>   (cyanuric acid), and sometimes algaecide or metals. Distillation removes salts and most of
>   these.
> - **Floor:** bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners.
>   Pool supplies include acids ("pH down", muriatic acid); keep them apart. The mix gives off
>   chlorine gas. (→ 30-01)
> - **Floor:** children do not have access to chlorine products or pool chemicals. (→ 30-01)

## Do this now

1. **Use stored, tap or bottled water first.** Distilling is slow (about 1 cup an hour with a
   pot on a stove). It is the fallback, not the main supply.
2. **Use untreated pool water freely for everything except drinking and cooking:** flushing
   toilets, washing floors, cleaning, fighting fires. This is the pool's real value: once the
   pool covers flushing and washing, every gallon of stored water can go to drinking.
3. **Never drink saltwater pool water straight, boiled or bleached.** The salt stays in.
4. **Fresh (chlorine) pool or hot tub water for drinking is a decision.** Your household's
   choice: {{choice DC-13}} (→ 30-14). Whatever you chose, follow it the same way every time.
5. **To distil:** boil the water and catch the **steam**, which turns back into clean water.
   The salt and most chemicals stay behind in the pot. Method below.
6. **Cover the pool** to cut evaporation and keep out leaves, animals and children.

## What kind of water is in it

| Water | What is in it | Without distilling it is | To drink |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Saltwater pool** (salt chlorinator) | Dissolved salt, chlorine made from the salt, stabilizer, maybe algaecide or metals | Utility water only | **Distil.** No other home method removes salt |
| **Chlorine pool** (fresh water) | Chlorine, stabilizer, maybe algaecide or metals; bacteria and algae once the pump stops | Utility water | Distil; or the household's choice on → 30-14 |
| **Hot tub or spa** | Bromine or chlorine, body oils and sweat from bathers, often a warm breeding ground for germs | Utility water | Distil; or the household's choice on → 30-14 |

A home saltwater pool is much less salty than the sea, but **far too salty to drink**. Your
salt chlorinator's manual gives the salt level it runs at; write it here: ______ ppm ("ppm"
means parts per million, → 29-05). Less salty does not mean safe to sip.

**The trade-off for fresh pools and hot tubs, in one sentence:** filtering and chlorinating
a fresh pool uses far less fuel than distilling it, but leaves in the stabilizer, algaecide
and any metals that distilling would remove, and hot tubs start dirtier than pools. The card
lays out the risks and options (→ 30-14).

## Why distillation works

Distillation boils water into steam and turns only the steam back into liquid. Salt, metals
and most chemicals do not boil off with the water, so they are **left behind** in the pot.
The CDC says distillation removes **germs, heavy metals, salts and most other chemicals**; it
is the only common home method that also removes salt (CDC, How to Make Water Safe in an
Emergency). Boiling and bleach kill germs but leave salt and chemicals in place.

### The cup-on-lid still (CDC method)

{{figure fig-cup-on-lid-still}}

1. **Pre-filter:** pour the water through a cloth or coffee filter to remove leaves, insects
   and grit. This keeps the pot cleaner and the still faster.
2. Fill a pot **halfway** with the filtered water.
3. Tie a cup to the handle of the pot lid so that, when the lid is put on **upside down**, the
   cup hangs **right side up** inside the pot. The cup must **not** touch the water.
4. Put the lid on upside down. Steam hits the lid, runs to the low middle point and drips into
   the cup.
5. **Boil for 20 minutes.** The water in the cup is distilled. Let it cool before drinking.

**Yield:** roughly **1 cup an hour**. The CDC's drinking-water share alone is half a gallon
per person per day: for your {{ household.size }} people, about half of your
{{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }}-gallon daily floor (→ 03-01). At a cup an hour, that is
eight hours of boiling per gallon. The cup-on-lid still is a demonstration and a stopgap, not
a supply. That is why the tube still below, fuel, and rain and snow (→ 03-05) matter.

### The larger still: pot, lid and tube condenser

The cup-on-lid wastes most of the steam. Piping the steam out through a tube and cooling it
outside the pot captures nearly all of it: same fire, several times the water.

{{figure fig-tube-condenser-still}}

**Materials (stores in a shoebox):**

- **10 to 20 ft of soft copper tubing, 3/8 or 1/2 inch.** Copper carries heat away fast and
  handles steam. Food-grade silicone tubing is fine for a short flexible joint. **Never use
  vinyl or PVC tubing**: it releases chemicals at steam temperature.
- **A lid you can seal the tube into:** drill a spare pot lid and fit a compression or barbed
  fitting, or, with no tools, seal heavy aluminum foil over the pot with the tube pushed
  through and crimped tight.
- **A cooling bath:** a bucket or basin of cold water (snow in winter works well) that the
  copper coil runs through, sloping **downhill** the whole way to the collection jar.
- A collection jar, and cloth or coffee filters.

**Running it:** pot half full of pre-filtered water at a low rolling boil. Steam leaves
through the tube, turns to water in the cold coil and drips into the jar. Keep the bath cold
(change the water or add snow). Keep the tube sloping so water cannot pool in it. **Never let
the pot boil dry**: the salts scorch and the pot warps. Throw away the salty liquid left in
the pot.

{{photo pool-still-setup}}

**Rules that keep the water clean:**

- Before the first drinking batch, run a new copper coil once with vinegar and water, then
  once with plain water. New copper carries oil from manufacturing.
- **Lead-free fittings only.** No lead solder, no brass of unknown origin.
- Pour the leftover brine far from gardens and rain barrels. Salt kills soil.
- **Do not look for a reverse-osmosis unit** to use on pool water. Home units need water
  pressure, power and replacement membranes. A still is the practical route.

**Planning numbers (estimates; time your own still once):**

- **Yield:** a sealed pot-and-coil still over a steady wood fire makes roughly **1 to 2 quarts
  an hour**, two to six times the cup-on-lid, depending on the seal and how cold the coil is.
  Time yours with a watch and write it here: ______ quarts an hour.
- **Fire time:** at 1 to 2 quarts an hour, each gallon needs 2 to 4 hours of fire. Your
  drinking share alone is several gallons a day, so **distilling cannot carry a household by
  itself.** Run the still on fires already burning for heat and cooking (→ 06-04), and use it
  to cover dry spells. Rain and snow must be the main supply.
- **Wood:** turning a gallon of water to steam takes about 2.5 kWh of heat. Seasoned wood
  holds about 2.5 kWh per pound, and an open-fire still captures perhaps 10 to 20 percent of
  it, so budget roughly **5 to 15 lb of seasoned wood per gallon distilled.** Over a winter
  that is a large bite out of the woodpile; put it on the consumables table (→ 23-02).
- **Check the output:** a cheap TDS meter ("total dissolved solids", a pen that reads how much
  is dissolved in water) should read near zero on distilled water. If it reads salty, the
  seal is leaking boiling splash into the tube. Reseat the seal and fix the slope.

**Do not distil on battery power.** Turning water to steam takes roughly **700 to 1,400
watt-hours per liter**, against about 110 watt-hours just to boil a liter for purification.
{{#if has.power_station}}Your power stations hold about {{ gear.station_wh_total }} watt-hours
in total: divide that by 700 to 1,400 to see how few liters a full charge would make.{{else}}A
large 2,000 watt-hour power station would make only about 1.5 to 3 liters.{{/if}}
Distillation is a wood-fire job. An electric countertop distiller running on a strong solar
day nets only a few liters: useful for drinking water, never the household's supply
(→ 09-02).

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Large stockpot with a domed lid that can sit upside down | The still | Stainless steel; a rounded lid sends drips to the center |
| Heat-safe cup and wire or cord | Catches the distilled water | A metal cup will not melt |
| 10 to 20 ft soft copper tubing, 3/8 to 1/2 inch, and a fitting | The tube still | Never vinyl tubing |
| A drilled spare lid, or heavy aluminum foil | Seals the tube into the pot | Foil needs no tools |
| Cloth or coffee filters | Pre-filter | Cheap; stock many |
| Unscented bleach or pool shock | Disinfecting distilled water before storage | **Dose only from → 03-04.** Pool shock only by the two-step method there, never as dry granules |
| TDS meter | Confirms the still is working | Reads near zero on good distillate |
| Food-safe storage containers | Finished water | Label "DRINKING" and "POOL / UTILITY" |
| Electric countertop distiller | Much faster if you have power | Power hungry; a supplement only |

**If you don't have it:**

- Any pot with a bowl set inside and an upside-down domed lid is a still. Weight the center of
  the lid so drips fall into the bowl.
- Clear tubing and two sealed containers over heat make a rough condenser.
- Plastic sheeting over a frame floating on the pool surface makes a solar still: roughly a
  liter per square meter per day for no fuel.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** a pool is a lot of *volume*. Your real limits are **fuel to boil it** and
  **time**. Wood or propane (→ 06-04) is the binding constraint, not water.
- **Ration:** distil only what you need to drink and cook with. Use untreated pool water for
  all washing, flushing and cleaning.
- **Resupply:** rain and snowmelt need only disinfecting, **not** distilling, which takes far
  less fuel (→ 03-05). In wet or snowy months, use those first and save the pool for dry
  spells.
- **Gardens:** do not water a garden with saltwater-pool water. Salt harms soil and plants.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** the pool is a large reserve already in place. Once the grid is
  down, **stop adding chemicals by default**, cover the pool, and treat it as your utility
  tank. Keeping a measured chlorine level to slow algae is an option with its own rules
  (→ 03-08).
- **B (moving):** you cannot take the pool. Carry stored or distilled water, and know the
  water sources on the route.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** a still kit is light. Bring it for brackish or doubtful
  sources even if you do not expect to need it. Fresh well water is disinfected, not
  distilled (→ 03-10).

## Cross-references

→ 03-01 how much you need · → 03-04 purifying fresh water · → 03-05 rain and snow ·
→ 03-08 keeping pool water from going bad · → 06-04 wood supply · → 30-14 the pool-water card ·
→ 29-05 chlorine products

pages.title: Purifying water: boil, chemical, filter

photo_slots.caption: Our treatment kit: bleach with its strength, dropper, pool shock bucket, filter

pages.body:
# Purifying water: boil, chemical, filter

**What this page is for.** How to make fresh water (rain, snow, rivers, ponds, wells, doubtful
tap water) safe to drink, with or without fuel. Salt water is different: it needs → 03-03.
New to the words? "Disinfect", "micron", "virus" and "turbidity" are explained in → 29-06;
bleach and pool shock in → 29-05.

> **SAFETY.**
> - Bad water causes diarrhea. In an infant, a young child, an elder or a person with
>   diabetes that is not an inconvenience: it is dehydration and a medical emergency with no
>   clinic to go to (→ 12-05).
> - **You cannot boil or disinfect away fuel, toxic chemicals or radioactive material**
>   (CDC). If water may hold those, do not use it; distil it (→ 03-03) or find another source.
> - **Floor:** bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners. The
>   mix gives off chlorine gas. (→ 30-01)
> - **Floor:** children do not have access to chlorine products. (→ 30-01)

## Do this now

1. **Cloudy water: clear it first.** Pour it through clean cloth, paper towel or a coffee
   filter, or let it settle and pour off the clear water. Then disinfect.
2. **Boiling is best.** Bring the water to a **rolling boil for 1 minute**. Above about 5,000
   feet, boil for **3 minutes** (EPA says above 5,000 ft; CDC says above 6,500 ft; use the
   lower, safer figure). {{#if is.high_altitude}}**Your home is at about {{ region.home.elevation_ft }} ft: boil for 3 minutes.**{{else}}Your home is at about {{ region.home.elevation_ft }} ft.{{/if}}
   Let it cool, then store it covered.
3. **No fuel? Use plain unscented household bleach (5 to 9 percent): 8 drops per gallon.**
   Stir, wait **30 minutes**, then drink. **Double the bleach** if the water is cloudy,
   colored or very cold.
4. **Filters do not remove viruses.** After filtering, still disinfect with chemicals or
   boiling.
5. **Salt water needs distilling, not this page** (→ 03-03).

## Three different jobs

People mix these up all the time.

- **Clarifying** removes dirt and particles (settling, cloth, filters).
- **Disinfecting** kills germs (boiling, chlorine, UV, sunlight).
- **Distilling** removes salts and chemicals (→ 03-03).

Boiling and bleach disinfect. They do **not** remove salt or chemicals.

## 1. Boiling: the most reliable

The CDC says boiling is the best way to kill germs. **One minute at a rolling boil**: a true
tumbling boil, not the first small bubbles. Let it cool on its own; do not add cold untreated
water to speed it up. A flat taste is normal: pour it between two clean containers to put air
back in, or add a pinch of salt per quart.

The catch is **fuel**. Boiling a household's water every day burns a lot of wood or gas
(→ 06-04). That is why chemical treatment is the everyday method when the water is already
clear.

## 2. Chlorine bleach: cheap, small, no fuel

Use **unscented liquid household bleach**. Check the label for "sodium hypochlorite" and its
percentage. Do not use scented, color-safe, splash-less or "with cleaners" bleach. **If the
label gives directions for disinfecting drinking water, follow the label.**

Published table (US EPA, Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water; CDC, How to Make Water Safe
in an Emergency), printed as published:

**5 to 9 percent sodium hypochlorite (typical US household bleach):**

| Water | Drops | Milliliters | Spoon |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 quart / liter | 2 drops | 0.1 mL | too small to measure |
| 1 gallon | 8 drops | 0.5 mL | slightly less than 1/8 tsp |
| 5 gallons | 40 drops | 2.5 mL | 1/2 tsp |

**1 percent sodium hypochlorite:**

| Water | Drops | Milliliters | Spoon |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 quart / liter | 10 drops | 0.5 mL | 1/8 tsp |
| 1 gallon | 40 drops | 2.5 mL | 1/2 tsp |
| 5 gallons | 200 drops | 12.5 mL | 2.5 tsp |

Stir well and let stand **at least 30 minutes**. **Double the dose** for water that is
cloudy, murky, colored or very cold. A faint chlorine smell afterwards is the point. No smell
at all can mean the dirt in the water used up the chlorine: treat again and wait again.

**Very dirty water that will not clear** after settling and filtering is a decision. The
published method is to clear the water first and then use the label or table dose (doubled for
cloudy water). Some households go further, adding more chlorine and waiting longer, which
raises the chlorine they drink and still may not reach germs hidden in dirt. Your household's
choice: {{choice DC-23}} (→ 30-24).

**Limits that matter:**

- Chemicals **do not work as well as boiling against parasites** (tiny organisms with tough
  shells).
- Iodine will **not** kill *Cryptosporidium*, a common parasite. **Chlorine dioxide tablets
  will**, if you follow the label exactly.
- **Do not drink iodine-treated water** if pregnant, with thyroid problems, or with iodine
  sensitivity, and nobody should drink it for more than a few weeks.

## 2b. Pool shock (calcium hypochlorite): the long-storage chemical

Bleach loses strength within months. Dry, sealed **granular calcium hypochlorite** ("pool
shock") keeps for years, and a small amount treats a very large volume of water. It is used
in **two steps**. This is the US EPA's published emergency method:

**Step 1. Make a stock solution** (somewhere with fresh air; wear eye protection):
**One heaping teaspoon (about 1/4 ounce) of granular calcium hypochlorite into 2 gallons of
water.** Stir until it dissolves. This makes roughly a 500 mg/L chlorine solution.

**The stock is itself a poison**, far stronger than drinking water. Keep it in a container
nobody could mistake for drinking water, **labeled "CHLORINE STOCK: DO NOT DRINK"** in
marker, lid on, up high and out of children's reach (→ 20-02). If anyone swallows it, call
Poison Control and see → 12-17.

**Step 2. Treat the water:** add **1 part stock solution to each 100 parts of water**: about
**1 pint (16 oz) of stock per 12.5 gallons** of water. That is about 1.3 fl oz (2½
tablespoons) of stock per gallon, or 6.4 oz per 5 gallons. Stir, wait **30 minutes**, and
expect a slight chlorine smell. No smell means add more and wait again. If the taste is
strong, pour it between clean containers and let it stand a few hours.

**Rules that keep this safe:**

- **Read the label:** it must be 65 to 73 percent calcium hypochlorite with **no algaecides,
  clarifiers or stabilizers**. "Multi-action" shock products cannot be made drinkable.
- Add granules **to water**, never water to granules. Use plastic or glass, never metal.
- **Do not store mixed stock solution**: it weakens within days to weeks. Mix it fresh.
- Never use pool shock as dry granules in drinking water, and never dose it like bleach
  drops.

**Storing pool shock.** Calcium hypochlorite is a strong oxidizer: it **feeds a fire**,
**gives off chlorine when it gets wet or hot**, and its dust burns skin, eyes and lungs (CDC
and ATSDR, Medical Management Guidelines for Calcium Hypochlorite). Store it:

- in its sealed bag inside a lidded plastic bucket, labeled "POOL SHOCK: OXIDIZER";
- **off the floor** (a flood or wet floor reaching it releases chlorine), dry, away from
  furnaces, water heaters and other heat;
- **never near fuel, acids, ammonia or ammunition** (→ 06-06), and **never on the same shelf
  or in the same bucket as trichlor or dichlor pool tablets**: calcium hypochlorite and
  trichlor can make chlorine gas or fire on contact;
- away from electronics and power stations (the fumes corrode them);
- where children cannot reach it.

If your only good dry spot is also your shelter room, a sealed, lidded bucket on a shelf
removes the two triggers that matter most: water and heat.

{{photo water-treatment-kit}}

## 3. Filters: clear water and remove parasites, not viruses

Portable filters do **not** remove all germs. The CDC says a filter needs an **absolute pore
size of 0.3 micron or smaller** to remove bacteria, and **1 micron or smaller** for parasites
such as *Giardia* and *Cryptosporidium* (a micron is a thousandth of a millimeter, → 29-06).
**No common portable filter removes viruses.** So filter first, then disinfect. Filter care:
→ 03-09; filter specifications: → 28-06.

## 4. UV and sunlight: the backups

- A portable **UV pen or bottle** works on small amounts of **clear** water.
- **Solar disinfection (SODIS):** fill **clear PET plastic bottles of 2 liters or less** (not
  glass, not colored or scratched plastic, not bigger: the sunlight has to reach the middle)
  with clear water. Lay them on their side in the sun for **6 hours** if sunny or **2 days**
  if cloudy. A dark surface underneath helps.
- Neither works on cloudy water.

**Never** drink water from car radiators or home heating boilers.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Unscented household bleach, 5 to 9 percent, fresh | Main fuel-free treatment | Weakens within months; rotate; note the percentage |
| Calcium hypochlorite (pool shock), additive-free | Years of shelf life in a small container | Strong oxidizer; store as above |
| Chlorine dioxide tablets | The chemical that handles *Cryptosporidium* | Follow the label timing exactly |
| Gravity or pump filter, 0.1 to 0.2 micron | Clears water and removes parasites and bacteria with no fuel | Still disinfect afterwards for viruses |
| Coffee filters, clean cloth | Pre-filter, always step one | Cheap; stock many |
| Large stockpot with lid | Boiling in volume | Also the still (→ 03-03) |
| Medicine dropper and measuring spoons | Measure bleach accurately | Guessing a dose is how people get sick |
| Clean lidded containers | Hold treated water | Label "TREATED" with the time |

Write where your treatment kit is kept: __________ (→ 22-04).

**If you don't have it:**

- **Pool shock** is concentrated chlorine; additive-free pool shock is usable for drinking
  water by the two-step method above.
- Any tightly woven cloth (a T-shirt, a bandana) pre-filters; fold it in layers.
- Clear PET bottles of 2 liters or less plus sunshine is disinfection with no equipment.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** count bottles of bleach and strips of tablets. A year-old jug of bleach is
  weaker than the tables assume. Pool shock stored dry lasts years.
- **Ration:** use chemicals for clear water and save fuel. Boil when the water is doubtful,
  someone is sick, or you cannot measure a dose with confidence.
- **Resupply:** boiling always works if you have fuel. Sunlight works with nothing but
  bottles. A good filter reduces how much chemical you need.
- **The real failure:** running out of *clean container space*, not treatment. Keep clean,
  labeled containers ready so treated water does not get dirty again.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** clear tap or stored water usually needs nothing. Treat rain and
  snow (→ 03-05){{#if has.pool}}, and distil pool water (→ 03-03){{/if}}. Keep both bleach and
  tablets.
- **B (moving):** tablets and a small filter: light, no fuel, fast. Treat everything you pick
  up on the way, no exceptions.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** a well or spring is usually fresh and needs only
  disinfecting. Test it when you can (→ 03-07); until then, treat it as unsafe.

## Cross-references

→ 03-03 pool water · → 03-05 rain and snow · → 03-06 winter water · → 03-07 testing ·
→ 03-08 keeping water from going bad · → 03-09 filter care · → 06-04 fuel ·
→ 12-05 dehydration · → 29-05 chlorine products · → 30-24 extra-strength chlorination card

photo_slots.caption: Our rain barrel: where it stands, the downspout or funnel, the screen, the WATER ONLY pump

pages.body:
# Rain catchment and melting snow and ice

**What this page is for.** Rain and snow are the cheapest water you can get in fuel terms:
they need disinfecting, not distilling. This page covers catching rain, melting snow and
ice, and keeping both safe.

> **CAUTION.** Rain is clean when it leaves the sky and dirty by the time it leaves your roof:
> bird droppings, grit, roofing residue and whatever blew onto it. **Treat harvested rain
> before drinking it** (CDC, Collecting Rainwater and Your Health). Snow is the same, plus
> whatever it landed on.

## Do this now

1. **Put barrels or any clean containers under downspouts.** A modest rain fills them.
2. **Always treat before drinking:** filter out the grit, then boil or disinfect (→ 03-04).
   Rain needs **disinfecting only**, not distilling.
3. **Skip the first flush.** The first minutes of runoff carry the worst of the roof. Send it
   to the garden and collect what comes after.
4. **Melt snow with a little water already in the pot.** Never eat snow to stay hydrated: it
   costs body heat you cannot spare (→ 03-06).
5. **Screen every barrel**, or empty and scrub it at least **once a week**. That is the CDC's
   rule for stopping mosquitoes breeding in it (→ 03-08).

## Setting up a barrel

- **Stand it on level, solid ground or a sturdy platform.** A full 55-gallon barrel holds
  about **460 lb of water** (55 gal x 8.34 lb). On a slope or soft ground it can tip over or
  split; a falling barrel can crush a child.
- **Lid and screen on**, against mosquitoes and debris (→ 03-08).
- **Draw from a spigot or a pump**, never by dipping.
- **A pump or hose used for drinking water is "WATER ONLY" for ever.** Anything that has
  touched fuel, diesel exhaust fluid or chemicals never touches drinking water again. Mark the
  pump "WATER ONLY" in marker and keep it in a separate bag from any fuel pump. Before first
  use, rinse barrel and pump with the container-cleaning solution on → 03-02 (1 teaspoon
  bleach per quart of water, 30 seconds), then with clean water.
- **No roof? Make a funnel.** A tarp strung as a funnel, or an upside-down ceiling-leak
  diverter hung from posts or a line with a hose to the barrel, collects rain without the
  roof's grit. (If your roof is leaking, that job comes first: → 16-12.)
- **Freeze rule: drain the barrel and bring it in before a hard freeze.** Water expands as it
  freezes and splits barrels and pumps. In winter, snowmelt replaces it.

Write where your barrel, pump and treatment supplies are kept: __________ (→ 22-04).

{{photo rain-barrel-setup}}

## How much water a roof gives

**One inch of rain on 1,000 square feet of roof gives about 600 gallons** (0.6 gallon per
square foot per inch, before losses). Allow for losses (first flush, splash, overflow) of
roughly a fifth.

Measure the footprint of your roof (length x width of the house from outside, not the sloped
surface) and write it here: ______ sq ft. Then:

- **Gallons per inch of rain** = roof square feet x 0.6 = ______
- Your area gets about **{{ region.home.precip_in }} inches of rain a year** and
  **{{ region.home.snow_in }} inches of snow**.

Even one downspout on a modest roof section fills a 55-gallon barrel in an ordinary rain. For
most houses, **storage barrels and treatment are the limit, not the rain.**

> **Before the collapse:** a few states limit how much rainwater a household may collect or
> how it may be used. Your state's water-rights agency can tell you. This never decides
> whether you collect water to survive.

## What is actually in it

The CDC says rain picks up contamination from the roof: animal droppings, dust, insects and
roofing material. Rainwater is not safe to drink untreated, and the risk is highest for young
children. Treat everything anyone drinks.

**Never mix rainwater into treated water.** The CDC warns that adding rain to treated water
(bottled or tap) can contaminate it. Keep "TREATED" and "RAW" containers strictly apart, and
never connect a catchment line to house plumbing.

**Roofing matters.** Asphalt shingles shed grit and some chemicals; metal roofs are the
cleanest common surface. Do not collect from anything with lead flashing, treated wood or moss
killer. If the roof is doubtful, use the water for flushing, washing and the garden, and drink
from a cleaner source.

**Treatment chain:** screen out leaves at the gutter → let it settle in the barrel → draw from
a spigot above the sediment → **filter** → **boil or disinfect** (→ 03-04) → store clean
(→ 03-02).

{{figure fig-first-flush-diverter}}

## Snow and ice

- **Melt, don't eat.** Eating snow lowers your core temperature and costs more energy than it
  gives back. Melt it and drink it warm.
- **Prime the pot.** Put an inch of water in the pot first, then add snow a little at a time.
  Snow packed into a dry hot pot scorches and can ruin the pot.
- **Volume is disappointing.** Fresh fluffy snow is mostly air: it can take around **10 pots of
  snow to make 1 pot of water**. Wet, dense snow and ice give far more.
- **Ice beats snow** for yield and fuel. Take icicles or hard-packed snow over powder.
- **Take clean snow.** Not near roads (salt, exhaust), not near the driveway, not discolored,
  not where pets or wildlife have been. The middle of an untouched yard, or a clean tarp, is
  best.
- **Still treat it.** Snow is not sterile. Clean fresh snowmelt is usually low-risk and has
  little sediment, but it gets the same treatment as rain.

{{#if is.snow_region}}**Where you live, snow is a real reserve.** A snowbank is a large store
of water sitting in the yard for months. In deep winter, snowmelt often beats every other
source on effort, but it costs **fuel**, so it competes with cooking and heat (→ 06-04).{{/if}}

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Rain barrels, food-grade, with spigot (two or more) | The catchment | Link in a row; raise them for gravity flow |
| Drum pump or siphon, marked WATER ONLY | Empties the barrel into jugs without dipping | Never used for fuel |
| Downspout diverter and first-flush device | Skips the dirtiest runoff | Can be built from pipe |
| Fine screen, gutter guards, barrel screens | Blocks leaves and mosquitoes | Mosquito control is not optional (→ 03-08) |
| Clean tarp and cord | Catch rain or clean snow away from the roof | The cleanest catchment surface you can own |
| Large melting pot | Snow to water in volume | A dark pot melts faster in sun |
| Filter and treatment supplies | Rain and snow both need them | → 03-04 |
| Food-grade containers | Move it to storage | → 03-02 |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Any clean container under a downspout:** trash cans, storage totes, buckets. Volume beats
  neatness.
- A **tarp strung as a funnel** into a barrel.
- Kiddie pools, coolers and totes all hold water; cover them against mosquitoes and debris.
- A **sled** is the best tool for hauling snow to the pot.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** rain and snow are seasonal and you cannot schedule them. Collect hard whenever
  they come, not when you need them.
- **Ration:** use rain and snowmelt for drinking and cooking *first*, because they are cheap
  in fuel.{{#if has.pool}} Save the pool for washing and flushing.{{/if}}
- **Resupply:**{{#if has.pool}} the pool (→ 03-03) is the constant backstop: huge volume,
  high fuel cost. Rain is the opposite: free but irregular. Run both.{{else}} keep stored water
  (→ 03-02) for dry spells and look for other sources (→ 17-07).{{/if}}
- **The fuel trade:** melting snow and boiling rain both burn fuel. In a hard winter, water and
  heat compete for the same woodpile. Put both in the consumables table (→ 23-02).

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** barrels on downspouts and snow from the yard are quiet water
  sources that nobody sees you collect, unlike hauling from a public source.
- **B (moving):** a tarp and a pot make rain and snow your water anywhere. This is the most
  portable water skill in the binder.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** scale it up: a cistern, more roof, more barrels. Clean
  and disinfect a new or unused cistern before trusting it (CDC, Cistern Safety and
  Disasters). Where a destination is on town or district water with no well, pressure dies
  with the grid, and **roof catchment becomes the water plan**, not a supplement: fill every
  container on arrival (→ 03-01), then live on the roof. Do the roof sum for each place you
  might go, and send barrels ahead if you can.
{{#if has.destinations}}
{{#each destinations as d}}  - **{{ d.name }}** gets about {{ d.region.precip_in }} inches of rain a year. Roof size: ______ sq ft; gallons per inch: ______; barrels there: ______
{{/each}}
{{/if}}

## Cross-references

→ 03-02 storing water · → 03-04 purifying water · → 03-06 winter water ·
→ 03-08 mosquitoes in barrels · → 06-04 fuel for melting · → 17-07 drought ·
→ 03-10 well water · → 01-05 destination water

pages.title: Water when everything is frozen

photo_slots.caption: Our main water shutoff valve, and the tool for it

pages.body:
# Water when everything is frozen

**What this page is for.** Winter brings two separate water problems: **your plumbing freezing
and bursting** (which can flood the house and destroy the water you have), and **every
outdoor source turning solid**. This page covers both.
{{#if is.cold_winters}}Your January nights average about {{ region.home.jan_low_f }} °F, so
this page applies to you every winter.{{/if}}

> **CAUTION.** Never thaw a pipe with an open flame: that is how houses burn down. Never eat
> snow to stay hydrated: that is how people become hypothermic (dangerously cold inside).

## Do this now

1. **Before the cold:** drain and store garden hoses. Close the inside valve to each outdoor
   tap and leave the outdoor tap **open** so trapped water can expand without bursting the
   pipe.
2. **During deep cold:** let taps on outside walls **drip**, and **open the cabinet doors**
   under sinks so house heat reaches the pipes.
3. **If the power fails in winter:** fill every container with water **at once**, before pipes
   freeze or pressure is lost: tub, pots, jugs, bottles.
4. **If a pipe freezes, one sequence:**
   - **main water valve OFF**;
   - **open the tap on the frozen line** so melt water has somewhere to go;
   - **warm the pipe starting from the tap end** and working back toward the frozen part, with
     a hair dryer, heating pad or hot towels. **Never a torch, a heater or any open flame.**
   - **Turn the water back on slowly and check the whole pipe for a split** before you trust
     it. A frozen pipe often cracks and only leaks once it thaws.
5. **Melt snow; never eat it.** Put a little water in the pot first (→ 03-05).

{{photo water-main-shutoff}}

Your main water shutoff is at: __________ (→ 22-04). Practice finding it in the dark now.

## Why pipes burst

Water expands as it freezes, with enough force to split metal or plastic pipe. The break is
often not found until the ice thaws and the pipe floods. The pipes at risk are in unheated
space: along outside walls, in crawlspaces, in the garage, in any unheated corner of a
basement.

**In a grid-down winter this gets worse.** With no furnace, the house cools toward the outside
temperature, and pipes *inside* start to freeze too. If you are heating only one room
(→ 08-01), the rest of the plumbing is exposed. Often the right move is to **drain the system
on purpose** rather than fight it:

1. **Fill every container first.** Draining means no running water at all. Fill first, drain
   second.
2. Shut off the main water valve.
3. Open the lowest tap and any drain valves; open the taps upstairs to let air in.
4. Flush the toilets to empty the tanks.
5. **Drain the water heater** using the six-step procedure on → 03-02. Do not do it from
   memory: the heat must go off first and the water can be scalding. Until you drain it, that
   tank is your safe **hot washing water** (a gas heater keeps it hot while gas flows), so use
   it for the first days' washing before you empty it.
6. Pour plumbing (RV) antifreeze, the non-toxic kind, into sink and tub drain traps and toilet
   bowls if you have it.

A drained system cannot burst. Toilets without water: → 13-05.

## Where winter water comes from

| Source | Effort | Fuel cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stored water indoors | None | None | Keep it where it cannot freeze |
| Snow | Low (shovel) | **High** (melting) | About 10 parts fluffy snow to 1 part water |
| Ice (icicles, hard-packed snow) | Low | Medium | More water per pot than powder |
| Pool or hot tub under its cover and ice | Medium (procedure below) | High if distilled | Still there; saltwater still needs distilling (→ 03-03) |
| Rain barrels | none | none | Usually frozen solid; drain them before the hard freeze |
| A well | Depends | Depends | → 03-10 |

### Drawing from a pool in winter: the cover comes first

{{#if has.pool}}This applies to your pool.{{else}}This applies if you have, or reach, a pool
with a safety cover.{{/if}} **A safety cover is a drowning barrier for small children, and it
matters as much in January as in July.** Never cut the cover, never fold it back in a way that
defeats it, never leave it open or half open. Cold adds another reason: a cover peeled back
in freezing weather can stiffen and ice into its tracks, and then it cannot be closed again.

1. **First choice: draw without touching the cover.** Use a skimmer opening at deck level, if
   it sits outside the cover and is open to the pool, or the cover's own pump or drain
   access. A bottle on a pole through the skimmer fills buckets slowly but touches nothing.
   **Check this before the first freeze:** many skimmers sit under the cover's lid box, are
   plugged for winter, or sit above a lowered water level. Skimmer reachable with the cover
   closed: ☐ yes ☐ no. Checked on: ________. If no, step 2 is your first choice and snow is the
   better answer.
2. **If you must open the cover: the smallest corner only, an adult there the whole time.**
   Open it 3 to 4 feet at the shallow end, draw fast, and **close and secure it at once**,
   before anything else. In freezing weather, check that ropes and tracks are free of ice and
   that you *can* close it **before** you open it. If you cannot be sure of closing it, do not
   open it: melt the snow lying on top of it instead.
3. **If there is ice under the cover:** break through **at the access point only**: one hole
   the size of the bucket, chipped with a bar (never an axe swung over water). Draw, then
   cover the hole again and **mark the spot** with a flag or stake at the edge so the next
   person knows where the ice is thin. Never walk on the cover or the ice.
4. **Watch the water level.** Many safety covers need the normal water level to carry weight
   (→ 03-08). Winter draws count. Draw sparingly; snow and ice around the yard are the bulk
   source.

### Protect what you have

{{#if has.garage}}Water stored in an unheated garage will freeze and can split its containers.{{else}}Water stored in any unheated space will freeze and can split its containers.{{/if}}
Keep the working supply inside the heated part of the house. Leave air space at the top of
any container that might freeze. Do not store water in glass where it can freeze.

**Winter is also a refrigerator.** The cold that threatens your pipes also keeps food
(→ 04-09). But some medicines must never freeze.

{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}> **Floor:** a frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded. It loses strength with no
> way to tell. Keep insulin and other refrigerated medicines in the heated room, never on a
> windowsill or in an unheated space (→ 29-07).
{{else}}> **Floor:** a frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded. It loses strength with no
> way to tell. If anyone in your group uses refrigerated medicine, keep it from freezing
> (→ 29-07).
{{/if}}

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Pipe insulation sleeves, heat tape | Prevention beats repair | UL-listed heat tape only |
| Hair dryer, heating pads, towels | Thawing pipes safely | Never an open flame |
| The main shutoff, its tool, and knowing where the drain valves are | Draining before a burst | Practice in the dark now |
| Plumbing or RV antifreeze (non-toxic) | Protects drain traps and toilets once drained | |
| Snow shovel, sled, large pot | Collecting and hauling snow | The sled saves the most work |
| Insulated containers or a cooler | Keeps stored water from freezing | Also keeps it cool in summer |
| Headlamps | All of this happens in the dark at 5 p.m. | → 10-01 |

**If you don't have it:**

- Towels soaked in hot water thaw a pipe with no equipment.
- Foam pool noodles, rags or blankets make rough pipe insulation.
- Any tarp collects clean snow; any dark container melts it faster in the sun.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** in winter the limit is **fuel to melt**, not water. Track wood or propane
  against the melting load (→ 23-02).
- **Ration:** melt in big batches while a fire is already going for cooking or heat. Never
  light a fire just to melt snow (→ 06-04).
- **Resupply:** ice before snow; on bright days, set dark containers of snow in the sun for
  free melting.
- **The real winter failure** is a burst pipe flooding the house while everyone keeps warm in
  one room. Drain the system early rather than gambling.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** fill everything, then drain the plumbing if the house is going
  cold. Snow from a fenced yard is clean and private.
- **B (moving):** winter travel with young children is among the riskiest moves in this
  binder. Carry water inside your coat against your body or it freezes; melt snow at stops
  (→ 11-02).
- **C (rural or at a destination):** protect barrels, cisterns and tanks against freezing.
  A well pump needs power; hand pumps, bailers, generators and keeping the wellhead from
  freezing are on → 03-10.

## Cross-references

→ 03-05 rain and snow · → 03-02 storing water and draining the water heater ·
→ 03-04 purifying water · → 03-08 pool cover rules · → 03-09 a frozen filter is a dead filter ·
→ 08-01 heating one room · → 08-03 winterizing the home · → 08-05 hypothermia and frostbite ·
→ 11-01 layering · → 13-05 winter sanitation

pages.title: Judging and testing water quality
pages.body:
# Judging and testing water quality

**What this page is for.** How to rank water sources from bad to worse, what a real test can
tell you, and which tests to buy now while labs and shops are open.

> **CAUTION.** You cannot see, smell or taste the things that matter most: bacteria, nitrate
> and most chemicals. **Clear water is not safe water** (→ 29-06). Treat every unknown source
> as contaminated and disinfect it (→ 03-04). This page helps you choose between sources; it
> is not a way to declare water safe by looking at it.

## Do this now

1. **Test now, while labs exist.** If you have a well or might ever use one, get a baseline
   test through a **state-certified lab** for **total coliform bacteria, nitrate, total
   dissolved solids and pH**: the CDC's yearly list (CDC, Guidelines for Testing Well Water).
   Your county or state health department can name a certified lab.
2. **Nitrate matters most for infants.** Babies are the people most harmed by nitrate in
   water (it stops their blood carrying oxygen properly). Know the number before you ever mix
   formula with well or surface water. **Boiling makes nitrate worse**, because it boils off
   water and leaves the nitrate behind.{{#if has.infant}} You have an infant: this is your
   most important water test.{{/if}}
3. **Buy test strips now** (free chlorine, pH, nitrate, hardness) and a pocket TDS meter. They
   are cheap, small, and impossible to buy later.
4. **At a new site with a well**, the first job is a coliform and nitrate test. Treat every
   gallon until you have the result (→ 03-04), and carry the kit so you can test on the first
   day. Record it below.
5. **When in doubt, distil** (→ 03-03). It is the only home method that deals with salt, most
   chemicals and germs in one step.

## What testing can and cannot tell you

**Private wells are not regulated.** The EPA's public-water rules do not apply to them;
nobody checks or treats that water but you (CDC, Private Drinking Water and Public Health).
The CDC recommends testing a well **at least once a year** for **total coliform, nitrate,
total dissolved solids and pH**, and more often if small children, elders, or anyone pregnant
or nursing lives in the house.

| Test | What it means | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **Total coliform** | Indicator bacteria. If they are present, harmful bacteria, viruses or parasites probably are too | The disease test. Positive means do not drink it untreated |
| **Nitrate** | Runoff from fertilizer, manure, septic systems, flooded sewers | **Dangerous to infants.** A real risk in farm country |
| **TDS** (total dissolved solids) | How much salt and mineral is dissolved in the water | Tells you whether distilling is needed (pool water, brackish sources) |
| **pH** | How acidic the water is | Affects pipe corrosion and how well chlorine works |

**Disinfecting does not remove nitrate, salts or most chemicals.** Boiling actually
*concentrates* them as water boils off. That is the most dangerous misunderstanding in
emergency water, and it is why nitrate and TDS deserve a real test.

### Well test record

Fill this in at the wellhead, for your well or any well you use.

{{#each destinations as d}}**{{ d.name }}** ({{ d.county }}, {{ d.state_name }}): water source __________
{{/each}}

- Well: __________ Date sampled: ________ Lab or kit: ________
- Total coliform: ☐ absent ☐ PRESENT (treat all water until it is fixed, → 03-04, → 03-10)
- Nitrate: ________ mg/L. **Over 10 mg/L (the EPA drinking-water limit) is not safe for an
  infant's formula or feeding.** Use other water for the baby; boiling makes it worse.
- TDS: ________ ppm · pH: ________
- Retest due (one year, or after flooding): ________

## Judging a source in the field

Use this to *choose between* sources and to decide how hard to treat. Never to skip
treatment.

**Prefer, in this order:** stored or bottled water → rain caught off a clean surface → clean
snow or ice → a working well or spring → a clear flowing stream → a still pond → pool water
(needs distilling).

**Warning signs that push a source down the list or off it:**

- **Any smell of fuel, solvent or chemicals:** reject it. Boiling, bleach and filters do not
  fix that, and boiling makes some of it worse.
- **A sheen, foam or oily rainbow on the surface:** reject.
- **A strong rotten-egg or sewage smell:** reject for drinking.
- **Dark color, very cloudy, floating material:** do not use it. If you must, clear it, then
  distil rather than only disinfect.
- **Dead animals, mats of algae or livestock upstream:** heavy germ load. Boil or distil,
  never chemicals alone.
- **Downstream of a crop field, feedlot, road or industrial site:** assume nitrate and
  chemicals. Distil only.
- **Near a flooded area:** assume sewage and chemicals are mixed in (→ 17-03).

{{#if is.rural}}**Farm country.** Where crops and livestock surround you, surface water often
carries nitrate and manure runoff, and spring floods mix sewage with field runoff. Rain, snow
and distilled water are often *safer* than the nearest creek: the opposite of what instinct
says.{{else}}**Towns and cities.** Urban streams and ponds collect road runoff, sewage
overflows and industrial waste. Rain off a clean surface and snow are usually safer than any
nearby creek or pond.{{/if}}

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Lab test of any well you might use | The only real answer on nitrate and coliform | State-certified lab; keep the report behind this page |
| Nitrate and nitrite test strips | The contaminant most dangerous to infants | Cheap; check the expiry date |
| Pocket TDS meter | Shows how salty a source is and whether a still is working | → 03-03 |
| Free-chlorine and pH strips | Confirms disinfection worked | Also for pool water (→ 03-08) |
| Total-coliform home test kits (present or absent) | Home check for bacteria | Not lab grade, far better than guessing |
| Clear glass sample jars with lids | Judge clarity, settling and smell in good light | |
| Printed results sheet | The numbers survive a dead phone | File it behind this page |

**If you don't have it:**

- **A clear jar and daylight.** Fill it, let it stand an hour, look at what settles and what
  floats, and smell the air at the top. Crude, but it separates obviously bad from possible.
- **Distilling** (→ 03-03) removes what you cannot test for. Slow and fuel hungry, but it is
  the honest answer.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** test strips expire. Check dates and rotate them like batteries.
- **Ration:** test the *source*, not every batch. Once a source is known and unchanged, treat
  it the same way every time, and re-test only when something changes: heavy rain, flooding,
  a new smell, or anyone falling ill.
- **Resupply:** when tests run out, rank sources and use the strongest treatment you can
  afford in fuel. Distil anything doubtful.
- **The health signal:** if people start having diarrhea, treat the water supply as guilty
  until proven otherwise (→ 12-05).

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** city water is tested until it is not. Once the grid is down,
  treat the last tap water as stored water and everything after as unknown.
- **B (moving):** no lab, no time. Rank the source, treat everything, and prefer rain, snow
  and springs over standing water.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** the first job at a new place is learning its water.
  Bring strips; test a well or spring before it becomes the family supply, and re-test after
  floods. On town water plus roof catchment, test the catchment.

## Cross-references

→ 03-04 purifying water · → 03-03 distilling · → 03-05 rain and snow · → 17-03 floods ·
→ 03-10 well water without power · → 20-01 infant needs · → 12-05 illness and dehydration
