photo_slots.caption: Our pool cover's manual override: where the tool is kept, the bolt or crank, how it closes

pages.body:
# Keeping stored and pool water from going bad (algae, bacteria, mosquitoes)

**What this page is for.** Standing water left alone goes bad: green, slimy, smelly, and full
of mosquito larvae. This page explains how to slow that down, how to stop mosquitoes breeding
in it, and how to make bad water usable. It matters most for pools, hot tubs, rain barrels and
ponds, but stored drinking water is covered too.

> **SAFETY.**
> - Water that has "gone bad" carries **bacteria and parasites that cause diarrheal
>   disease**, which can kill infants and young children, and **breeds mosquitoes** that
>   spread **West Nile virus** and other illnesses. **Never drink scummy, green or smelly
>   water untreated.** For drinking, distil it (→ 03-03).
> - **Floor:** bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners. The
>   mix gives off chlorine gas. (→ 30-01)
> - **Floor:** children do not have access to chlorine products. (→ 30-01)
{{#if has.young_child}}> - **A pool is a drowning hazard for your young children.** Every rule below keeps the
>   cover closed except for the minutes you are drawing water with an adult present.
{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Cover the pool or tub.** The single most useful move. A solid cover blocks sunlight (which
   stops algae), keeps debris out, and **stops mosquitoes laying eggs**.
2. **Treat the pool as utility water**, not drinking water. You cannot keep a pool swimming-
   clear without power, so don't try. Keep it usable for flushing, washing and firefighting,
   kill the mosquito larvae, and **distil the small amount you drink** (→ 03-03). Drinking
   fresh pool water any other way is a household decision: {{choice DC-13}} (→ 30-14).
3. **Kill mosquito larvae** in standing water with **Bti "mosquito dunks" or "bits"**. Bti is
   safe for people and pets and kills only larvae. Re-apply about **monthly** (per the label).
4. **Empty every other container of standing water** in the yard each week: buckets, tires,
   toys, gutters, plant saucers.
5. **Replace stored drinking water about every 6 months** (CDC). Keep it cool, dark and
   sealed (→ 03-02).

## If your pool has an automatic (electric) safety cover

**If the cover cannot be worked without power, the pool is not a water source.** Find the
manual override in the cover's manual now, while the power is on, and practice it.

- **Many covers open with a hand tool (often a ratchet on the drive shaft) but close only by
  pulling, which can take two strong people.** The rule most cover makers print: **confirm you
  can close it before you ever open it.** With children in the house, an open pool you cannot
  close is a worse problem than a water shortage.
- **Never fully open it.** Open **3 to 4 feet at the shallow end**, draw water, close it. A
  bucket-sized gap is enough and the barrier stays in place. **Never cut the cover.**
- **Many safety covers need the normal water level** to work and to carry weight. Drawing the
  pool down weakens the barrier: draw sparingly and watch the level, winter included (→ 03-06).
- **Keep the override tool with the pool equipment**, and write here what it is and where it
  lives: __________

{{photo pool-cover-override}}

## Why pool water turns bad

A pool stays clear because a **pump** moves the water, a **filter** strains it, and
**chlorine** kills germs and algae. Cut the power and all three stop. Within days to weeks the
chlorine is used up, sunlight feeds **algae** (green, then black), leaves and debris rot,
**slime and bacteria** grow, and the still surface becomes a **mosquito nursery**. It goes
from a pool to a pond.

## Three ways to control it

### 1. Block sunlight and debris (cheapest; always do it)

A cover (solid is better than mesh for this) stops algae growing and mosquitoes laying eggs.
A shaded, covered pool goes bad far more slowly than an open, sunny one.

### 2. Keep some chlorine in it (optional; uses up your stock)

If you want clearer utility water and have the chemicals, keep a **free-chlorine level**
("free chlorine" is the chlorine still able to kill germs; → 29-05) using a pool test kit as
your guide.

**Chlorine products, best to worst for long storage:**

- **Calcium hypochlorite** ("cal-hypo", pool shock, 65 to 73 percent): the most chlorine per
  pound, and it keeps for years **dry, sealed, cool, and away from anything flammable and from
  other pool chemicals.** Store it as described on → 03-04.
- **Sodium hypochlorite** (liquid pool chlorine, or plain unscented bleach at 5 to 9 percent):
  easy to measure, but **weakens within months** and is mostly water, so heavy to store.
- **Dichlor granules:** contain stabilizer (cyanuric acid), dissolve cleanly, store well.
- **Trichlor tablets:** release slowly, store very well, acidic, need a floating feeder.
  **Never store trichlor with calcium hypochlorite, or use a scoop that touched one for the
  other.** The two react to make chlorine gas or fire. Keep them on different walls.

**How much:** do not dose from memory. **Measure with strips or a kit, add small amounts to
reach about 1 to 4 ppm free chlorine**, then test again. For a stronger "shock" dose, follow
the product label for your pool's gallons and confirm with the test kit, because strengths
vary.

**Reality check:** keeping a whole pool chlorinated for months uses a lot of chemical. It is
usually better to **cover, use Bti and distil what you drink**, and spend chlorine only where
it is worth it.

### 3. Kill the mosquitoes (always, in warm months)

- **Bti** (*Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis*) dunks or bits are a natural bacterium that
  kills mosquito larvae (and blackfly and fungus-gnat larvae) when they eat it. The EPA has
  registered it and **judged that it does not pose a risk to people**, and larvae rarely
  become resistant (US EPA, Bti for Mosquito Control). Drop dunks in the pool and any standing
  water; **re-apply roughly monthly** per the label.
- **Methoprene** (a growth regulator that stops larvae becoming adults) and **surface oils or
  films** (which smother larvae at the surface) are the other two larvicide types if Bti is not
  available (CDC, Larvicides for Mosquito Control).
- **Chlorine in the water and a tight cover** also stop larvae.
- **Around the yard:** get rid of all other standing water weekly, screen rain barrels
  (→ 03-05), keep gutters clear. Mosquitoes breed in a bottle cap of water.

## Making bad water usable

- **For drinking:** strain out the chunks (cloth or coffee filter), then **distil** (→ 03-03).
  Distilling deals with algae, bacteria and chemicals in one step.
- **To clear cloudy water** before disinfecting (if you are not distilling): let it **settle**,
  or stir in a pinch of **alum** (a powder sold for pickling and pools that makes particles
  clump and sink), then pour off the clear water, filter it, and **then** disinfect (→ 03-04).
  Disinfecting alone does not clear algae or particles, and dirty water uses up chlorine, so
  clear it first.
- **For utility use** (flushing, firefighting, laundry): use it as it is.
- **"Utility" stops where mouths begin.** Dishes, hands before cooking, food surfaces, teeth
  brushing and washing a child's face all get **treated** water, or a sanitizing final rinse
  (→ 13-10). Stale raw water on an eating surface ends up swallowed.
- **"Utility" stops at broken skin.** Untreated pool or pond water (and salty water from a
  saltwater pool) on an open cut, a cracked winter hand or a scraped knee is an infection
  route. Wash wounds with treated water only (→ 12-02), and keep anyone with open cuts away
  from pool-water chores.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Solid pool cover, or a heavy tarp with tie-downs | Blocks sun, debris and mosquitoes | The most useful single item here |
| Bti mosquito dunks and bits, a season's worth or more | Kills larvae; safe for people | Re-apply about monthly |
| Calcium hypochlorite (pool shock) | Compact, long-keeping chlorine | Store as on → 03-04 |
| Pool test kit or free-chlorine and pH strips | Dose by measuring, not guessing | Aim for 1 to 4 ppm free chlorine |
| Unscented household bleach, 5 to 9 percent | Disinfecting stored or cleared water | **Dose only from the table on → 03-04** |
| Alum | Clears cloudy water before disinfecting | Small amount; settle, then pour off |
| Fine mesh, cloth or coffee filters | Strain debris and algae | Before distilling or clearing |
| Food-safe containers and labels | Rotating stored drinking water | "DRINKING" or "UTILITY" |
| Long-handled skimmer or brush | Remove debris and algae mats | Filtering by hand |

**If you don't have it:**

- Any tarp with weights makes a pool cover. Even partial shade cloth slows algae.
- Plain unscented bleach stands in for pool chlorine for a while (weaker; use more, by test).
- Screen or netting over barrels stops egg-laying if you have no larvicide.
- A thin film of cooking oil on the surface of a **non-drinking** container smothers larvae.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** each Bti dunk lasts about 30 days; count months of mosquito season times the
  number of pools and containers. Calcium hypochlorite stores for years kept dry; liquid
  bleach weakens within months. **A cover does not run out**, which is why it is the backbone
  of the plan.
- **Ration:** stop chlorinating for clarity. Spend chemical only on hygiene and on batches you
  will disinfect. Rely on cover, Bti and distilling.
- **Resupply:** pool shops, hardware stores and pool sheds are where chlorine and dunks are
  found. Bleach is everywhere but weak and does not keep. Long term, **prevention beats
  treatment**: keep water covered and shaded.
- **Disease is the real cost of failure.** A mosquito-borne illness or a diarrhea outbreak
  with no clinic is a catastrophe, not an inconvenience.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** a covered, Bti-treated pool is a large reserve for sanitation
  and utility water; distil drinking water from it (→ 03-03).
- **B (moving):** you leave the pool behind. What travels is the skill: larvae control and
  clearing water at any source you camp near.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** ponds, stock tanks and rain barrels all breed mosquitoes
  and grow algae. Same three levers: cover or shade, larvicide, clear then disinfect or distil.

## Cross-references

→ 03-02 storing water · → 03-03 distilling pool water · → 03-04 purifying water ·
→ 03-06 winter water · → 06-06 chemical storage · → 13-03 greywater · → 17-03 floods ·
→ 30-14 the pool-water card

pages.body:
# Filter care: straws, bottles, squeeze and gravity filters

**What this page is for.** How to choose, use, clean, store and retire the portable water
filters most households buy. Specifications by filter class are on → 28-06; what "micron" and
"virus" mean is on → 29-06.

> **SAFETY. A filter fails silently.** A damaged filter looks and works exactly like a good
> one: water still comes out. **You will not know.**
>
> **Freezing is the failure that matters.** Water left inside a used hollow-fiber filter (a
> bundle of tiny porous tubes) expands when it freezes and splits the fibers. The makers of
> these filters warn against it, and **the damage cannot be seen**: the filter still flows,
> but it no longer filters.{{#if is.cold_winters}} Where you live, a used filter left in a
> vehicle or an unheated garage overnight is the most likely way to lose your water
> treatment (→ 03-06, → 22-05).{{/if}}
>
> **Most filters do not remove viruses** (CDC). Filtering is not the end of the chain
> (→ 03-04).

## Do this now

1. **Find every filter you own and write on it, in marker, whether it has ever been used and
   whether it has ever been below freezing.** A filter with an unknown history cannot be
   trusted.
2. **Move used filters out of garages and vehicles** for the winter. They live in the heated
   part of the house (→ 08-01).
3. **Buy the backflush syringe or cleaning tool for your filter now,** and spare elements
   (→ 26-04). A filter without its cleaning tool has a much shorter life.
4. **Practice the full chain once:** pre-filter → filter → disinfect with chemical or boiling
   → store covered (→ 03-04). Doing it for the first time in an emergency is how steps get
   skipped.

{{photo our-filters}}

## What each type is for

| Type | How it works | Best for | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Straw** | You suck water through it at the source | Emergency use by one person; go-bag weight | **You cannot store or carry treated water.** Useless for cooking, or for a child who cannot suck hard |
| **Bottle filter** | Filter built into a bottle | One person on the move | Small; the filter limits the flow |
| **Squeeze** | Squeeze a pouch through a filter in the line | Light, fast, fills containers | Pouches split; carry spares |
| **Gravity** | Hang a bag and let it drip through | **Households.** Volume with no effort | Bulky; slow when cold or clogged |
| **Pump** | Hand pump through a cartridge | Shallow or awkward sources | Moving parts and seals that break |
| **Ultrafilter (0.01 micron)** | Hollow fiber with pores small enough for viruses | Removes viruses too, says the CDC | Costs more, slower, needs more pressure |

**For a household of {{ household.size }}, a gravity filter is the right main filter**, with a
squeeze filter to carry and a straw only as a go-bag backup. **Do not build the household
plan on straws.**

## What filters do and do not remove

The CDC is direct: **pore size is the main thing that decides how well a filter works**, and
**many filters do not reliably remove viruses.** Its advice for anyone using a microfilter is to
treat the water with chlorine as well, to deal with viruses (CDC, Water Disinfection for
Travelers).

So the chain is:

1. **Pre-filter:** cloth, coffee filter, or let it settle (→ 03-04).
2. **Filter:** removes parasites and bacteria, and clears the water.
3. **Disinfect:** chlorine or boiling. **This is the virus step.**
4. **Store:** in a covered, clean container (→ 03-02).

The CDC also notes that filtering **does not prevent the water getting dirty again in
storage.** A perfectly filtered gallon poured into a dirty jug is dirty water.

**Ultrafilters at 0.01 micron are the exception:** the CDC says they should remove viruses,
bacteria and parasites. If you own one, know it. If you do not, **assume you need step 3.**

## Freezing: read this twice

Once a hollow-fiber filter has been used, water stays inside the fibers. **When that water
freezes it expands and splits them.** After that the filter passes water freely, and passes
everything in the water with it.

- **There is no reliable field test.** You cannot see, taste or measure it at home.
- **Makers say to protect these filters from freezing.** Your filter's own instructions
  govern.
- **A brand-new filter that has never been wet is not at risk.** The danger starts the first
  time it gets wet.
- **The rule: if a used filter has been below freezing, or you cannot be sure, retire it.**
  Use it only to pre-filter dirty water, or throw it away. **Do not gamble a child's health on
  it** (→ 12-05).

**What that means in practice:**

- Used filters do not live in a garage, a shed or a vehicle in winter.
- The vehicle kit gets **chemical treatment and a metal cup for boiling**, not the good filter
  (→ 22-05, → 03-04).
- After winter use, **shake it as dry as you can and bring it inside** (→ 03-06). In very cold
  weather, carry it inside your coat.

## Clogging and backflushing

The CDC notes that filters **eventually clog** with particles and then need replacing,
maintenance or repair. Slower flow is normal ageing, not necessarily failure.

**Pre-filtering is the biggest single thing that extends filter life.** Cloth, a coffee filter,
or letting sediment settle and pouring off the clear water costs nothing and makes the element
last many times longer.

**Backflushing** means pushing clean water backwards through the element to knock trapped dirt
loose. It restores flow on filters designed for it:

- [ ] Backflush with **clean, already-treated water**, never dirty source water.
- [ ] Use the syringe or tool made for **your** filter, by its instructions.
- [ ] Do it when flow slows noticeably, and before storage, not after.
- [ ] Some filters are shaken, tapped or scrubbed instead (ceramic elements are scrubbed and
  slowly wear thin). Know which you have.
- [ ] Never poke anything into the element to clear it.

## Storing a filter between uses

- **Dry it as far as its instructions allow** before long storage, then keep it **inside,
  above freezing**.
- **Some filters are stored with a preservative solution and some must not be.** Your
  instructions govern; there is no universal rule.
- **Keep new spare elements sealed and dry.** They keep well, and they are the part that runs
  out (→ 26-08).
- **Label each filter with the date of first use** and roughly how much water has gone
  through it.

## When to retire a filter

Retire it (not "keep an eye on it") if any of these is true:

- [ ] It has been below freezing after being used, or you cannot be sure it has not.
- [ ] It was dropped hard, or the housing is cracked or damaged.
- [ ] Flow does not come back after a proper backflush.
- [ ] It has passed its rated volume, or you have lost track of the volume.
- [ ] It was stored wet and smells, or shows mold or growth.
- [ ] Its history is unknown: scavenged, borrowed or found (→ 22-02).

**A retired filter still has a job:** pre-filtering muddy water before boiling. Mark it clearly
so it is never used as a main filter again.

## Why spare elements are the real purchase

The housing lasts. **The element is what wears out**, and a filter with no spare has a hard
deadline. Buy at least two spares with each filter and count them in → 23-02. That count is
your real filtering runway, not the filter itself (→ 23-04).

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Gravity filter and 2 spare elements** | Household volume with no effort | The main filter; elements are the consumable |
| **Squeeze filter and spare pouches** | Portable; fills containers | Pouches split before elements fail |
| **The backflush tool for your model** | Restores flow, extends life | Buy it with the filter |
| Straw filters, two | Go-bag backup only | Not a household plan |
| **Chemical disinfectant** | **The virus step** filters miss | → 03-04 |
| Cloth or coffee filters | The cheapest life-extender there is | Stock many |
| A clean container for backflush water | Never backflush with source water | |
| Permanent marker | First-use date, volume, freeze history | The habit that makes this page work |

**If you don't have it:** cloth and settling clear water. **Boiling replaces filtering
entirely** and needs nothing but fuel (→ 03-04, → 06-04). Sand-and-charcoal home-made filters
clear water but **do not make it safe**: they are a pre-filter, and the disinfecting step still
applies.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** the rated volume per element, and **far less on dirty water** without
  pre-filtering. Write the number in → 23-02.
- **Ration:** pre-filter everything. Use the filter for drinking and cooking water, not
  washing (→ 13-04).
- **Resupply:** spare elements while shops exist. **After that there is none**, which is why the
  boiling path matters.
- **Substitute:** **boiling**, at a fuel cost (→ 06-04). Chemicals deal with germs but not
  cloudiness or chemicals (→ 03-04). **Filters are a stock that runs down; boiling is the
  answer that lasts** (→ 23-04).

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** gravity filter at the sink, chemicals as backup, spares stocked,
  everything above freezing.
- **B (moving):** the squeeze filter and chemical treatment travel. **The good filter does not
  sit in a cold vehicle** (→ 22-05).
- **C (rural or at a destination):** protect the elements you have and move the daily load onto
  boiling, because a filter you cannot replace is a filter on a countdown.

## Cross-references

→ 03-04 the treatment chain (filtering is step 2 of 4) · → 03-02 clean storage ·
→ 03-06 winter water · → 03-07 judging the source · → 28-06 filter specifications ·
→ 26-04 checklist · → 26-08 dates · → 23-02 your real runway

The well pump breaker in the panel, the pressure tank and the pressure switch

pages.body:
# Well water without power

**What this page is for.** Getting water out of a drilled well when the grid is down, at your
own home or at any place you might go that has one. A drilled well's water really comes from
an **electric pump** at the bottom of a narrow pipe: no power, no pump, no water, unless you
have planned one of the four ways round it below.
{{#if has.well}}Your home is on a well: this page is for you now.{{else}}Your home is on
{{ dwelling.water_supply }}. Keep this page for a destination, a relative's farm, or a
neighbor's well.{{/if}}

> **CAUTION.** Two ways to get hurt here.
> - **Electricity.** Generator-to-pump wiring is dangerous (→ 09-04, → 09-08, → 29-04).
>   **Floor:** never connect a generator to house wiring without a transfer switch, an
>   interlock, or a cord-and-plug conversion with the main breaker locked off. Never backfeed
>   through an outlet. Backfeeding electrocutes line workers and neighbors and starts fires.
>   (→ 30-01)
> - **Floor:** never run a generator indoors, in a garage, or near an open window. Carbon
>   monoxide kills in minutes with no warning. (→ 30-01)
> - **Contamination.** One dirty rope lowered down the well can foul the water everyone
>   drinks. Everything that goes down the pipe is clean.

## Do this now

1. **Buy a well bucket (cylinder bailer) and enough rope to reach the water, with margin.** It
   fits in a tote, and it is the one option that works on any drilled well with no power and
   no information. An ordinary bucket will not fit down a well.
2. **Fill in the well survey below** for your well and any well you might use. Ten minutes at
   the wellhead with a flashlight and a phone camera answers every open question on this page.
   Pull a water sample the same visit (→ 03-07).
3. **At someone else's place, ask what already exists.** A working farm has often solved this
   before: a standby or tractor-driven generator, a windmill stock well, a spring. Plugging
   into their system may be the right first move. Arrive assuming nothing is there for you.
4. **Do not open a well cap casually.** Sealed is safe. Open it only with clean hands, cleaned
   gear and a reason.

## What a drilled well is

{{figure fig-drilled-well-parts}}

- **The casing:** a steel or plastic pipe, usually **4 to 6 inches across** for a home well,
  set down to the water-bearing rock or gravel, often 100 to 300 feet or more. A sanitary
  **well cap** seals the top. Below it is a narrow, dark, wet tube.
- **The submersible pump:** an electric pump hanging near the bottom on a **drop pipe**,
  pushing water up. Most home submersible pumps run on **240 volts**; smaller ones (1/2
  horsepower) are sometimes 120 volts. That one fact decides the generator question.
- **The pitless adapter:** the underground fitting where the water line leaves the casing
  **below the frost line** and runs to the house. It is why a well works in winter.
- **The pressure tank and switch:** inside the house or a well house, a tank (commonly
  labeled 20 to 80 gallons) holds water under pressure so the pump starts and stops instead
  of running at every tap. The pressure switch (often set at 30/50 or 40/60 psi) turns the
  pump on and off.

{{photo wellhead}}

## Four ways to get water with no grid, fastest first

### 1. What is left in the pressure tank (minutes of water, not days)

The tank keeps delivering until its pressure is gone. A tank delivers only about a quarter of
its labeled size before the pump would normally restart: a "30-gallon" tank gives perhaps
**5 to 10 usable gallons** (University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension). Draw it into containers
from the lowest tap, on purpose, before it disappears into toilet flushes and hand washing.

### 2. A generator to run the pump (the fast fix, if the electrics match)

Check, in this order:

- **Pump voltage.** Find the well pump's breaker in the panel. **A double-width (2-pole)
  breaker means a 240-volt pump; a single breaker means 120 volts.** Confirm on the pump's
  control box or nameplate.
- **Generator voltage.** Read the generator's label. **A 120-volt-only generator cannot run a
  240-volt pump at any wattage.** Many small and inverter generators are 120 volts only.
  {{#if has.generator}}Your generator: {{ gear.generator_watts }} running watts. Its voltage
  (from the label): ______ V.{{/if}}
- **Starting surge.** Pump motors draw two to three times their running watts for a moment to
  start. A 1/2-horsepower pump runs on about 1,000 watts but may need 2,000 to 3,000 to start;
  a 1-horsepower pump may need 4,000 to 6,000 (Water Systems Council, What if the Power
  Fails?). **Size the generator to the start surge, not the running number.** A "soft-start"
  kit fitted to the pump circuit roughly halves the surge.
- **Connection.** Through a transfer switch or interlock, or by a proper connection at the
  pump's own disconnect: **never backfed through a wall outlet** (floor above; → 09-04,
  → 09-08). Rewiring a pump to a plug yourself is a decision with its own card: your choice
  {{choice DC-07}} (→ 30-08).
- **Run it hard and briefly.** Run the generator, refill the pressure tank and every
  container, shut down. A well pump is the textbook short, heavy job for a generator (→ 09-04).

{{photo well-breaker-and-tank}}

### 3. The well bucket (no power, no information needed: buy now)

A 4 to 6 inch casing takes no ordinary container. A **purpose-made well bucket** is a slim
cylinder, about **3 to 3.5 inches across and 3 to 6 feet long**, of galvanized steel or
plastic pipe with a one-way valve in the foot. It holds **1 to 2 gallons per pull**. Lower it
on rope past the drop pipe and the pump wires (go slowly; do not snag the wire), let it fill,
haul it up. Slow, honest work, and it works at any depth your rope reaches. This plus good rope
is the guaranteed floor under this whole page.

### 4. A deep-well hand pump (the permanent fix)

Purpose-built deep-well hand pumps (for example the Simple Pump or Bison types) fit **beside
the existing electric pump in the same casing**, under a two-hole well cap, and lift water
from around **200 feet down (some to 325 feet)** (Simple Pump Co., Deep Well Hand Pumps). The
cheap "pitcher pumps" sold for shallow wells stop working at about 25 feet of lift. **You
cannot choose one without the survey:** casing inside width, how far down the water stands,
and how much room the drop pipe leaves. Before the collapse, it is the project that turns a
well from grid-dependent to hand-powered for good.

## Keeping the wellhead from freezing

The buried line and pitless adapter are safe below the frost line. What freezes is the
**equipment above ground**: the pressure tank, the switch and exposed pipe in a well house or
basement. In a grid-down winter with the building unheated: insulate the tank and pipes, heat
a small well house if you safely can, or **drain the above-ground side between generator
runs** and treat each run as "fill everything, then drain" (→ 03-06). Never leave a full
pressure tank in a space going below freezing. The capped casing itself survives winter fine.

## Keeping the well clean

A well is the one water source that one careless draw can *ruin*, for everyone who drinks
from it.

- **Everything that goes down the casing is clean.** Wipe the bailer and the first several
  feet of rope with the container-cleaning solution on → 03-02 (1 teaspoon of 5 to 9 percent
  bleach per quart of water, 30 seconds), then rinse with treated water. The drinking-water
  dose on → 03-04 is far too weak to clean a surface. Keep the rope in a sealed bag, never
  coiled on the ground, and wash your hands first.
- **Keep the cap on** except during a draw. Rodents, insects and surface water running down the
  casing are the classic ways wells get contaminated.
- **Keep fuel, the generator and animals away from the wellhead** (20 feet or more), and check
  that the ground slopes *away* from the casing. Keep latrines and septic systems well away too
  (→ 13-07, → 13-12).
- **After anything gets in** (bailer work, pump repair, flood water over the wellhead):
  disinfect the well as below and re-test before trusting it (→ 03-07). Treat all water until
  then (→ 03-04).

> **Floor:** bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners. The
> mix gives off chlorine gas. (→ 30-01)

### Disinfecting ("shock-chlorinating") a well: the CDC method

Do this after flood water covers the wellhead, after any work down the casing, or after a
positive coliform test. It takes a day; everyone uses stored or treated water meanwhile.
Steps from the CDC (How to Disinfect Wells After an Emergency), in plain words:

1. **Bypass or close the valves to any water softener**, and take carbon filters and UV units
   out of the line: strong chlorine ruins them.
2. **Work out the depth of water in the well**: total well depth minus the depth down to the
   water (from the survey, the well record, or a weighted line).
3. **Find the bleach amount in the table below.** Use only unscented household bleach.
4. **Mix that bleach with 3 to 5 gallons of water** in a 5-gallon bucket.
5. **Remove the vent cap and pour the mixture into the well** through a funnel. Keep clear of
   all electrical connections.
6. **Circulate it:** attach a clean hose to the nearest outside tap and run water back down
   the well for thorough mixing (this needs the pump, so a generator; see above). Rinse the
   inside of the casing with the hose or a bucket for 5 to 10 minutes. If the pump cannot run,
   pour the mixture, then bail and pour back several bucketfuls to mix it.
7. **Open every tap in the house** and run each until you smell a **strong chlorine (bleach)
   smell** at it. Then close them all.
8. **Leave it at least 12 hours.** Nobody drinks, cooks with or bathes in the water.
9. **Drain it:** run a hose from an outside tap onto an area **with no plants**, such as a
   driveway, until the chlorine smell is gone. Do not drain it into streams or ponds, and do
   not send it into a septic system (it kills the bacteria a septic tank needs, → 13-12). Then
   run the indoor taps until the smell is gone.
10. **Until the water is tested, boil it** (rolling boil, 1 minute) or use another source.
    **Wait at least 7 to 10 days**, then have the water tested (→ 03-07). Testing cannot be
    done until all the chlorine is flushed out.

A second positive test means contamination is still getting in (a cracked casing, surface
water, a nearby septic system or latrine). Find the cause; do not keep re-shocking.

**Approximate amount of bleach for disinfecting a drilled or driven well** (CDC, printed as
published; bleach of 5 to 9 percent; amounts reach a chlorine level above 100 mg/L):

| Depth of water | 2 in casing | 4 in casing | 6 in casing | 8 in casing | 10 in casing | 24 in casing | 36 in casing |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 feet | 3/4 tbsp | 3 1/4 tbsp | 1/2 cup | 3/4 cup | 1 1/4 cups | 7 cups | 1 gal |
| 20 feet | 1 1/2 tbsp | 6 1/2 tbsp | 1 cup | 1 1/2 cups | 2 1/2 cups | 14 cups | 2 gal |
| 30 feet | 2 1/4 tbsp | 9 3/4 tbsp | 1 1/2 cups | 2 1/4 cups | 3 1/4 cups | 1 1/4 gal | 3 gal |
| 40 feet | 3 tbsp | 13 tbsp | 2 cups | 3 cups | 5 cups | 1 3/4 gal | 4 gal |
| 50 feet | 3 3/4 tbsp | 1 cup | 2 1/2 cups | 3 3/4 cups | 6 1/4 cups | 2 1/4 gal | 5 gal |
| 100 feet | 7 1/2 tbsp | 2 cups | 5 cups | 7 1/2 cups | 12 1/2 cups | 4 1/2 gal | 10 gal |

1 cup = 8 fluid ounces = 16 tablespoons; 1 gallon = 16 cups. For water deeper than 100 feet,
the CDC table stops; the target is the same strong chlorine smell at every tap.

If you have only pool shock (calcium hypochlorite), dissolve it in a bucket of water first;
never pour dry granules down a well. The strong chlorine smell at every tap is still the
target (→ 29-05).

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Cylinder well bucket (bailer)** | Works with no power and no information | About 3 to 3.5 inches across, with a foot valve; must fit a 4-inch casing |
| Rope long enough to reach the water with margin, and a carabiner | Reaching the water | Braided rope; kept bagged and clean |
| Well-cleaning kit | Protects the well during draws; disinfects it | Fresh unscented bleach, gloves, eye protection, a sealed rope bag, a clean 5-gallon bucket, a funnel, a garden hose |
| Soft-start kit | Roughly halves the generator surge the pump needs | Fit after the survey: pump horsepower and voltage first |
| A spare pressure switch, and knowing how it works | The most common well electrical failure | Photograph the existing switch during the survey |
| Water test supplies | Same visit as the survey | → 03-07 |

**If you don't have it:**

- A bailer can be made from **3-inch plastic pipe, a foot check valve and an eye bolt**: farm
  store parts and one afternoon.
- A neighbor's larger generator that can supply 240 volts can run a pump yours cannot: a
  mutual-aid trade waiting to happen (→ 18-01).
- A windmill or solar stock well elsewhere on a farm is water already solved. Ask where the
  animals drink in winter.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** the groundwater is effectively unlimited at household scale. The runway is
  **generator fuel**, or **arms and rope** with the bailer. At 1 to 2 gallons a pull, your
  {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} gallons a day (→ 03-01) is a manageable number of pulls by
  hand.
- **Ration:** the well changes none of the treat-and-test rules. Until test results are in,
  treat every gallon you draw (→ 03-04).
- **Resupply:** roof catchment, stock tanks, and snowmelt in winter (→ 03-06). A hand pump is
  the permanent way off the fuel treadmill.
- **The failure to fear** is not a dry well. It is a **fouled** one: a contaminated casing
  after careless draws or a flood. Discipline at the wellhead is the whole game.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** {{#if has.well}}fill in the survey now, buy the bailer and rope,
  and know your pump's voltage and your generator's.{{else}}you are on {{ dwelling.water_supply }}.
  If any place you might go has a well, buy the bailer and rope now and pack them with the
  survey sheet and test strips.{{/if}}
- **B (moving):** wells along a route are sealed and private. Carry water (→ 03-01).
- **C (rural or at a destination):** on arrival, water is job one (→ 01-04). Check what is left
  in the pressure tank, find out what the place already uses to run the pump, and fall back to
  the bailer the same afternoon if needed. Do not wait for a perfect generator answer before
  you start drawing and treating water.

### Well survey (photograph everything)

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Which well (home or destination): | ________ |
| Casing diameter (measure the cap): | ________ in |
| Total well depth / depth down to the water (well record, owner, or a weighted line): | ________ / ________ ft |
| Pump voltage (breaker poles and control box): 120 V ☐ 240 V ☐ | Horsepower: ________ |
| Pump breaker location and amps: | ________ |
| Pressure tank location and size: | ________ |
| Well house? Heated how in winter? | ________ |
| Generator on site (watts; can it supply 240 V?): | ________ |
| Hand pump, windmill or stock wells nearby: | ________ |
| Well log or driller's record available? | ________ |
| Water sample taken (→ 03-07)? ☐ coliform ☐ nitrate | Date: ________ |

{{#if has.destinations}}Destinations to survey:
{{#each destinations as d}}- **{{ d.name }}** ({{ d.county }}, {{ d.state_name }}): well? ☐ yes ☐ no ☐ unknown
{{/each}}{{/if}}

## Cross-references

→ 03-07 testing water · → 09-04 generators · → 09-08 wiring and safety · → 28-03 generator
specifications · → 30-08 the cord-and-plug card · → 01-04 arrival · → 03-06 freezing ·
→ 03-04 treat until tested · → 13-12 septic

pages.title: Calorie planning and stockpile math
pages.body:
# Calorie planning and stockpile math

**What this page is for.** How much food your household needs each day, how to turn that into
pounds of food on a shelf, and how to work out how many days the food you already have will
last (your **runway**). Every other food page uses the numbers printed here.

> **CAUTION.** Calories are only half of a food plan. If anyone in the house has a food
> allergy, diabetes, celiac disease or another condition that limits what they can eat, their
> safe food is a second, separate number, and it is usually the one that runs out first. Plan
> both numbers together, or you will find the problem when it is too late to fix (→ 02-04).

## Do this now

1. **Know your daily number.** Your household needs about **{{ derived.calories.day }}
   calories a day** at an ordinary, moderately active level. Two weeks is about
   **{{ derived.calories.two_weeks }} calories**.
2. **Plan more in winter and for hard work.** Cold, hauling wood and water, and washing by
   hand all burn more. For most adults the "active" column of the same government table is
   200 to 400 calories a day higher than the moderate one (USDA/HHS, Dietary Guidelines
   2020-2025, Appendix 2).
3. **Count, do not estimate.** Your current estimate is **{{ gear.food.pantry_days }} days**
   of pantry food and **{{ gear.food.freeze_dried_servings }} freeze-dried servings**. Most
   households are wrong about this number. Count the shelf once, with the method below.
4. **Track any restricted diet separately.** If one person can eat only some of the food,
   work out their runway from their safe food only.
5. **Build in stages:** two weeks, then one month, then three months. Depth of food you
   already eat beats variety.
6. **Write the runway down** where everyone can see it (→ 23-02, → 22-04).

## How your number is worked out

The binder adds up one line per person from the published USDA/HHS table of estimated
calorie needs, using the **moderately active** column (USDA/HHS, Dietary Guidelines for
Americans 2020-2025, Appendix 2).

{{#each members as m}}
- **{{m.label}}**: {{m.age_text}}, {{m.sex}}. Daily need from the table below: ________ calories.
{{else}}
- No household members are entered yet. Add them in settings and this list fills in.
{{/each}}

**Household total: {{ derived.calories.day }} calories a day.** If the total shows a blank,
someone's age is missing in settings.

| Age | Male, moderately active | Female, moderately active |
|---|---|---|
| 12 to 23 months | about 1,000 (kit uses the top of the published 700 to 1,000) | about 1,000 |
| 2 | 1,000 | 1,000 |
| 3 | 1,400 | 1,200 |
| 4 to 5 | 1,400 | 1,400 |
| 6 | 1,600 | 1,400 |
| 7 to 8 | 1,600 | 1,600 |
| 9 | 1,800 | 1,600 |
| 10 | 1,800 | 1,800 |
| 11 | 2,000 | 1,800 |
| 12 to 13 | 2,200 | 2,000 |
| 14 | 2,400 | 2,000 |
| 15 | 2,600 | 2,000 |
| 16 to 18 | 2,800 | 2,000 |
| 19 to 25 | 2,800 | 2,200 |
| 26 to 45 | 2,600 | 2,000 |
| 46 to 50 | 2,400 | 2,000 |
| 51 to 65 | 2,400 | 1,800 |
| 66 and over | 2,200 | 1,800 |

Source: USDA/HHS, Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2020-2025, Appendix 2, printed as
published. Where sex is not entered the binder uses the higher figure, so the store is not
planned short.

- **Pregnant:** the binder adds **340 calories a day** (the published second-trimester
  figure). **Nursing:** it adds **450**. Both come from the same Guidelines and are printed as
  published.
- **Babies under 12 months are not in the food total.** The Guidelines give no calorie figure
  for them: they live on breast milk or infant formula. Their plan is on → 02-13 and → 20-05.
  **Powdered or canned milk is not infant formula** (→ 04-14).
- **Toddlers 12 to 23 months need whole-fat food.** The dairy rule for them is on → 04-14 and
  the feeding plan on → 20-05.

## Turning calories into pounds

Rules of thumb that make this workable:

- **1 lb of dry staples (rice, beans, flour, oats) is about 1,500 to 1,700 calories.**
- **Pounds of dry staples per day, if you ate staples alone:** {{ derived.calories.day }} ÷
  1,600. Multiply by 30 for a month and by 90 for three months.
- **Fats and oils are about 4,000 calories per pound,** more than double any grain. They are
  the easiest way to close a calorie gap in a small space (→ 04-12).

### The runway is a sum

Count every layer: staples, canned goods, fats, and freeze-dried food. The number that goes on
the consumables table (→ 23-02) is:

> **(calories of staples on hand + calories of canned and other food on hand + calories of
> freeze-dried food on hand, from → 04-19) ÷ {{ derived.calories.day }} = days of runway**

No single layer is the number. If one person eats a restricted diet, work out their runway
the same way **from their safe food only**, using their own line from the table above.

How to count calories on hand: read the label (calories per serving × servings per package;
→ 29-14). For bulk buckets, weigh them and use the per-pound figures above. A kitchen scale
helps; → 29-13 has ways to estimate without one.

### The water cost: when water is short, eat the food that brings its own

Freeze-dried food is the best food when water is plentiful and the worst when it is not,
because you must add your stored water to eat it (→ 07-07, → 03-01). When the water runway is
the shorter one, turn the menu around:

| Food | Water it costs you to eat | Eat it when water is |
|---|---|---|
| **Canned goods** | **Lowest**: packed in their own liquid; drink it | **Short: eat these first** |
| Dry staples (rice, beans, oats) | Middle: real cooking water, some absorbed | Adequate |
| **Freeze-dried meals** | **Highest**: about 2 cups per pouch (the label governs) | **Plentiful: eat these last** |

## Medical diets change the plan

- **Food allergy.** One allergic person can remove a large share of the usual preparedness
  pantry. Build the family's staples from **single-ingredient foods** everyone can eat, keep any
  separate supply physically apart and labelled, and give the allergic person's supply the
  **longest** runway in the house, not the shortest: everyone else can eat almost anything; they
  cannot. → 02-04. {{#if has.anaphylaxis}}**Someone in your household has an allergy marked
  severe enough for anaphylaxis.** Their safe-food runway is the number that binds.{{/if}}
- **Diabetes.** Carbohydrate is dosing information, not just calories. Write the carbohydrate
  content on each container of staples; repeat known meals with known carbohydrate; keep fast
  sugar for treating lows separate and protected (→ 02-01, → 02-05, → 04-18).
- **Celiac disease and other gut conditions:** → 02-19.
- **Unlabelled, traded or scavenged food for someone with a food allergy** is a decision card:
  {{choice DC-18}} → 30-19.

## What to store, by role

| Role | Foods | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Calorie base** | Rice, wheat, oats, corn, beans, potatoes | Cheap, dense, long-storing (→ 04-03) |
| **Fat** | Oil, lard, tallow, shortening | Calorie density; cooking (→ 04-12) |
| **Protein** | Dried beans, canned meat and fish, jerky | Beans and grain eaten together give complete protein |
| **Vitamins** | Canned and dried vegetables and fruit, sprouts (→ 04-16) | Scurvy (vitamin C lack) is a real risk over months |
| **Morale** | Sugar, coffee, tea, spices, cocoa | Not optional over months (→ 21-02) |
| **Medical** | Fast sugar for diabetics, oral rehydration salts | → 02-01, → 12-05 |

**Do not overlook vitamins.** A family living on rice and beans for six months develops real
deficiencies. Sprouting (→ 04-16), preserved vegetables and a garden (→ 05-01) are the
practical answers. A multivitamin is cheap insurance; check its label for allergens.

## Building it in stages

1. **Two weeks** of normal food you already eat.
2. **One month,** adding bulk staples and fats (→ 04-02, → 04-03).
3. **Three months,** adding the ability to preserve food (→ 04-04 to → 04-08).
4. **Beyond that** needs **production**: garden, animals, hunting, trade (Section 05, → 18-02).

**Storage alone does not carry a household through a long grid-down.** Every stored pound is
eaten once. Storage buys time to start producing.

## Leaving home: calories per pound decide what rides

When you leave home (Phase B) the limit is weight and space in the vehicle, not shelf space
(→ 01-03). Load by calories per pound, with one exception that comes first.

| Food | About calories per lb | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Rendered fat, lard, shortening | **4,000** | Densest food in the house (→ 04-12) |
| Cooking oil | **4,000** | Jugs pack tight |
| Sugar | 1,750 | Dense and keeps for ever (→ 04-13) |
| Jerky | **1,800** | Ready-to-eat protein (USDA FoodData Central: about 410 calories per 100 g) |
| Freeze-dried pouches | 1,600 to 1,800 | Ready to eat; needs your water (→ 04-19) |
| Dry staples | 1,500 to 1,700 | Needs cooking fuel and water |
| Canned goods | **400 to 600** | You are hauling its water: cheap water, expensive weight |

**One 50-lb bin, worked out:**

- of **freeze-dried** at about 1,700 calories per lb = about **85,000 calories**
- of **dry staples** at about 1,600 per lb = about **80,000 calories**
- of **canned goods** at about 500 per lb = about **25,000 calories**

Divide each by {{ derived.calories.day }} to get household-days per bin. Same bin, same weight,
about three times the difference. Load dense.

**Grab order (write it on the bin lids):**

1. **Any allergy-safe or medical-diet bin, first, always.** It is the one kind of food that
   scavenging and charity cannot replace (→ 02-04). Density does not apply to it.
2. **Fats and oils:** the most calories per pound.
3. **Freeze-dried pouches:** dense and no cooking, but check the water plan (→ 03-01).
4. **Sugar, jerky, dry staples:** dense, but staples need fuel and water to become food.
5. **Canned goods last,** and only if weight remains; or on purpose, as food-plus-water for
   the first day on the road.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Bulk staples: rice, beans, oats, flour, sugar, salt | The calorie base | Storage method → 04-03 |
| Cooking oil, shortening, lard | Calorie density | Check labels for allergens (→ 04-12) |
| Plain canned vegetables, fruit, meat | Vitamins and protein | Single-ingredient, readable labels |
| Separate stock for any restricted diet | Usually the binding number | Longest runway in the house |
| Kitchen scale and measuring cups | Real numbers; carbohydrate counting | Also for canning and curing |
| Written inventory and calorie sheet | Planning needs numbers | → 22-04, → 23-02 |
| Multivitamins | Cheap insurance against deficiency | Check allergens on the label |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Single-ingredient staples in sealed original packaging** are the safest food to scavenge
  or trade for, and the easiest to check for allergens.
- Garden produce (→ 05-01) is fully traceable.
- Fats are the hardest food to find later and the most valuable per pound. Get them early.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** total calories on hand (every layer, summed) ÷ {{ derived.calories.day }}. Write
  it on → 23-02. Then work out each restricted diet's separate runway from that person's safe
  food only; it is usually shorter.
- **Ration:** many households cut adult portions before children's. Keep a diabetic's
  carbohydrate steady rather than cut. Never ration an allergic person into eating unchecked
  food.
- **Resupply:** production (Section 05), preserving gluts (→ 04-04 to → 04-08), trade (→ 18-02).
- **The honest limit:** storage buys months. Only production buys years.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** build the stockpile now; it is the cheapest phase to do it in.
- **B (moving):** you carry days, not months: dense, ready to eat, and safe for everyone who
  travels (→ 01-03). Use the grab order above.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** storage plus growing; the planting calendar becomes the
  plan (→ 25-01).

## Cross-references

→ 04-02 building a pantry · → 04-03 bulk staples · → 04-12 fats · → 04-19 freeze-dried food ·
→ 03-01 water · → 02-04 food allergy · → 02-01 diabetes · → 02-13 infant feeding ·
→ 23-02 consumables table

pages.title: Starting fire reliably (multiple methods)

photo_slots.caption: Our three ignition kits and where each one lives

pages.body:
# Starting fire reliably (multiple methods)

**What this page is for.** Without power, fire cooks food, makes water safe and keeps people
warm. It is also the fastest way to lose a house. This page covers when not to light a fire,
how to build one that catches the first time, and which ways of lighting it still work when it
is cold and wet.

> **CAUTION.** **Never burn treated, painted or pressure-treated wood, plywood, particleboard,
> plastics or trash**: the smoke is toxic (EPA, Burn Wise). Inside the house, fire for heat or
> cooking belongs only in an installed, vented fireplace or wood stove, because every flame
> makes carbon monoxide (CO), a gas you cannot see or smell (CDC; → 29-03). **Never use
> gasoline to start or restart a fire** (CPSC; → 29-01). **Fuel is never stored or transferred
> near an open flame or a running appliance.** Vapour ignition. **Children do not have access
> to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products.** Fixed in every source. Lighters and
> matches count as fuel here.

## Do this now

1. **Keep three different ways to light a fire, in three places**: lighters, storm-proof
   matches, and a ferrocerium rod (below).
2. **Keep manufactured tinder** (fire-starter cubes or similar). It works wet, cold and
   one-handed, which is exactly when you need it.
3. **Practise once in bad weather now.** Lighting a fire with numb hands in freezing wind is a
   different skill from lighting one in the yard in summer.
4. **Keep dry kindling inside**, under cover, before every storm.
5. **Clear the spot**: nothing that burns within a few feet, and water or an extinguisher
   beside you (→ 29-12).

{{photo ignition-kits}}

## The gate: when not to light an outdoor fire

Knowing how to light a fire includes knowing when the answer is no. Run these checks before
any open fire outdoors.

| Check | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Burn ban?** | Counties and states ban open burning in dry spells because the grass and brush really will carry fire. Under a ban: contained appliances only (a camp stove outdoors), no open flame. The reason holds whether or not anyone enforces it |
| **Red Flag Warning?** | The National Weather Service's warning for **critical fire weather: strong wind plus very low humidity over dry fuels**. Each forecast office sets its own exact criteria (NWS Glossary, Red Flag Warning). **On a Red Flag day, no open fire**, no ash dumping outside and no spark-making work outdoors (→ 17-05) |
| **Wind right now?** | Wind carries embers past any fire ring you control. Pick a wind limit before you need it, lower than the conditions that bring a Red Flag Warning, and write it here: no open fire above ______ mph |
| **Dry-fuel season?** | Any time the grass is brown and cured, and any drought. Treat every other check one step more cautiously |

{{#if is.wildfire_region}}Your home county is rated for wildfire risk. Treat dry, windy days as
no-fire days by default (→ 17-14).{{/if}}{{#if is.drought_region}} Your home county is rated for
drought; dry spells can last for months.{{/if}}

> **Before the collapse:** burn bans for {{ home.county }} are issued by the county or state.
> Check the current status while there is someone to issue it.

**How you hear it with no internet.** Red Flag Warnings and fire-weather watches come over a
NOAA Weather Radio (→ 15-01, → 29-09). When no warning service exists, the wind check and the
season check still work: **you can always feel the wind and look at the grass** (→ 17-10).

## Why fires fail

A fire needs fuel, heat and air. Fires almost always fail for one of three ordinary reasons:
**wet fuel**, **too big too fast**, or **not enough air**. Build small, build dry, leave gaps.

## The fuel ladder: the part beginners skip

You need **four sizes**, all ready **before** you strike anything:

1. **Tinder** catches a spark: a cotton ball smeared with petroleum jelly, birch bark, dryer
   lint, fatwood shavings, char cloth, a commercial fire starter.
2. **Kindling**: from pencil-lead to pencil thickness. Dry twigs, thin split shavings.
3. **Small fuel**: finger to wrist thickness.
4. **Fuel wood**: the real logs (→ 06-03).

**Have three times more kindling than you think you need.** Running back for more while a weak
flame dies is the most common failure.

{{figure fig-fuel-ladder}}

## Ways to light it, ranked for reliability

| Method | Reliability | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Butane lighter** | High, when warm | **Fails in deep cold**: butane will not turn to gas well below freezing. Keep one in an inside pocket against your body |
| **Storm-proof or waterproof matches** | High | Work cold and wet; there are only so many. Keep them in a waterproof case with the striker |
| **Ferrocerium ("ferro") rod** | Very high | A metal rod that throws hot sparks when scraped. Works wet and cold for thousands of strikes. **Needs good tinder** and practice |
| **Magnifying lens** | Depends on weather | Free and unlimited, but needs bright sun, which winter often does not give |
| **Battery and steel wool** | Good improvised method | A 9-volt battery touched to fine steel wool lights it at once. **Store them apart**: together in a drawer they are a fire hazard |
| **Bow drill or other friction** | Low | Hard, especially in damp cold. Learn it; do not rely on it |

**The cold-weather lesson:** a lighter kept in your pocket works; a lighter left in a cold shed
often will not. Keep ignition warm and dry, on your body.

## Building it: a method that works in the wet

1. **Platform.** Lay split wood or bark so the tinder is not on cold, wet ground or snow.
2. **Windbreak.** Your body, a wall of split wood, or the fireplace itself.
3. **Tinder bundle** on the platform.
4. **Kindling** over it in a teepee or lean-to, with air gaps.
5. **Light the tinder low, on the side the wind is coming from**, and shield it.
6. **Feed small first.** Add bigger pieces only once the flame is steady.
7. **Do not smother it.** Most dying fires need air and patience, not more wood.

**In snow or rain**, the platform matters more than anything else. A fire on snow melts itself
out. Build up, not down.

## Tinder you can make or find

- **Cotton balls and petroleum jelly** in a pill bottle: cheap, nearly waterproof, burn for
  minutes.
- **Fatwood**: resin-rich pine. Lights when damp and shaves easily.
- **Birch bark**: burns even when wet.
- **Dryer lint** from natural fibres, **char cloth**, waxed cardboard, egg-carton-and-wax pucks.
- **Cattail fluff, dry grass, milkweed down** where they grow.

## Gear

**Have now:**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Lighters, a bag of them | Easiest method; cheap; good barter | Keep some on your body in winter |
| Storm-proof matches and a waterproof case | Work when lighters fail | Include the striker |
| Large ferrocerium rod and striker | Thousands of lights | Practise **before** you need it |
| Commercial tinder or fire-starter cubes | Work wet, cold, one-handed | Cheap; keep plenty |
| Fatwood | Natural, keeps indefinitely, lights damp | |
| Dry kindling stored inside | The real bottleneck | Restock before every storm |
| Hatchet and knife | Dry wood is **inside** wet wood: split it to reach it | → 16-01, → 16-02 |
| Fire extinguisher and a bucket of water | Things go wrong | Beside the fire, not behind it (→ 29-12) |
| Metal ash bucket with a lid | **Ashes stay hot for days** and start house fires | Never a cardboard box or plastic bin (→ 06-02) |

**If you do not have it:**

- A 9-volt battery and steel wool is the best improvised way to light a fire in a house.
- Petroleum jelly, lip balm, candle wax and cooking oil all help weak tinder burn longer.
- Paper, cardboard and untreated wood scraps are everywhere in town (→ 06-04).
- **Never gasoline.** It flashes, explodes and kills people every year (CPSC; → 29-01).

## When it runs out

- **Count** lighters and matches. A ferro rod lasts for thousands of strikes, which is why it
  belongs in every kit: it turns something you use up into something that lasts.
- **Use one lighter until it is empty** rather than starting several.
- **Keep a fire going rather than relighting it** (→ 06-02). Banked coals save lighters,
  matches and kindling all at once.
- Lighters and matches are common things to scavenge and good to barter (→ 18-02).

## Fire indoors

A fireplace or wood stove is the only indoor place for a wood fire. Before the first fire of
the season, check the chimney (→ 06-09). Using one that has not been inspected this year is a
trade-off: {{choice DC-21}} → 30-22. Candles and open-flame cooking indoors are a separate
trade-off: {{choice DC-20}} → 30-21. Keep CO alarms working in every room with a flame
(→ 08-02).

## Children and fire

{{#if has.young_child}}There is a child under 6 in this household. Lighters, matches and
ferro rods stay locked or out of reach, and a marked line around any fire is a household rule
for everyone (→ 20-02).{{else}}Lighters and matches stay out of reach of any visiting children,
and a marked line around any fire keeps everyone back (→ 20-02).{{/if}} Whether older children
light or tend fires is the household's call: {{choice DC-24}} → 30-25.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** {{#if has.outdoor_fire}}your outdoor fireplace or fire pit is
  your cooking and boiling fire (→ 07-01).{{else}}a fire-pit ring, a rocket stove (→ 07-02) or
  a camp stove outdoors (→ 07-05) does the cooking.{{/if}}{{#if has.fireplace}} The indoor
  fireplace is for heat once the chimney is checked (→ 06-09).{{/if}}{{#if has.wood_stove}} The
  wood stove is for heat once the chimney is checked (→ 06-09, → 08-08).{{/if}} Keep kindling
  and ignition indoors and dry, and one set in each go-bag (→ 22-03).
- **B (on the move):** ignition on your body, tinder in a pocket, a ferro rod as backup.
  Practise with gloves on.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** more natural tinder and wood, often harsher weather. A
  reliable ignition kit is a survival item.
