pages.title: What actually needs power (load triage)
pages.body:
# What actually needs power (load triage)

**What this page is for.** Before you buy a single panel, battery or generator, decide what *must*
run when the grid is down, add up how much energy that takes in a day, and size everything else to
that number. Most households do it backwards: they buy a generator or a "solar generator" first and
then find out what it can run. This page is the list and the arithmetic. If watts and watt-hours
are new to you, read → 29-02 first; this page uses them without re-explaining.

## Do this now
- **Buy a plug-in watt meter (the kind a lamp plugs into) and measure your real devices.** The
  label on an appliance gives its *maximum* draw, not what it uses over a day. A refrigerator
  labelled 700 W may average 60 to 90 W across a day because the compressor cycles on and off.
  Guessing here is the single biggest cause of systems that turn out too small.
- **Fill in the table at the bottom of this page** with measured numbers. It is the input to
  → 09-02, → 09-09 and → 09-10. Nothing downstream works without it.
- **Sort every load into the four tiers below and put the tier on a label on the device.** You
  make these decisions once, calmly, now, not at 2 a.m. in a cold house.
- **Know your Tier 0 loads by name.**
  {{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}This household has a refrigerated medicine: keeping it cold is a
  Tier 0 load and usually the biggest one (→ 09-10).{{/if}}
  {{#if has.cpap}}A CPAP machine is on the Tier 0 list (→ 02-24, → 09-06).{{/if}}
  {{#if has.oxygen}}An oxygen concentrator is on the Tier 0 list, and it is a large load
  (→ 02-08, → 09-06).{{/if}}
  Everything else on this page is comfort by comparison.

## Why it works this way

**The number that matters is the watt-hour (Wh).** Watts are how fast a device uses energy;
watt-hours are how much it used. Watts × hours = watt-hours: a 10 W LED bulb for 5 hours is
50 Wh. A battery is rated in watt-hours, or in amp-hours at a voltage (amp-hours × volts =
watt-hours; a 100 Ah 12 V battery is roughly 1,200 to 1,280 Wh depending on whether you count it
at 12.0 or 12.8 V). Every sizing decision in this section is that one piece of arithmetic
(→ 29-02).

**Two numbers describe every load, and you need both:**
- **Power (W)** decides whether a battery and its inverter can run the device *at all*. A
  1,500 W microwave trips a 300 W power station instantly, however large its battery is.
- **Energy (Wh per day)** decides how long you can keep doing it.

**Heat and motors are the two budget-killers.** Anything that makes heat (kettle, toaster, hair
dryer, space heater, coffee maker) or drives a compressor or motor (refrigerator, freezer, well
pump, furnace blower) draws ten to a thousand times what electronics draw. **A survival power
system does not make heat.** Heat comes from fire and fuel (Sections 06, 07 and 08). Electricity
is for information, medicine and light.

**Two deliberate exceptions** (→ 07-06):
- **Boiling small amounts of water.** An electric kettle is efficient, silent and makes no carbon
  monoxide. Budget about **110 Wh per litre boiled, about 55 Wh per freeze-dried meal**. A vacuum
  flask filled from one morning boil roughly halves that.
- **Heated blankets (50 to 100 W)** warm the person, not the room: the best heat per watt you
  can get from a battery.

### The four tiers

**Tier 0: life-critical. This is the reason the system exists.**

| Load | Why | Typical draw |
|---|---|---|
| Phone(s) used for medical devices, alerts and contact | Information; for some households the phone runs a medical device (→ 09-06) | About 10 to 20 Wh a day with the screen mostly off |
| Cooling for refrigerated medicine | Some medicines lose strength when warm (→ 29-07, → 09-10) | **200 to 1,500 Wh a day, depending on what does the cooling** |
| Medical devices that plug in or charge (CPAP, oxygen concentrator, pump accessories, nebuliser) | Breathing and medicine delivery (→ 09-06) | From a few Wh to hundreds; read the label and measure |
| One reliable light source at night | Falls, stairs, children, injuries | 10 to 50 Wh a day |

**Tier 1: high value, low cost.** Radio and scanner (→ 15-02, → 15-04), headlamps and
rechargeable AA and AAA cells (→ 10-01), a small fan to move warm air in one room (→ 08-01), a
tablet or laptop holding this binder, rechargeable tool batteries, a water filter pump.

**Tier 2: quality of life, when there is a surplus.** A refrigerator or freezer for food (as
opposed to medicine), laundry, children's devices for morale (→ 21-02), power tools, a sewing
machine.

**Tier 3: do not run these on batteries.** Electric space heat, electric cooking, electric water
heating, air conditioning, a well pump on a small system, a clothes dryer. **These are fuel jobs,
not electricity jobs.** Each one empties a battery bank in well under a day and buys almost
nothing.

### Typical draws (planning placeholders; measure your own)

| Device | Typical W | Typical Wh per day | Tier |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phone charge | 5 to 20 W | 10 to 20 Wh | 0 |
| LED bulb or lantern | 3 to 10 W | 15 to 50 Wh | 0 or 1 |
| Headlamp recharge | 2 to 5 W | 5 to 10 Wh | 1 |
| Handheld radio charge | 5 W | 10 to 20 Wh | 1 |
| Laptop | 30 to 65 W | 100 to 300 Wh | 1 or 2 |
| CPAP-class medical device | 30 to 60 W | 200 to 400 Wh | 0 if you use one |
| 12 V compressor cooler (medicine) | 40 to 60 W while running | 200 to 500 Wh | 0 |
| **The power station's own draw** (its idle use while it runs a load) | commonly 3 to 10 W, more with the AC inverter on | 70 to 240 Wh | 0: unavoidable; keep it small by using the 12 V port and switching the AC inverter off (→ 09-10) |
| Full-size refrigerator (efficient, modern) | 60 to 150 W average | 800 to 1,500 Wh | 0 or 2 |
| Chest freezer | 40 to 100 W average | 600 to 1,200 Wh | 2 |
| Box fan | 50 to 100 W | 400 to 800 Wh | 1 or 2 |
| Microwave | 1,000 to 1,500 W | | 3 |
| Electric kettle | 1,200 to 1,800 W | | 3, except the small-boil exception above (→ 07-06): tea and meals yes, bulk heating never |
| Space heater | 1,500 W | 36,000 Wh per day if run continuously | 3, never |
| Well pump | 1,000 to 2,500 W, much more at start | | 3 on small systems (→ 03-10) |

Look hard at the space heater row. One space heater running all day uses about 36,000 Wh. Compare
that with what your panels make on a clear December day (→ 09-05): for most households it is a
few hundred to a couple of thousand watt-hours. That is why heat comes from combustion, clothing
and one warm room (→ 08-04), not from batteries.

{{#if has.house_connection}}A furnace blower is a motor load (often several hundred watts running,
two to three times that for a moment at start). It can run from a generator or a large station
only through a safe connection: this household's is "{{ gear.house_connection }}" (→ 09-04).
{{else}}A gas furnace needs electricity for its blower and controls. It can run from a generator
or a large station only through a safe connection: a transfer switch or interlock fitted by an
electrician, or a cord-and-plug conversion, which is a decision card (→ 09-04, {{choice DC-07}},
→ 30-08). Never by plugging a generator into an outlet (→ 30-01).{{/if}}

### Doing the triage
1. List every device you would want. Measure or estimate its watts and hours per day.
2. Multiply for watt-hours per day. Add up each tier.
3. **The Tier 0 total is your must-have design number.** Add about 30% for inverter and charging
   losses (inverters are typically 85 to 90% efficient, and batteries lose a little too).
4. **Tier 0 plus Tier 1 is the realistic target.** If that is affordable, build to it.
5. **Everything above Tier 1 is a fair-weather bonus** you run only on a sunny surplus day.
6. **Check the plan against December, not June** (→ 09-05). A system sized in summer
   disappoints in the month you need it most.

## Gear and items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Plug-in watt meter | Turns guesses into a real design | The highest-value purchase in this section |
| DC watt meter (inline 12 V or USB) | Measures the DC side: 12 V loads, USB loads, panel output | For → 09-09 |
| This page's table, filled in | The design document for everything downstream | Copy the totals to → 23-02 |
| Label maker or masking tape and marker | Tier label on every device | Removes decisions from a crisis |
| Power strips with switches | Kills standby draw at once | Standby draw adds up over weeks |
| USB power banks, 20,000 mAh or larger | About 70 Wh each; covers phone loads for days (→ 09-06) | The cheapest useful battery there is |

**Scavenge or substitute:**
- **Measuring without a meter:** appliance labels give maximum watts (a ceiling, not a daily
  figure, → 29-14); a car's 12 V socket fuse rating bounds what you can pull from it; the
  percentage drop on a power station over a known time is a crude but usable meter.
- **Storage:** laptop batteries, tool batteries with USB adapters, car batteries (with the
  cautions in → 09-14), any power bank in a drawer.
- **Cutting the load beats making power.** A headlamp instead of a room light, a hand-crank radio,
  cooking on fire, hanging laundry: every watt you do not need is a watt you do not have to make,
  store and maintain.

## When it runs out
- **Batteries are the consumable, not panels.** Panels degrade slowly over decades; batteries wear
  out in years and faster if abused (→ 09-03, → 09-07). Your power runway is a battery question.
- **Ration by tier, in order.** Tier 3 is already off; drop Tier 2, then Tier 1. **Tier 0 is
  defended to the end**, and if Tier 0 cannot be met, that is not a power problem, it is a medical
  emergency and an input to the go/no-go decision (→ 01-02).
- **Substitutes for each tier:** light → lamps and flashlights first, candles only with care
  (→ 10-02; candles indoors are a decision, {{choice DC-20}}, → 30-21); refrigeration → cold
  storage and evaporative cooling (→ 04-09, → 12-21); information → this binder and a hand-crank
  radio; tools → hand tools (→ 16-01).
- **Write the Tier 0 number on the consumables table (→ 23-02)** and track how many days of it
  your storage holds, the same way you track food and water.

## Our loads

{{#if has.power_station}}Our power stations total **{{ gear.station_wh_total }} Wh**.{{/if}}
{{#if has.solar}}Our panels total **{{ gear.solar_w_total }} W**. On a clear December day at
home ({{ region.home.sun_hours_dec }} peak sun hours) that is roughly
{{ gear.solar_w_total }} × {{ region.home.sun_hours_dec }} × 0.75 = ________ Wh; in June
({{ region.home.sun_hours_jun }} sun hours), ________ Wh (method on → 09-02).{{/if}}
{{#if has.generator}}Our generator is rated **{{ gear.generator_watts }} W** running on
{{ gear.generator_fuel }} (→ 09-04).{{/if}}

Measure each device, then write it in. Correct in pencil as you learn.

| Device | Measured W | Hours per day | Wh per day | Tier |
|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}| Medicine cooler (→ 09-10) | | 24 (cycling) | | 0 |
{{/if}}{{#if has.cpap}}| CPAP (→ 09-06) | | | | 0 |
{{/if}}{{#if has.oxygen}}| Oxygen concentrator (→ 09-06) | | | | 0 |
{{/if}}| Phones and medical charging | | | | 0 |
| Night light or headlamp recharge | | | | 0 |
| Power station idle draw | | 24 | | 0 |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| **Tier 0 subtotal** | | | | |
| **Tier 0 × 1.3 = design target** | | | | |
| **Tier 0 + Tier 1 subtotal** | | | | |

## Phase notes
- **A (at home):** the whole system lives here: panels in the yard, batteries indoors where they
  stay warm (→ 09-07), Tier 0 and Tier 1 running.
- **B (moving):** you carry a fraction: a folding panel, one power station or battery, power
  banks and the medical loads. **Tier 0 only.**
- **C (settled somewhere new):** rebuild bigger. This is also where fuel generation (→ 09-04) is
  least sustainable and solar matters most, because there is no fuel resupply.

## Cross-references
→ 09-02 solar basics and sizing · → 09-03 batteries and power stations · → 09-05 solar in winter ·
→ 09-09 a small solar build · → 09-10 power for refrigerated medicine · → 09-16 outage day one ·
→ 29-02 batteries and power stations explained · → 28-07 reading your own gear

pages.title: Solar power basics and sizing
pages.body:
# Solar power basics and sizing

**What this page is for.** How a solar setup is put together, how to work out how many panels and
how much battery you need, and the one wiring mistake that destroys equipment on the first cold
morning. Do the load list on → 09-01 first; you cannot size anything without its watt-hour number.
Volts, amps and watts are explained on → 29-02.

> **CAUTION.** A grid-tied rooftop solar array **shuts down when the grid goes down**, by design,
> to protect line workers. If your house has rooftop solar with no battery and no inverter that
> can run on its own (often called "islanding" or "backup-capable"), **you will have no power in
> an outage despite the panels on the roof.** Find out which kind you have before you need it.
> Also: **a panel in daylight is live.** There is no off switch on a solar panel; you cover it or
> you disconnect it.

## Do this now
- **Finish → 09-01 first.**
- **If the house has rooftop solar, find out whether it is grid-tied, hybrid or off-grid.** Grid-tied
  without a battery is no help in an outage. This is a phone call to the installer today.
- **Size on the December number, not the June number** (→ 09-05). This is where most plans fail.
- **Start small and modular.** A few hundred watts of panels, a lithium iron phosphate battery or a
  power station, and a good charge controller cover Tier 0 and much of Tier 1. Buy parts you can
  add to, not a sealed box you cannot expand.
- **Read the label on every panel and station you own** and write the numbers in the tables on
  → 09-03 (how to read them: → 28-07).

## Why it works this way

**Four parts, four jobs.** Every solar setup, from a folding kit to a whole-house array, is the
same four blocks (US Department of Energy, Solar Photovoltaic System Design Basics):

| Part | Job | If it fails |
|---|---|---|
| **Panels** (PV modules) | Turn light into DC electricity | No generation. Very reliable; decades of life |
| **Charge controller** | Regulates panel output into the battery safely | Overcharges and destroys the battery, or will not charge |
| **Battery** | Stores energy for night and cloud | Power only while the sun shines |
| **Inverter** | Turns battery DC into 120 V AC for household plugs | Only DC devices work |

A **power station** is all of these except the panels, in one box (→ 09-03).

**Skip the inverter where you can.** Running 12 V DC loads directly (USB charging, LED lights, a
12 V compressor cooler) avoids the 10 to 15% lost in each conversion. Direct DC is the easiest
efficiency gain there is. Run the medicine cooler and the lights on DC; keep the inverter for the
few things that truly need AC.

**"Sun hours" is the sizing unit.** A panel rated 100 W makes 100 W only in full, square-on,
clear-sky noon sun at a mild temperature: a laboratory condition. A "peak sun hour" is one hour of
that full-strength sun; a December day may give two or three of them even though it is light for
eight or nine. Real daily output is roughly:

**Daily Wh ≈ panel watts × peak sun hours × 0.75**

The 0.75 covers wiring and controller losses, dust, heat and imperfect aim. Be pessimistic.

**Your home's sun hours** (from the region data for {{ region.home.county }} County,
{{ region.home.state_name }}): June **{{ region.home.sun_hours_jun }}**, December
**{{ region.home.sun_hours_dec }}**. Use December for sizing. Overcast and snow cut December far
below even that (→ 09-05).

**Size the system with this arithmetic:**
1. **Daily need** (Wh per day) from → 09-01, including the 1.3 loss factor.
2. **Panel watts needed ≈ daily need ÷ (December sun hours × 0.75).**
   Example: 600 Wh per day ÷ (2.5 × 0.75) ≈ **320 W of panel** to break even on a clear December
   day. Yours: ________ Wh ÷ ({{ region.home.sun_hours_dec }} × 0.75) = ________ W.
3. **Battery ≈ daily need × days of autonomy** (days you can run with no sun at all). Two to three
   days is the practical minimum where overcast or snow can last several days. Then divide by the
   usable depth of discharge (→ 09-07): lithium iron phosphate about 80 to 100%; lead-acid only
   about 50%, so a lead-acid bank must be **twice** the size.
   Example: 600 Wh × 3 days = 1,800 Wh usable → about 2,000 Wh of lithium iron phosphate, or about
   4,000 Wh of lead-acid.
4. **Inverter size ≈ the largest set of AC loads that run at the same time**, plus headroom for
   motor start (a compressor can pull 3 to 5 times its running watts for a second).
5. **Charge controller** must handle the panels' voltage and current with margin. **MPPT beats
   PWM**, typically by 15 to 30%, and by more in cold weather and low light. (MPPT and PWM are the
   two kinds of controller; MPPT converts surplus panel voltage into extra charging current, PWM
   throws it away.) Buy MPPT. Every power station has an MPPT controller inside.

### Series and parallel: the wiring choice that matters most

{{figure fig-series-vs-parallel}}

When you connect two or more panels you choose:
- **Series** (plus of one panel to minus of the next, in a chain): the **voltages add**; the
  current stays at the level of the weakest panel. Three panels of about 20 V each make a string of
  about 60 V.
- **Parallel** (all pluses together, all minuses together, usually with a Y-branch connector): the
  **currents add**; the voltage stays near the lower panel's voltage.

**The failure modes are not the same.** **Too much voltage kills a charge controller instantly
and permanently.** Too much current, at most station and controller inputs, is simply clipped:
the input takes what it can use and ignores the rest. (Check your manual: if it lists a maximum
short-circuit current, stay under that too.) So when in doubt, **choose the configuration with the
lower voltage.**

**Cold raises panel voltage.** A panel is rated at 77 °F (25 °C). For every degree colder, its
open-circuit voltage (Voc, the voltage with nothing connected, printed on the label) rises a
little: typically about 0.3% per °C. A string that is safely under a controller's limit on a mild
afternoon can be over it at sunrise on a clear, frozen morning. Cold never raises current, so
**series is the configuration winter can push over the edge, and parallel is the one it cannot.**

**The cold-voltage check, every time you plan a series string:**
1. Add up the label **Voc** of every panel in the string (warm Voc).
2. **Multiply by 1.20.** At a typical 0.3% per °C, a factor of 1.20 covers panel temperatures down
   to about −40 °F. Your home's record low is **{{ region.home.record_low_f }} °F**; if your
   panel's label gives a larger temperature coefficient, or you are planning for colder, work it
   out: factor = 1 + (coefficient as a decimal, without its minus sign) × (25 − lowest
   temperature in °C). Example: 0.003 × (25 − (−40)) = 0.195, so a factor of about 1.20.
3. **The result must be below the station's or controller's maximum PV input voltage**, with a
   margin. A few volts of margin is no margin.
4. Never drop the factor because "it is only 20 degrees this morning". Every winter morning is far
   below the 77 °F rating.

The worked tables for your own panels and stations, and which configuration goes into which
station, are on → 09-03. The short version that prevents almost every disaster: **a station with
a high input-voltage ceiling and a low current limit takes series strings; a station with a low
voltage ceiling and a high current limit takes parallel pairs or single panels, never a series
string that its ceiling cannot hold cold.**

### Mounting decisions that matter
- **Face true south.** A compass points to magnetic north, which can be well off true north in
  much of the country. Set panels by the shadow at solar noon (when shadows are shortest, they
  point true north).
- **Tilt steep in winter.** Roughly your latitude plus 15° catches the low winter sun and sheds
  snow (→ 09-05). Adjustable tilt is worth the trouble twice a year.
- **Shade is disproportionately bad.** Shading part of one panel can cut the output of the whole
  series string, not just that panel. Trees, chimneys, a neighbour's roof and the low winter sun
  angle all matter.
- **Ground-mount or portable is better than roof for an emergency setup.** You can sweep snow off
  it, re-aim it, move it, and bring it inside at night. A roof array in a blizzard is
  unreachable, and a lit house in a dark neighbourhood is a signal (→ 14-03).
{{#if has.solar}}
**Our panels:**

| Panel | Watts each | How many | Voc (label) | Isc (label) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each panels as p}}| {{p.model}} | {{p.watts}} | {{p.count}} | ______ V | ______ A |
{{/each}}

Total: **{{ gear.solar_w_total }} W**. Model-by-model figures for common panels and controllers:
→ 28-02.
{{/if}}

## Gear and items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Rigid panels, 100 to 200 W each, several | Modular, cheap per watt, decades of life | More smaller panels give more redundancy than one big one |
| One folding or portable 100 to 200 W panel | Phase B, and aiming at the low winter sun | The panel that leaves with you |
| **MPPT** charge controller with voltage headroom | 15 to 30% more harvest; survives the cold-voltage rise | Check its maximum PV input voltage against the cold check above |
| Lithium iron phosphate battery, 100 Ah (about 1.2 kWh) or more, or a power station | Deep cycles, long life | Note the **cold-charging limit** (→ 09-07) |
| Pure sine inverter, 300 to 1,500 W | Medical gear and electronics want pure sine | Modified sine can damage or buzz some devices |
| 12 V DC distribution: sockets, USB, fuse block | Skips inverter losses | The efficient path for Tier 0 |
| Fuses, breakers, correctly sized wire | Not optional (→ 09-08) | Fire risk otherwise |
| Adjustable tilt mounts or a simple A-frame | Winter angle and snow shedding | Buildable from 2×4s |
| Soft broom or snow rake with a non-abrasive head | A snowed-over panel makes nothing | Never a metal scraper |
| Multimeter | Checks Voc and polarity before every first connection | → 09-12 |

**Scavenge or substitute:**
- **Panels** from RVs, campers, boats, construction signs, solar yard lights and derelict arrays.
  **Large grid-tie panels are high-voltage** (30 to 40 V or more each) and need an MPPT controller
  that accepts that input; they are not a direct 12 V battery charger.
- **Controllers and inverters** from RVs, boats and campers; car inverters for small AC loads.
- **Batteries** from vehicles, boats, RVs, UPS units, floor scrubbers, mobility scooters and golf
  carts (→ 09-13, → 09-14).
- **Mounts:** 2×4 A-frames, pallets, fence posts, a ladder, a leaned sheet of plywood: anything
  that holds a panel steep and facing south.
- **Wire:** automotive and battery cable, welding cable. **Do not undersize it** (→ 09-08).

## When it runs out
- **Panels are the durable part.** They lose a fraction of a percent a year and can last 25 years
  or more. Hail is the real risk: store a spare panel flat and indoors.
- **The controller and inverter are the fragile electronics.** They fail from heat, water, surges
  and reversed polarity. **Buy a spare charge controller now**; without it the panels cannot
  safely charge anything. It is the highest-value spare in this section.
- **The battery is the true consumable** (→ 09-03, → 09-07).
- **When generation drops below Tier 0** (a snowed-in December week), fall back in order: stored
  battery, then a short generator run to bulk-charge the bank (→ 09-04), then vehicle and
  hand-crank charging (→ 09-11), then shedding to Tier 0 alone (→ 09-01).

## Phase notes
- **A (at home):** ground-mounted or yard-deployed panels you can sweep and re-aim, batteries
  **indoors** where they stay warm (→ 09-07).
- **B (moving):** one folding panel, one battery or station, power banks. Solar on foot or in a
  vehicle is a **trickle**: it keeps a phone and a small medical device alive, not a household.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** the permanent build. More panel than you think you need, real
  ground-mount racking, a battery room that stays above freezing. **Over-panel deliberately**:
  extra panels are cheap and they are what carry you through December.

## Cross-references
→ 09-01 load triage, do this first · → 09-03 batteries, stations and your wiring tables ·
→ 09-05 solar in winter, read before finalising any size · → 09-07 battery chemistry ·
→ 09-08 wiring and fusing · → 09-09 step-by-step build · → 28-02 panels and controllers ·
→ 29-02 batteries and power stations explained

pages.body:
# Batteries and power stations

**What this page is for.** Storage, not generation, is what keeps a phone and a medicine cooler
alive through a night and a cloudy day. This page covers the two kinds of battery you will meet
(lithium iron phosphate and lead-acid), power stations versus home-built systems, how to look after
them, and how to connect solar panels to your stations without destroying them. What a power
station is, and volts, amps and watt-hours, are on → 29-02. Model-by-model station specs are on
→ 28-01.

> **SAFETY. Three ways batteries hurt people.**
> **(1) Lithium fire.** A damaged, defective or wrongly charged lithium-ion battery can go into
> **thermal runaway**: an intense, self-sustaining fire that is very hard to put out and gives off
> toxic smoke. The warning signs are **heat, an odd smell, swelling or a change in shape, leaking,
> smoke, or unusual noise**; if you see them, get people out and call for help (NFPA,
> Lithium-Ion Batteries). Charge on a hard, non-flammable surface, away from exits and sleeping
> areas, and **never charge a battery that has been damaged, crushed, punctured or soaked.**
> **(2) Lead-acid gas and acid.** Charging lead-acid batteries gives off **explosive hydrogen**,
> and they hold **sulfuric acid**. Ventilate, no sparks or flames nearby, eye protection (OSHA,
> 29 CFR 1926.441).
> **(3) Short circuit.** A 12 V battery will push hundreds of amps through a dropped wrench and
> set the wire, the tool and the room on fire. **Fuse everything** (→ 09-08). Take off rings and
> watches before working on a battery.
> {{#if has.child}}**Children live in this house: batteries live where they cannot reach them, on a
> hard surface, with a working smoke alarm in the room.**{{else}}Keep batteries where children
> cannot reach them, on a hard surface, with a working smoke alarm in the room.{{/if}}
> **Never connect a power station's AC output to house wiring or into a wall outlet.** That is
> backfeeding, the same floor as for generators (→ 09-04, → 30-01).

## Do this now
- **Own one good lithium iron phosphate battery or one quality power station before anything else
  electrical.**
- **Put a fire extinguisher and a smoke alarm where the batteries live** (→ 29-12). Not optional
  with lithium.
- **Store lithium stations and banks at 40 to 60% charge, not full.** A cell held at 100% wears
  measurably faster, and manufacturers say the same for units unused for months. **Exception:
  when a storm is forecast, charge everything to 100%.** A few days full costs nothing; an outage
  that arrives with the station at 50% does.
- **Cycle them every three months:** note the charge you find (a bank that fell from 100% to 55%
  in 90 days has a drain or a fault), run it down to about 30%, charge to 100%, settle back to 50
  to 60%, check every port works, and **write it in the log** (→ 25-05). The failure you are
  guarding against is finding a dead unit after years of neglect.
- **Heat is the main enemy of stored lithium:** conditioned space, never a summer car or an
  attic. And **lithium iron phosphate must not be charged below freezing (32 °F).** Discharging
  cold is fine; charging cold is what damages it.
- **Turn off any power-saving ("ECO") setting on a port that runs a medicine cooler.** Many
  stations switch an output off after an hour or more of tiny load, and a compressor cooler
  resting between cycles looks like nothing is plugged in. Check the screen does not show the
  ECO symbol before the cooler goes on.
- **Fill in the station and panel tables below from the labels** (how: → 28-07), and take the
  photos: {{photo station-ports}} {{photo panel-labels}}
- **Buy several 20,000 mAh USB power banks.** About 70 Wh each, cheap, no wiring, no knowledge
  needed, and they cover phone loads for days (→ 09-06).

## Why it works this way

**Batteries are rated three ways and you need all three:**
- **Capacity:** watt-hours, or amp-hours at a voltage (Ah × V = Wh). A 100 Ah 12 V battery is
  about 1,280 Wh.
- **Usable capacity:** what you can take out without wrecking it. This is where chemistries
  differ enormously (→ 09-07).
- **Continuous and surge current:** how fast you can pull it out. A big battery with a small
  inverter still cannot start a compressor.

**The comparison that decides a purchase:**

| | **Lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4)** | **Lead-acid (AGM, flooded, gel)** |
|---|---|---|
| Usable depth of discharge | About 80 to 100% | **About 50%**: deeper kills it fast |
| Cycle life | Thousands of cycles | Hundreds (AGM), fewer if abused |
| Weight for the same usable Wh | About a third to a quarter | Heavy |
| Tolerates sitting part-charged | Yes | **No**: it sulfates and dies |
| **Charging below freezing** | **No: permanent damage.** Needs a heated battery or a battery management system with a low-temperature cutoff | Yes, at a reduced rate |
| Fire risk | Lower than other lithium types, but real | Hydrogen gas and acid, not fire |
| Cost per usable Wh over its life | **Lower** | Higher |
| Can you find more in a crisis? | Rarely | **Everywhere: every car, truck, boat, RV** |

**Read the cold-charging row twice.** {{#if is.cold_winters}}Your winters here are cold enough that
this decides where the bank lives: **inside the heated space** (→ 08-01), not in the garage, a
shed or on the porch.{{else}}Even where winters are mild, a cold snap, a garage or a car in January
can put a battery below freezing.{{/if}} Many quality batteries include internal heating or a
low-temperature charge cutoff; check the spec sheet for that feature specifically.

**Power station or component system?**

*Power station* (one box: battery, inverter, charge controller, outlets):
- **For:** works out of the box, no wiring knowledge, portable, protected by design, one thing to
  grab in Phase B. **The right first purchase for most households.**
- **Against:** expensive per Wh, cells usually not repairable, and when the electronics fail the
  whole unit is gone. Expansion only with the maker's add-ons.

*Component system* (separate battery, controller, inverter: → 09-09):
- **For:** cheaper per Wh, **repairable and expandable**, any part can be replaced or scavenged,
  runs 12 V loads directly with no conversion loss.
- **Against:** you must understand fusing and wire sizing (→ 09-08) or you will start a fire.

For many households the answer is both: a power station as the grab-and-go and the simple backup,
and a component 12 V system as the house bank that can be repaired and grown.

### Our stations

{{#if has.power_station}}Total: **{{ gear.station_wh_total }} Wh** across all stations.{{else}}No
power station is recorded in this household's settings. If you get one, add it in the app; until
then use this table on paper.{{/if}}

Fill the blank columns from each station's label or manual (→ 28-07). The solar input numbers are
the ones that protect the station.

| Station | Wh | AC output W (continuous / surge) | Solar input: max volts | Solar input: max amps | Solar input: max watts | Number of solar inputs, socket type | Charging temperature range | Where kept |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each stations as s}}| {{s.model}} | {{s.wh}} | ______ / ______ | ______ V | ______ A | ______ W | ______ | ______ to ______ °F | ______ |
{{else}}| ______ | ______ | ______ / ______ | ______ V | ______ A | ______ W | ______ | ______ to ______ °F | ______ |
{{/each}}

**Operating rules for any station:**
- **AC output never into house wiring** (above).
- **Idle draw is real.** With the AC inverter on and nothing plugged in, a station uses its own
  battery. Run DC loads from the 12 V and USB ports and switch the AC inverter off when you do not
  need it (→ 09-10). Measure yours: fully charged, inverter on, nothing plugged in, note the
  percentage after 12 hours.
- **Motor starts.** A motor (a blower, a pump, a compressor) draws two to three times its running
  watts, or more, for a moment at start. Check that against the station's surge figure before you
  rely on it. Some stations have a high-power mode meant for heating elements; read the manual for
  whether it suits motors.
- **UPS or pass-through mode.** Some stations can sit plugged into the wall with a load attached
  and switch to battery in milliseconds when the grid drops. If yours can, it is a good everyday
  home for a medicine cooler (→ 09-10). Read the manual's switchover time and whether the maker
  approves it for continuous use.
- **Temperature.** Most stations list a charging range that starts at 32 °F. A station does not
  live in a parked car in summer or winter.

### Connecting solar panels to a station without destroying it

{{figure fig-series-vs-parallel}}

The full explanation is on → 09-02. In one breath: **series adds voltage** (current stays at the
weakest panel's level); **parallel adds current** (voltage stays near the lower panel's). **Too
much voltage destroys a station's solar input instantly and permanently; too much current is
normally just clipped.** Cold raises voltage, never current, so series is what winter can push over
a station's ceiling.

**Our panels** (from each label; {{#if has.solar}}total {{ gear.solar_w_total }} W{{else}}none
recorded yet{{/if}}):

| Panel | Watts | How many | Voc | Vmp | Imp | Isc | Measured Voc (multimeter, in sun) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each panels as p}}| {{p.model}} | {{p.watts}} | {{p.count}} | ______ V | ______ V | ______ A | ______ A | ______ V |
{{else}}| ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ V | ______ V | ______ A | ______ A | ______ V |
{{/each}}

(Voc: voltage with nothing connected. Vmp and Imp: voltage and current at full working output.
Isc: current if the leads were shorted. All are printed on the label; → 28-07.)

**Work out every configuration before the first connection.** For each one:
- **Series:** voltage = sum of the Voc of every panel in the string; cold voltage = that × 1.20
  (→ 09-02 for where 1.20 comes from and when to use more); current = the **lowest** Imp in the
  string.
- **Parallel:** voltage = the **highest** single Voc; cold voltage = that × 1.20; current = the
  **sum** of the Isc of all panels.
- **Compare with each station's input window.** The cold voltage must be below the station's
  maximum input voltage, with real margin. Current over the station's limit is clipped (a little
  harvest wasted), unless the manual sets a maximum short-circuit current, which you then respect.

| Configuration | Warm V | Cold V (× 1.20) | Current | Into which station? (OK / NEVER) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| All panels in series | | | | |
| Two in series | | | | |
| Two in parallel | | | | |
| One panel alone | | | | |
| | | | | |

**Read the pattern in your own table.** A station with a high voltage ceiling and a low current
limit is a *series* machine. A station with a low voltage ceiling and a high current limit is a
*parallel* machine: it takes parallel pairs or single panels, and **never a series string whose
cold voltage reaches its ceiling, in any season.** Write your standing configurations here, pick
one each time, and do not improvise at first light:

1. ________________________________________ → ________________
2. ________________________________________ → ________________
3. ________________________________________ → ________________

The same table, cut down to a card, is on → 09-16; keep a copy with the panels.

**Rules that go with every configuration:**
- **Three or more strings in parallel need a fuse on each string** (→ 09-08). Two do not.
- **Mismatch:** series cares about matched *current* (the string runs at the lowest Imp);
  parallel cares about matched *voltage*. Pair the most alike panels in parallel.
- **Measure the string's Voc with a multimeter before any first-time connection.** On an MC4
  connector, red probe to the + end (the connector with the male pin), black to the − end. A
  **minus sign** on the meter means a connector is reversed: swap it before anything is plugged
  in. A station's input may survive reverse polarity, but a reversed panel *inside* a series chain
  silently subtracts its voltage. {{figure fig-mc4-polarity-check}}
- **Connect in the order the station's manual gives.** Where it gives none, the safe habit is:
  panels positioned and chained first, cable laid, then plugged into the station, then the station
  switched on.
- **Suitcase kits with a separate controller box.** Some folding panels come with a small charge
  controller and clips meant for a 12 V car battery. That box puts out *regulated battery-charging
  voltage*, not panel power. **The controller box, its clips and its adapter tips never go into a
  series string and never into a power station.** Use the panel's own bare MC4 leads, and store
  the controller box separately so nobody grabs it in the dark.
- **Small stations have small limits.** A small DC-only or USB-class station can have an input
  voltage and wattage limit that one large panel exceeds on its own, especially cold. Run the same
  check for it; it usually gets only its own small panel.

Full input specs for common stations and panels: → 28-01, → 28-02.

### What a station runs (estimates; the percentage on the screen is the truth)
- **A typical full-size refrigerator** (about 1,200 Wh a day): our station bank,
  {{ gear.station_wh_total }} Wh, runs one for roughly **{{ derived.station_fridge_days }} days**.
  That is an estimate: it assumes about 85% of the rated Wh is usable and does not count the
  station's own idle draw or anything else plugged in. **Measure your own:** fully charge, plug in
  only the fridge, and note the percentage every few hours for a day.
- **A small 12 V compressor medicine cooler** (often 200 to 500 Wh a day): days per charge =
  station Wh × 0.85 ÷ (cooler Wh per day + 24 × idle watts). Work it per station on → 09-10.
- **Kettle boils:** about 135 Wh per one-litre boil once kettle and inverter losses are counted
  (→ 07-06). Boils per charge ≈ station Wh × 0.85 ÷ 135.
- **Phones, lights, radios, laptops:** trivially.
- **A furnace blower** only through a safe connection: a transfer switch or interlock fitted by an
  electrician, or a cord-and-plug conversion ({{choice DC-07}}, → 30-08; write-up on → 09-04).
  Check the blower's running watts and start surge against the station's figures first.

### Lead-acid: the scavenger's chemistry
In a long event, every abandoned car, truck, tractor, boat, RV and mobility scooter holds a
lead-acid battery. They are heavy, inefficient and short-lived, and they may be the only batteries
you can find in year two (→ 09-13, → 09-14).
- A **starting battery** (from a car) is built for short bursts, not deep cycling. It works as
  storage but dies quickly if deeply discharged again and again.
- A **deep-cycle battery** (marine, RV, golf cart, floor scrubber) is the one you want.
- **Only discharge to about 50%**: roughly **12.0 to 12.1 V at rest** for a 12 V battery. Below
  about 11.8 V you are damaging it. **A resting 12 V lead-acid battery reads about 12.6 to 12.7 V
  full.** A cheap voltmeter is your fuel gauge (→ 09-07 has the full table).
- Never mix old and new, or different types, in one bank.

**Capacity reality check.** With Tier 0 and Tier 1 loads of roughly 500 to 800 Wh a day, two to
three days of autonomy needs about **1.5 to 2.5 kWh of usable storage**: one or two 100 Ah
lithium iron phosphate batteries, a large power station plus a spare, or roughly **four to six**
100 Ah lead-acid batteries (because of the 50% rule).

## Gear and items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Lithium iron phosphate 100 Ah battery (one or two) | The house bank | **Insist on low-temperature charge protection or internal heating** |
| Power station, 1 to 2 kWh, pure sine | Grab-and-go; runs AC out of the box | → 28-01 for how to compare them |
| 20,000 mAh USB power banks (three or four) | About 70 Wh each; phones and small medical devices | Cheapest useful storage |
| Charger with a **lithium iron phosphate profile**; a lead-acid smart charger | The wrong profile ruins a battery | The lead-acid one is for scavenged batteries |
| Multimeter and a 12 V battery monitor | Your fuel gauge | A shunt-based monitor beats voltage alone on lithium |
| Fuses, breakers, correct wire | Prevents the fire this page warns about | → 09-08 |
| Fire extinguisher near the batteries, smoke alarm in the room | Lithium and electrical fires | → 29-12 |
| Vented battery box | Contains acid, keeps children out | **Required** for lead-acid |
| Insulated battery blanket or a warm interior spot | Cold stops charging | Cheaper than a new battery |
| Safety glasses and baking soda | Acid neutraliser for lead-acid | Keep both with the batteries |
| MC4 Y-branch pair, spare MC4 connectors, the station's own solar cable | Parallel wiring and repairs | → 09-12 |

**Scavenge or substitute:**
- **Vehicle batteries:** the most abundant storage in a town. Vehicles also give you alternator
  charging (→ 09-11).
- **UPS units** (computer battery backups): sealed lead-acid, often nearly new (→ 09-13).
- **Mobility scooters, wheelchairs, floor scrubbers, golf carts:** real deep-cycle batteries.
- **Cordless tool batteries:** usable with USB adapters for small loads.
- **Laptop and e-bike packs:** high energy and **the most dangerous to repurpose.** Use whole
  packs with their own charger; never take them apart.
- **What you cannot scavenge:** a proper charge controller and a good charger. Buy spares.

## When it runs out
- **Batteries die of age, deep discharge, heat and cold, and the death is often sudden.** Track
  real capacity: note how long a known load runs, and watch that number shrink. A bank that held
  two days and now holds half a day is telling you it is ending.
- **Runway:** lithium iron phosphate gives **many years** of daily cycling if never charged below
  freezing and never left flat. Lead-acid gives **a few years at best**, much less if regularly
  run below 50%.
- **Ration:** shed loads by tier (→ 09-01). Charge and run loads during the sunny hours: power used
  while the sun is up is capacity you do not have to store.
- **Resupply:** scavenged lead-acid, in quantity, accepting the weight.
- **Substitute:** move loads off electricity entirely: light to lamps (→ 10-02), refrigeration to
  cold storage (→ 04-09, → 09-10), information to this binder on paper. **The final fallback for a
  phone is a hand-crank or vehicle charge** (→ 09-11).
- **End of life:** a dead lead-acid battery is still lead and acid. Do not burn it, do not open it,
  and keep it from freezing and splitting near children or the garden.

## Phase notes
- **A (at home):** house bank indoors in a warm room, fused, boxed, out of children's reach, smoke
  alarm overhead. Stations charged to storage level and staged where you can reach them.
- **B (moving):** the power stations and power banks go; a lead-acid bank does not (weight).
  **Charge everything to 100% before you leave.**
- **C (settled somewhere new):** build a larger bank in a space that stays above freezing. Collect
  scavenged lead-acid into a big, ugly, serviceable bank and keep the lithium for what has to be
  portable and reliable.

## Cross-references
→ 09-01 load triage · → 09-02 solar basics and the cold-voltage check · → 09-05 winter ·
→ 09-07 battery chemistry · → 09-08 wiring and fusing, read before wiring anything ·
→ 09-10 power for refrigerated medicine · → 09-16 outage day one and the hard-limits card ·
→ 28-01 power stations · → 28-02 panels and controllers · → 28-07 reading your own gear ·
→ 29-02 batteries and power stations explained

pages.body:
# Generators: fuel, siting, carbon monoxide and backfeed

**What this page is for.** How to use a portable generator without killing anyone, what it is
really for in a long outage (charging batteries fast, then off), how to start one that has never
been run, the ways it can safely connect to the house, and the cord-and-plug conversion for a
furnace or well pump if your household chooses to do it itself. Fuels are explained on → 29-01,
carbon monoxide on → 29-03, the breaker panel and transfer switches on → 29-04.

> **SAFETY. Generators kill people every year in two ways, and both are preventable.**
>
> **1. Carbon monoxide.** **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage,
> or near an open window.** Carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no warning; alarms fail; there
> is no mitigation that works every time (→ 30-01). One portable generator can produce as much
> carbon monoxide as hundreds of cars, and more than 80 people die in the US every year from
> carbon monoxide from portable generators (CPSC, Portable Generator Safety). Opening a door or
> window does **not** make an enclosed space safe. Run it **outdoors only, at least 20 feet from
> the house**, exhaust pointed away from your home and anyone else's (CPSC; CDC, Carbon Monoxide
> Poisoning: Basics). Battery-powered carbon monoxide alarms on every level and outside sleeping
> areas (→ 08-02). Some newer generators have a carbon monoxide shutoff; many do not, and **a
> generator without one runs happily while it poisons a room.** Only distance protects you.
>
> **2. Backfeed.** **Never connect a generator to house wiring without a transfer switch,
> interlock, or a cord-and-plug conversion with the main breaker locked off. Never backfeed
> through an outlet.** Backfeed electrocutes line workers and neighbours, and causes fires
> (→ 30-01). Plugging a generator into a wall outlet with a two-male-ended cord pushes power
> backward through your service onto the street lines.
>
> **3. Fuel.** **Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance**
> (vapour ignition, → 30-01). Never refuel a running or hot generator; spilled gasoline on a hot
> engine ignites. Let it cool.

## Do this now
- **Install carbon monoxide alarms now, before you own a generator.** Battery-powered, every
  level, outside sleeping areas. Test them; keep spare batteries. The single highest-value item on
  this page.
- **Choose the generator's exact outdoor spot today** and mark it: 20 feet or more from the house,
  exhaust aimed away from your house and the neighbours', not under a deck or overhang, on a dry,
  level, solid surface, sheltered from snow but open to air. {{photo generator-spot}}
  {{figure fig-generator-siting}}
- **Decide how the generator will reach anything in the house** (section below): extension cords
  only, a transfer switch or interlock fitted by an electrician, or a cord-and-plug conversion.
  Our connection: **{{ gear.house_connection }}**. Cord-and-plug done yourself is a decision card:
  {{choice DC-07}} (→ 30-08).
- **Think of the generator as a battery charger, not a power supply.** For this plan it fills the
  battery bank fast, then shuts off.
- **Fuel plan:** which fuel first, where it is stored, how it is rotated (→ 06-06, → 09-15).
  Propane cylinders larger than 1 lb live outdoors or in an outbuilding, upright, valves closed,
  away from doors and vents. Keeping gasoline or propane in an attached garage is a decision card:
  {{choice DC-05}} (→ 30-06).
- **Copy these from your generator's manual onto this page now** (you will not have the internet):
  oil type and capacity ________ · break-in load and hours ________ · first oil change after
  ________ · lowest rated operating temperature ________ °F · fuel allowed (octane, maximum ethanol)
  ________ · starting-battery charging instructions ________. Model specs for common generators:
  → 28-03.
{{#if has.generator}}
**Our generator:** {{ gear.generator_watts }} W running, fuel: {{ gear.generator_fuel }}.
{{#if has.inverter_generator}}It is an inverter generator: clean power, suitable for charging
stations and for electronics.{{else}}It is a conventional generator: fine for tools and pumps;
charge electronics through a power station or a pure sine charger rather than directly where you
can.{{/if}} {{photo generator-panel}}
{{/if}}

## First start: a generator that has never been run

Many households own a generator that has sat in its box. **The first start should not happen in
an emergency, by someone who has never done it.** If it has to, follow this in order.

**Step 0: before you start (5 minutes).**
- **Carbon monoxide alarm on inside**, on the side of the house nearest the generator. Anyone
  inside who feels sick, dizzy or weak: everyone out to fresh air, then call for help.
- **Find the box parts:** the propane hose and regulator (dual-fuel models), the battery charger,
  the oil funnel, the spark-plug wrench, any remote. No propane hose means gasoline only.
- **Pick the spot** (above). It must not sit in rain or snow while running: an open-sided cover
  only, never an enclosure.

**Step 1: move it outside first, empty.** Most are heavy: two people, the wheels and handle. **Keep
it upright.** Fuel and oil go in **outdoors, at the spot**, never in the garage. If it has been
sitting in deep cold, below its rated operating temperature, warm it first.

**Step 2: oil first. Nothing else until this is done.** Many generators ship **without oil**, and
starting one dry destroys the engine. On level ground, open the oil cover, pull the dipstick, and
pour the **4-stroke engine oil** grade your manual names (never 2-stroke oil) slowly, checking the
dipstick as you go. Small engines hold very little. **Stop between the marks; do not overfill.**
If oil has sat in it for years, change it anyway: oil absorbs moisture. A **low-oil shutdown** that
stops the engine means it was already running low.

**Step 3: battery (electric start).** On a new machine the battery plug may be held apart with a
tie: cut it and push the plugs together. A battery stored for years is probably flat. Charge it
with the supplied charger as the manual says, and unplug it after the manual's maximum time if the
charger is not a maintainer. A power station's AC outlet can run the charger in an outage. If
there is no charge, **plan on the pull cord, in gloves.**

**Step 4: propane hookup (dual-fuel).** Use **the hose and regulator that came with the
generator**, not a heater's hose.
1. Generator off. **Cylinder upright, valve on top, on the ground, on a flat surface, away from the
   exhaust side.**
2. Cylinder valve **fully closed** (turn clockwise). The cylinder needs an **OPD valve** (a
   triangle-shaped handwheel) and an **in-date requalification stamp** on the collar.
3. Thread the hose on by hand, then snug it as the manual says. **Do not over-tighten.** Unless the
   manual says otherwise, no thread tape or sealant.
4. Open the cylinder valve. **Leak test:** brush **soapy water** on every joint. Bubbles that
   appear or grow mean a leak: close the valve, tighten, retest. Still leaking: **do not use
   propane.**
5. **If you ever smell propane, do not start it.** Close the cylinder valve first.

**Step 5: start.**
- **Propane:** nothing plugged in, any economy or idle-down switch off, fuel selector on propane,
  cylinder valve open, start as the manual says (button, remote or pull cord: pull slowly until you
  feel resistance, then fast). Wait for the ready light. A little roughness at first is normal.
- **Gasoline:** engine off and cool. **Read the can's label before you pour** (→ 29-01): colour
  is not proof of what is inside. Fresh gasoline only, the octane and ethanol your manual allows;
  most small-engine manuals forbid E15 and E85 and fuel-oil mix. Pour slowly to the fill mark, do
  not overfill, cap on, wipe spills and let them dry before starting.

**Step 6: break-in.** Follow the manual: usually a light, varied load for the first few hours and an
early first oil change. A power station on a slow charge setting is a good break-in load.

**Step 7: connect loads with extension cords only** (unless a transfer switch, interlock or
cord-and-plug conversion exists, below). Outdoor-rated, grounded three-prong, heavy enough for the
load (12 AWG for 15 to 20 A runs, → 09-08), fully unrolled. **Biggest load first, one at a time.**
**Never plug a cord into a house outlet.** Do not prop a door or window open for the cord:
openings let exhaust in.
- **Medical devices run from a power station or battery that the generator charges, not straight
  from the generator.** Many generator manuals say this too.
- **Charging a power station:** a station's fast AC charge can draw close to 20 A. Divide its AC
  charging watts by 120 to get amps. Keep that well under the generator outlet's breaker rating and
  under the cord's and plug's rating (ordinary household plugs and cords are 15 A). If the station
  has a slower "standard" charge setting, use it from an ordinary outlet. Faster rates need the
  generator's larger outlet with the matching heavy cord and adapter, or they trip the breaker and
  heat the plug.
- **Overload light?** Unplug everything, reset, reconnect fewer loads.

**Step 8: shut down in the manual's order.** Usually: unplug loads, let it run a few minutes with
no load, switch off, battery switch off, **close the propane valve fully** and disconnect the hose
when not in use. Let it cool (the manual gives the time) before moving or covering it.

**Step 9: write it down** on a label on the machine: date, run hours, fuel used. Maintenance and
the no-start sequence: → 09-15.

## Why it works this way

**A generator's role in a long outage is narrow.** It burns a finite, hard-to-store fuel to make
electricity. Run continuously, it exhausts the fuel you own within days, and it is **loud**,
audible a long way off in a silent, dark neighbourhood (→ 14-03). Its real job:

**Run it hard, briefly, to bulk-charge the batteries and run the big one-time loads, then shut it
off and live from the batteries.** A generator burns a lot of fuel even lightly loaded, so idling
one for a couple of lights is the worst use of it. Charge the bank, run the well pump, pull the
freezer down, do the laundry, then off.

**Generator types:**

| Type | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Inverter generator** (mostly 1 to 3 kW, some larger) | Clean pure-sine power, quieter, sips fuel at low load | Best fit for battery charging and electronics |
| Conventional portable (3 to 8 kW) | Cheap watts, loud, rougher power | Fine for tools and pumps; questionable for sensitive electronics |
| Dual- or tri-fuel | Gasoline, propane, sometimes natural gas | **Propane stores for years without going stale** |
| Standby (whole-house, natural gas) | Automatic, powerful | Depends on the gas utility still flowing |

**Fuel is the real limit** (→ 29-01, → 06-06):
- **Gasoline** goes stale. Untreated it may be questionable in a few months; **stabilised and
  sealed, roughly a year or more** (check the stabiliser's own instructions). Ethanol-free stores
  better. It is volatile and dangerous to store in quantity. Old fuel in an engine is a decision
  card: {{choice DC-17}} (→ 30-18).
- **Propane** effectively **does not go bad** and stores safely in steel cylinders outdoors.
- **Diesel** stores longer than gasoline but gels in hard cold without treatment.
- **Do the arithmetic honestly.** Run hours = fuel on hand ÷ fuel per hour at your usual load (the
  manual gives fuel use). Even a lot of stored fuel is **weeks of intermittent use, not months.**
  Build the plan on solar and batteries; use the generator to cover gaps.

**Sizing.** Match the generator to the largest thing you must start (motors surge 3 to 5 times
their running watts), not your average load.

**The duty cycle that multiplies fuel:** run it about as long as it takes to refill the station or
bank (often under an hour at the station's standard rate), then shut it down. Do not charge a
station at its fastest rate and run another large load at the same time if together they approach
the generator's running watts.

## Connecting the generator to anything in the house

{{figure fig-generator-connection-options}}

| Way | What it is | Who does it |
|---|---|---|
| **Extension cords to individual appliances** | Cord from the generator outlet to the appliance's own plug | Anyone. Always allowed |
| **Transfer switch** | A switch, usually beside the panel, that connects chosen circuits to either the grid or the generator, never both | Licensed electrician; needs a generator its manual says is suitable |
| **Interlock and inlet** | A plate on the panel that physically prevents the main breaker and the generator breaker being on together, fed from an outdoor inlet | Licensed electrician; same generator requirement |
| **Cord-and-plug conversion** | A hard-wired appliance (furnace, well pump) is given a plug and a receptacle, so it can be unplugged from the house and plugged into a generator cord | Electrician, or yourself if your household chooses: {{choice DC-07}} (→ 30-08) |
| **Backfeed through an outlet** | A cord with two male ends from the generator into a wall outlet | **Never. Floor (→ 30-01)** |

**Why a transfer switch or interlock may not fit your generator.** A standard residential inlet and
interlock are 240 V (often a twist-lock four-prong inlet) and feed both halves of the panel. A
generator with only 120 V outlets cannot properly drive them; adapters that bridge both halves
from one 120 V outlet can overload shared neutral wires, and the generator's neutral arrangement
must match the transfer equipment. **Read your manual's specifications: if it says it is not
transfer-switch ready, or has no 240 V outlet, a transfer switch or interlock is not for it.** Ask
an electrician. Our connection: **{{ gear.house_connection }}**.

### If you choose the cord-and-plug conversion yourself (DC-07)

**The trade-off in one sentence:** a cord-and-plug furnace or pump is a hard-wired appliance made
unpluggable, and a wrong plug, a backfeed or a cord with two male ends can energise house wiring or
a person; doing it yourself instead of hiring an electrician accepts the risk of a wiring mistake.
Read the card first: {{choice DC-07}} (→ 30-08). If you chose an electrician, give them this
write-up. If you chose to do it yourself, every step below is part of the choice. {{figure fig-cord-and-plug-conversion}}

**The conversion, in order:**
1. **Power off and locked.** Switch the **main breaker off and lock or tape it**, and switch off the
   appliance's own breaker and tape it. **Verify dead at the appliance with a non-contact tester AND
   a meter** (black probe to ground, red to the hot conductor: 0 V). The gas supply to a furnace can
   stay as it is: this is electrical work only.
2. **Find the appliance's disconnect or junction box.** Usually a switch in a box on or beside the
   furnace cabinet, or a junction box where the house cable enters.
3. **Match the circuit.** Read the breaker and the cable. A 15 A circuit (commonly 14 AWG copper)
   gets 15 A parts (NEMA 5-15) and 14 AWG cord; a 20 A circuit (12 AWG) gets 20 A parts (NEMA 5-20)
   and 12 AWG cord. **If the appliance is 240 V (many well pumps), the plug, receptacle, cord and the
   generator outlet must all be 240 V; if you are unsure, stop and call an electrician.**
4. **Give the appliance a plug. Either:**
   - **(A) a male flanged inlet** of the right rating, mounted in a knockout on the cabinet or the
     disconnect box and wired to the appliance's hot, neutral and ground; the appliance is then fed
     by a cord with a female end; **or**
   - **(B) a cord with a male plug**, three-conductor SJ or SJT of the right gauge, entering the
     junction box through a strain relief and wired to the appliance's hot, neutral and ground.
5. **End the old hard-wired circuit in a receptacle.** The house cable that used to enter the
   appliance now ends in a receptacle box of the same rating, within cord reach. **The appliance's
   neutral and ground travel with its cord;** nothing is left floating or re-bonded.
6. **Normal use: the appliance plugs into that wall receptacle.** Breakers back on, test through a
   full cycle.
7. **Never a cord with two male ends. Never a connection into any house wiring** (no dryer-plug
   cords, no outlet-to-outlet cords). The only cord that touches the appliance has one male end and
   one female end.
8. **Label the plug** ("FURNACE: generator or station in an outage") and label the receptacle.
9. **Check the start surge before trusting a generator or station.** A blower or pump motor draws
   about **two to three times its running watts** for a moment at start. From the motor plate or
   cabinet label: running ______ W × 3 = ______ W surge. Compare with the generator's running watts
   ({{ gear.generator_watts }} W) and each station's continuous and surge figures (→ 09-03). Newer
   variable-speed blowers start softly; older motors surge hardest.
10. **Test it before you need it:** once on the generator (outdoors, 20+ ft), once on a station.
    Let the blower start and run a full cycle; watch for an overload light. Date it on the label:
    conversion done ☐ · tested on generator ☐ ______ · tested on station ☐ ______.
    {{photo furnace-plug}}

**Using it in an outage:**
1. Generator outdoors, 20+ ft, running and steady; carbon monoxide alarms on inside.
2. **Main breaker off and locked or taped**, and the appliance's breaker off.
3. Unplug the appliance from its wall receptacle. Plug it into the extension cord from the
   generator (or the station). Nothing else changes.
4. **A gas furnace also needs gas.** If the gas supply has stopped, the furnace gives no heat
   (→ 08-04).
5. **When the grid returns:** unplug the appliance from the generator cord, plug it back into its
   wall receptacle, then turn the breakers back on.

## Cold weather and propane

Check your manual's lowest operating temperature. Below it, store the generator somewhere above
that temperature while it is off (if gasoline is in its tank, that is fuel storage: → 30-06), wheel
it out warm for the run, and bring it back between runs. **Never run it inside, not for a second.**

**What deep cold does to propane:**
- **A 20-lb cylinder's vapour supply weakens in deep cold.** Propane must boil off the liquid to
  feed the engine, and the colder the cylinder, the slower it boils. A small cylinder feeding a
  large load in sub-zero cold can starve the engine (surging, stumbling) while the cylinder frosts
  over and still reads "full".
- **The regulator can ice** below zero, choking the flow minutes into a run.

**Fixes, in order of value:**
1. **A larger cylinder**, or two 20-lb cylinders teed together: more liquid surface, more vapour.
2. **Keep the duty cylinder sheltered outdoors** (a shed or covered rack out of wind and snow).
   **Never indoors, never in a basement or living space** (→ 06-06).
3. **Swap warm cylinders:** move the sheltered spare onto the generator and put the frosted one
   back under cover to recover.
4. **Optional:** during the no-load idle at shutdown, close the cylinder valve for the last minute
   so the regulator runs dry, and switch off **before** it stalls. This adds to the manual's
   shutdown; it never replaces it.

Keep the starting battery charged and know the pull cord in gloves.

## Commissioning checklist (a generator that has sat for years)

```
[ ] READ THE MANUAL for your model. Copy its key numbers onto this page now.
[ ] OIL FIRST. Many ship dry. If old oil has sat in it for years, change it.
[ ] RODENTS. Look inside the shroud, air filter housing and exhaust for nests
    and chewed wiring.
[ ] AIR FILTER clean and present.   [ ] SPARK PLUG present, gapped, not corroded.
[ ] RUBBER: fuel lines, primer bulb, any propane hose and regulator. Cracked or
    hard = replace.
[ ] BATTERY (electric start): probably flat; plan to replace it (09-14).
[ ] DUAL-FUEL? First start on PROPANE: nothing goes stale, nothing varnishes.
[ ] FIRST RUN OUTDOORS, 20+ ft, exhaust away, CO alarms already installed.
    Then ONE load within the break-in limit for 20-30 minutes, not a bare idle.
[ ] Only then plug in anything you care about.
[ ] WRITE the date and run hours on a label on the machine.
```
A generator that was never fuelled usually starts fine once it has oil and a charged battery. Oil
and rodents are the two things most likely to be wrong, and both are visible in ten minutes.
Keeping it alive between uses: → 09-15.

## Taking it with you
- **A generator and its fuel travel outside the passenger cabin**: on a trailer or an external
  carrier. Fuel inside a passenger vehicle is a decision card: {{choice DC-06}} (→ 30-07). A
  propane cylinder in an enclosed cabin is a leak away from an explosive atmosphere.
- **At a destination, check what fuel exists.** A gasoline/propane generator cannot run on natural
  gas without a conversion kit, and a kit lowers its output; check the kit's figures. Until a kit is
  fitted, it runs on the fuel you brought.

## Noise and light discipline
A running generator in a dark, silent neighbourhood announces fuel, power and probably food
(→ 14-03). Run it in daytime when other noise exists, keep runs short, and break up the sound with
distance and barriers that **do not restrict airflow or trap exhaust**. Never let noise push it
toward an enclosed space: carbon monoxide kills faster than anything else here.

## Gear and items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Battery-powered carbon monoxide alarms**, every level and outside bedrooms | The real life-saver on this page | Buy before the generator; test monthly |
| Generator suited to charging batteries | Inverter type preferred | Specs by class: → 28-03 |
| Heavy outdoor extension cords (12 AWG, 50 to 100 ft) | Lets you site it 20+ ft away and still reach | Undersized cords overheat (→ 09-08) |
| Transfer switch or interlock (electrician), or cord-and-plug conversion parts | The only safe ways to run a hard-wired appliance | Decision card DC-07 (→ 30-08) |
| Propane cylinders and the generator's own hose and regulator | Fuel that does not go stale | Stored outdoors, upright (→ 06-06) |
| Stabilised gasoline in approved cans, labelled with fill date | Second fuel, shared with vehicles | → 06-06, → 09-15 |
| Spare oil of the manual's grade, air filter, spark plug | Small engines need oil on a schedule | Two changes' worth, stored with the machine |
| Open-sided cover | Rain and snow protection **without enclosing it** | Must not trap exhaust |
| Battery charger that runs from generator AC | Bulk-charging the bank is the whole point | Pair with → 09-03 |

**Scavenge or substitute:**
- **A running vehicle is a generator you already own** (→ 09-11). Same carbon monoxide rules:
  **never run an engine in an attached garage.**
- **An inverter on a car battery** runs small AC loads with no engine running (→ 09-14).
- **Fuel:** from vehicles and stored equipment (→ 06-07 for the technique and why a hose down a
  modern filler neck usually fails). Give the generator the freshest fuel you have.
- **Cords:** heavy appliance cords, welding leads.
- **What you cannot substitute: the carbon monoxide alarm.** Buy several now.

## When it runs out
- **Fuel is the whole story.** Work your runway in **hours of run time**: fuel on hand ÷ fuel per
  hour at your usual load. Write it on → 23-02. Most households find the honest answer is days to a
  few weeks.
- **Ration from day one.** Batch every run: charge the bank to full, run every big load together,
  then shut down. Never idle it for a light.
- **Shared fuel:** if the same propane also feeds a heater or a cooking stove, every hour of those
  comes out of the generator's runway (→ 06-05).
- **Resupply:** stored fuel, then fuel from vehicles, then nothing. There is **no renewable
  resupply** for a generator, which is why this section leads with solar.
- **Plan for the generator to be a memory by month two and be fine anyway.**
- **Maintenance parts are a consumable too:** a generator run hard without oil changes dies before
  the fuel does (→ 09-15).

## Phase notes
- **A (at home):** the generator's best week is the first: bulk-charging, pulling the freezer down,
  laundry, filling water containers. After that it is an occasional charging tool. Noise discipline
  starts at once.
- **B (moving):** heavy, loud, and it needs fuel you would rather put in the vehicle. It travels
  only outside the cabin, with its fuel, or it stays behind.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** the main electrical tool until solar is set up, then back to
  storm-bridge duty. Keep fuel for real emergencies.

## Cross-references
→ 08-02 carbon monoxide safety · → 06-06 fuel storage · → 06-07 moving fuel · → 08-04 the heat
ladder · → 09-03 batteries (what the generator charges) · → 09-08 wiring and cords · → 09-15
generator maintenance and no-start troubleshooting · → 09-16 outage day one · → 28-03 generators
