pages.body:
# Outage day one: the live grid-down procedure

**What this page is for.** The page you run, in order, when the grid drops. It defends the loads that
matter most (→ 09-01): medical devices, refrigerated medicine, phones, light and, in cold weather,
heat. It then sets up the next morning's charging. The last part is a hard-limits card for your
stations and panels: print it and keep it with the panels.

> **SAFETY.** **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open
> window**: carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no warning; alarms fail (→ 30-01). Generator outdoors
> only, 20 feet or more from the house, exhaust away (CPSC, Portable Generator Safety).
> **Never connect a generator to house wiring without a transfer switch, interlock, or a cord-and-plug
> conversion with the main breaker locked off. Never backfeed through an outlet**: it electrocutes
> line workers and neighbours and causes fires (→ 30-01). The same goes for a power station's AC
> output.
> **The one wiring mistake that destroys a station instantly** is a panel string whose voltage is over
> the station's solar input limit. Use only the configurations on the card at the bottom. When in
> doubt, stop and read the card.

## Do this now (the power just went out)
1. **Is it just us?** Look outside. If neighbours have power, check the main breaker and the panel
   ({{photo breaker-panel}}). Report the outage: {{ contacts.utility.electric.provider }},
   {{ contacts.utility.electric.phone }}.
2. **Medical devices first.** {{#if has.cpap}}CPAP onto its battery or a station tonight. {{/if}}{{#if has.oxygen}}Oxygen: switch to cylinders or the portable concentrator's battery now and start
   counting hours. {{/if}}Phones and medical devices onto power banks (→ 09-06).
3. **Keep the fridge and freezer shut.** A closed refrigerator keeps food safe for about 4 hours; a
   full freezer about 48 hours, a half-full one about 24 (USDA and HHS, Food Safety During a Power
   Outage; → 04-17).
4. {{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}**Refrigerated medicine: set up the cooler within the first hour**
   (step 3 below), and move the medicine once the cooler's thermometer reads within the label range.
   {{else}}Any refrigerated medicine: set up a cooler within the first hour (step 3 below).{{/if}}
5. **Switch off and unplug non-essential loads and sensitive electronics** so a surge when the grid
   returns cannot damage them (American Red Cross, Power Outage Safety). Leave one light switched on so
   you know when power is back. Leave smoke and carbon monoxide alarms alone.
6. **Light: flashlights and lanterns, not candles** (US Fire Administration, Candle Fire Safety).
   Candles indoors are a decision: {{choice DC-20}} (→ 30-21).
7. **If you smell gas, leave first and call from outside** ({{ contacts.utility.gas.phone }}; FEMA,
   Utility Shut-off and Safety).
8. **Decide what kind of outage this is** (→ 17-08): hours, overnight, or unknown. Overnight or
   unknown: carry on down this page.

## Before any outage
- **Print this page and the card at the bottom; keep the card in the panel bag.** {{photo panel-bag}}
- **Photograph the breaker panel and mark the fridge, freezer and furnace breakers.**
  {{photo fridge-breaker}}
- **Know your posture for refrigerated medicine** (→ 09-10): either the cooler lives on a station in
  UPS mode, or the medicine lives in the kitchen fridge and the cooler, station and designated
  thermometer are staged. Ours: ________________________________.
- **Test the cooler for 24 hours on the station's 12 V port** with the designated thermometer inside;
  turn the station's power-saving ("ECO") setting off for that port (→ 09-03).
- **Stations:** stored at 40 to 60%, charged to 100% when a storm is forecast. Power banks charged.
  Panel bag staged with cables, Y-branch and multimeter. {{photo station-ports}}
- **Carbon monoxide alarms installed** (we have {{ gear.co_alarms }}), tested, spare batteries.
- **Walk this sequence once on a calm day and time it.** The first real run should be the second run.

## The sequence

### T+0: the first hour
1. **Fridge and freezer shut** (above). Start the clock.
2. **Kill non-essential house loads.** Walk the house once: power strips off, unplug anything with a
   standby light. Five minutes; it stretches every stored watt-hour and protects against the surge when
   power returns.
3. **Set up the medicine cooler** (if anyone uses refrigerated medicine):
   - Cooler, station and the designated thermometer to the **warm room** (→ 08-01), away from any
     heater; never an unheated room in winter.
   - **Plug the cooler into the station's 12 V port, not the AC outlets.** The inverter's idle draw
     alone can be most of what the cooler uses. Switch the 12 V port on; **power-saving mode off.** If
     the cooler's display is ever dark, re-enable the port.
   - **Thermometer inside, lid shut.** Move the medicine in **only when the thermometer reads within
     the label range** (for insulin, 36 to 46 °F, 2 to 8 °C, never frozen: US FDA, Information
     Regarding Insulin Storage). Wrap the medicine so it never touches the cooler walls; if it reads
     too cold, raise the setting.
4. **Runtimes to plan on** (→ 09-10): each station's days for the cooler, worked out there. **The
   percentage on the screen is the truth.** Move the cooler to the next station at ______ %.
5. **Before dark:** every phone and power bank charging from the remaining station capacity; set out
   tomorrow's panel plan in your head.

{{#if has.well}}**Water:** the well pump stops with the power (→ 03-10).{{/if}}

### T+0 to T+6 hours: heat (any outage in cold weather, or when the house is cooling)
{{#if is.cold_winters}}**In a winter as cold as yours, heat is the clock right behind medicine.**{{else}}When it is cold, heat is
the clock right behind medicine.{{/if}} Start while the house still holds its warmth, not late at
night. In this order (→ 08-04):
1. **Furnace, only if gas still flows and a safe connection exists.** Our connection:
   **{{ gear.house_connection }}**. A station or generator can run the blower only through a transfer
   switch or interlock, or a cord-and-plug conversion ({{choice DC-07}}, → 30-08; how to use it:
   → 09-04). Run the blower in bursts, coast, repeat. **Never backfeed.** {{figure fig-generator-connection-options}}
2. **Close down to one warm room** (→ 08-01): blankets over doorways, everyone (and the medicine) in
   one room. The warm room must meet the heater's air rules.
3. **Carbon monoxide alarms on and tested BEFORE any heater is lit:** one in the warm room, one where
   people sleep (→ 08-02).
4. **One combustion heater at a time.** Portable heater manuals generally forbid another fuel-burning
   appliance in the same space. Kerosene: → 08-10. Propane: → 08-09; a cylinder larger than 1 lb
   indoors is a decision: {{choice DC-02}} (→ 30-03). Shared propane also feeds the generator and
   any cooking stove: count it (→ 06-05).
5. **Overnight:** an unvented heater running while people sleep is a decision card:
   {{choice DC-01}} (→ 30-02). Whatever you chose, heated blankets from a station for the sleepers
   help either way (→ 09-01). Anyone waking with a headache or nausea: everyone out to fresh air.

### The first morning: panel deployment
{{#if has.solar}}Our panels: {{ gear.solar_w_total }} W.{{/if}} Deploy in this order, unless the
station's manual says otherwise: **position the panels → chain them as the card says → lay the cable →
plug into a station that is switched off → switch on.**

**Decision rule: charge whichever station is lowest.** Use **only the standing configurations on the
card** (worked out on → 09-03). {{figure fig-series-vs-parallel}}
- **Before the first connection of any string, measure its voltage (Voc)** with the multimeter: red
  probe to the + end (the MC4 connector with the male pin). **A minus sign means a connector is
  reversed: swap it.**
- **Re-check the card every time you move panels between stations.**
- **Suitcase kits:** the panel's bare MC4 leads only. A separate controller box never joins a string
  or a station.
- **Wind:** stake or weight kickstand panels. **Concealment:** out at dawn, in at dusk, never left
  unattended (→ 14-03).

### Who runs on what

| Load | Runs on | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Medicine cooler | **A station's 12 V port, power-saving off, AC inverter off** | Tier 0; no inverter loss; give it a dedicated station if you have two (→ 09-10) |
| CPAP, oxygen concentrator | Its own battery pack or DC cord, then a station | Tier 0 (→ 09-06) |
| Phones, medical charging, power banks | Power banks and the smallest station | Keeps the pocket tier off the big stations |
| Kettle boils, heated-blanket sessions | **Whichever station is fullest** | Big optional draws come from surplus, never from the cooler's station |
| Furnace blower | A station or generator, **only through the safe connection** | Never backfed (→ 09-04); check the start surge first |
| Lights, radio, laptop | Power banks and the smallest station first | Tier 1 stays off the AC tier when it can |

### The daily rhythm
- **Charge at midday; run loads while the sun is up.** Every watt-hour used while the panels are
  producing is storage you did not need (→ 09-05).
- **Kettle and blanket sessions in the afternoon**, from the day's surplus, not at 10 p.m. from the
  night's reserve.
- **The cooler's station is topped up before dark, every day.** The one hard daily requirement.
- **Panels in at dusk**, folded, indoors: inspection, concealment and hail insurance in one habit.

{{#if is.cold_winters}}### Winter variant
- **Panels go out only in usable sun.** A grey whiteout day is not worth the cold exposure or the wind
  risk (→ 09-05).
- **Stations charge INDOORS, above 32 °F, always.** Lithium iron phosphate charged below freezing is
  permanently damaged (→ 09-03). Run the panel cable in through a window or door gap with a towel seal.
- **Check winter's gift first:** below-freezing outdoor air may let the cooler's job move to passive
  cold, with freeze protection and a min/max thermometer (→ 09-10, → 04-09).
{{/if}}

### When solar fails for two days or more: the generator bridge
{{#if has.generator}}Our generator: {{ gear.generator_watts }} W, {{ gear.generator_fuel }}.{{/if}}
Outdoors, 20 feet or more, exhaust away, carbon monoxide alarms on (→ 09-04). Run it long enough to
refill a station at the station's **standard** charge rate on a 12 AWG cord, then off. That cycle is
the storm plan, not continuous running. In deep cold, start it warm and bring it back in between
runs (→ 09-04). **If it has never been run, follow the first-start steps on → 09-04 (oil
first).**

### When the power comes back
1. Leave the generator running only until the house is back on the grid; then switch it off, outdoors.
2. If the furnace or a pump was on the generator cord, **unplug it from the cord, plug it back into its
   wall receptacle**, then switch the breakers back on (→ 09-04).
3. Plug things back in one at a time.
4. Check the fridge and freezer and decide on food (→ 04-17). Medicine goes back to its normal
   storage.
5. Recharge everything, return stations to storage charge later, and write what happened in the log.

## Hard-limits card: print, cut out, keep with the panels
*(Fill in from the labels and the worksheet on → 09-03. Cold rule: a string's Voc × 1.20 must stay
below the station's maximum input voltage, with margin: → 09-02.)*

| Station | Solar input: max V · max A · max W · socket | OK to connect | **NEVER** |
|---|---|---|---|
{{#each stations as s}}| {{s.model}} ({{s.wh}} Wh) | ______ V · ______ A · ______ W · ______ | ______________ | ______________ |
{{else}}| ______ | ______ V · ______ A · ______ W · ______ | ______________ | ______________ |
{{/each}}

**Standing configurations:** (1) ______________ → ______ · (2) ______________ → ______ ·
(3) ______________ → ______.

**Never-rules for every station:**
- Measure Voc with the multimeter before any first-time connection; a **minus sign** means a reversed
  connector.
- The × 1.20 cold factor is never dropped on a "mild" morning.
- No series string whose cold voltage reaches a station's maximum input, in any season.
- No suitcase controller box, its clips or its adapter tips in a string or a station.
- No station's AC output into house wiring or a wall outlet, ever.
- No charging any lithium station below 32 °F.
- Power-saving mode off on any port running a medicine cooler.
- Generator outdoors only, 20 feet or more, exhaust away.

## When it runs out
- **Day three or later with no sun and no generator fuel:** shed to Tier 0 (→ 09-01), move the
  cooler's job to passive cold if the season allows (→ 09-10), and charge phones from a vehicle
  (→ 09-11, → 09-14).
- **If a station dies:** with two or more, the system is redundant: the cooler runs on any station's
  12 V port (power-saving off on whichever it moves to). One dead unit is a log entry, not a crisis.
- **If Tier 0 cannot be met**, that is a go/no-go input (→ 01-02), not something to endure.

## Phase notes
- **A (at home):** this page as written.
- **B (moving):** this page does not apply. Phase B power is power banks, the smallest station and the
  vehicle (→ 09-06, → 09-11).
- **C (settled somewhere new):** the same sequence; the generator bridge matters more until solar is
  set up (→ 09-04).

## Cross-references
→ 09-03 stations, panels and the wiring worksheet behind this card · → 09-10 the medicine cooler ·
→ 09-04 generator bridge and house connections · → 09-05 winter solar · → 09-06 medical devices ·
→ 09-01 load triage · → 08-04 the heat ladder · → 08-01 the warm room · → 08-02 carbon monoxide ·
→ 04-17 food safety in an outage · → 17-08 power grid failure · → 00-06 the first 60 minutes

# Medical and first aid

**What this section holds.** 21 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 12-01 **Building a real first-aid and trauma kit**: It lists what to buy and store so your household can handle the injuries and illnesses that actually happen when no clinic is open.
- → 12-02 **Bleeding control and wound care**: Stopping serious bleeding in the first minutes, then cleaning and caring for a wound over the following weeks so it does not become infected.
- → 12-03 **Burns (high risk around fire)**: Preventing burns, giving first aid in the first minutes, judging how serious a burn is, and caring for it afterwards when no hospital is reachable.
- → 12-04 **Infection, fever and antibiotics**: Spotting infection early, recognising sepsis, knowing when a wound needs a tetanus booster, and what a household can do when antibiotics are scarce or absent.
- → 12-05 **Common illness, diarrhoea and dehydration**: Recognising dehydration, treating it with oral rehydration solution, knowing when it is beyond home care, and the other common illnesses of a long emergency.
- → 12-06 **Dental emergencies**: Keeping teeth healthy when there is no dentist, and buying time when something goes wrong.
- → 12-07 **Family medicine stockpile and over-the-counter list**: Your household's own "my meds" table, the over-the-counter (OTC, no prescription needed) categories worth stocking, how to store medicines without power, and…

pages.body:
# Building a real first-aid and trauma kit

**What this page is for.** It lists what to buy and store so your household can handle the
injuries and illnesses that actually happen when no clinic is open. It is a supply list only.
How to use each item is on the treatment pages it points to.

> **Supplies are the smaller half of this.** A kit you do not know how to use is a bag of
> expensive props. **Take a Stop the Bleed course and a hands-on first-aid and CPR course
> now**, while classes still exist. They are short and inexpensive, and they are worth more
> than anything on this list. Nobody in your household needs to be a doctor; this binder is
> written for people who are not.

> **Life-critical medicines do not go in this kit.** Epinephrine auto-injectors (a pen that
> injects adrenaline into the thigh for a severe allergic reaction, → 02-03), insulin
> (→ 02-01, → 02-02) and any other medicine someone cannot go without belong in their own
> known place, reachable in seconds, never buried in a general first-aid bag.
> {{#if has.epinephrine}}Your household carries epinephrine: everyone, including older
> children, should know exactly where it is.{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Take the courses.** Stop the Bleed (about an hour) and a Red Cross or equivalent first
   aid and CPR class. Every adult who could be the one responding.
2. **Count what you already own** against the "buy first" table below and write the counts on
   → 22-04. Assume you do not have a trauma kit until those counts are written down.
3. **Check everyone's tetanus vaccination** while clinics are open. A puncture wound with no
   clinic and an out-of-date tetanus shot is a dangerous combination, and it is easy to fix
   now (CDC, About Tetanus; → 12-04).
4. **Build the everyday kit first, then the trauma kit.** You will use adhesive bandages,
   tweezers and pain relief a hundred times for every time you need a tourniquet.
5. **Put a trauma kit where wood is cut and fires are lit.** Axes, saws, chainsaws and stoves
   are where serious injuries happen (→ 16-06, → 06-01).
6. **Stock quantities, not a boxed kit.** Commercial kits hold about six of everything. For
   {{ household.size }} people in a long event you want **boxes** of gauze, not packets.
7. **Photograph where each kit lives** and add the photo below and on → 12-08.

{{photo kit-locations}}

## Design the kit around what will actually happen

Forget television. In a long emergency at home, the realistic list of injuries and illness
looks like this:

| How often | What | Where it is covered |
|---|---|---|
| **Constant** | Cuts, scrapes, splinters, blisters, minor burns | → 12-02, → 12-03 |
| **Very likely** | Axe, saw and knife wounds from processing wood and food | → 12-02 |
| **Very likely** | Burns from stoves, open fires and hot liquids{{#if has.child}}, especially children{{/if}} | → 12-03 |
| **Very likely** | Diarrhoea and vomiting; dehydration (losing more water than you take in) | → 12-05 |
| **Likely** | Sprains, falls{{#if is.cold_winters}} on ice{{/if}}, broken bones | → 12-09, → 11-06 |
| **Likely** | Infected wounds, the thing that kills when there are no antibiotics | → 12-04 |
| **Likely** | Cold injuries | → 12-10, → 08-05 |
| **Likely** | Dental problems | → 12-06 |
| **Ongoing** | Long-term conditions and the medicines they depend on | → 12-11 |
| Less likely | Massive bleeding; this is what the trauma kit is for | → 12-02 |

**Design for the top of that list.** Most of your supplies should be gauze, tape, wound
cleaning and burn care, not exotic gear.

## The three tiers (detail on → 12-08)

1. **Everyday kit**: in the kitchen, used weekly. Bandages, antiseptic, tweezers, pain
   relief{{#if has.child}}, children's supplies{{/if}}.
2. **Trauma kit**: for serious bleeding. Small, fast to reach, in the places injuries happen:
   the woodpile or work area, the vehicle, the go-bag.
3. **Long-haul supplies**: the bulk stock. Boxes of gauze, tape, saline, splint material and
   over-the-counter (OTC, no prescription needed) medicines in quantity. Stored, rotated,
   counted.

## The core list

**Bleeding and wounds** (→ 12-02)
- **Tourniquet ×2 to 3** (a strap with a stick-like handle, the windlass, that you twist to
  stop blood flow to a limb), and **training in how to use one.** Buy a genuine
  windlass-type tourniquet of a model the Stop the Bleed course teaches. Cheap copies can snap
  or slip under load.
- **Hemostatic gauze ×2 to 4** (gauze treated with a substance that speeds clotting) and plain
  **compressed gauze** in quantity.
- **Pressure bandages ×2 to 4** (a roll bandage with a built-in pad and a clip you can put on
  with one hand; often sold as "emergency" or "Israeli-type" bandages).
- **Sterile gauze pads** in many sizes, **by the box**. This is your highest-volume item.
- Roller gauze, self-adherent wrap, medical tape (cloth and paper).
- Non-adherent dressings (pads that do not stick to a wound) and large abdominal pads.
- **Nitrile gloves by the box.** Not latex: latex allergy is common. Gloves protect the
  person giving care, which matters when there is no clinic for them either.
- Trauma shears, fine-point tweezers for splinters, an irrigation syringe (20 to 60 mL) for
  washing wounds.
- Sterile saline or clean drinkable water for washing wounds (→ 03-04).
- Wound-closure strips and skin adhesive. **Read → 12-14 before closing any wound.** Most
  wounds in a long emergency should not be closed.
- Antiseptics: povidone-iodine, chlorhexidine, alcohol wipes.
- Antibiotic ointment (→ 12-07).

**Burns** (→ 12-03)
- Sterile non-adherent burn dressings, clean cling film (a recommended burn covering), and
  plenty of clean water for cooling.

**Splints and support** (→ 12-09)
- **Moldable padded splint ×2** (a flexible aluminium-and-foam strip you bend to shape),
  elastic bandages, triangular bandages, athletic tape, a sling.

**Checking a patient**
- Thermometers (**several**, plus batteries), a blood pressure cuff, a pulse oximeter (a
  fingertip clip that reads oxygen level and pulse; needs batteries), a good headlamp
  (→ 10-01), a notepad and pen for a treatment log, and a watch with a second hand.

**Medicines**: see → 12-07 and → 12-13. Follow the label. For children, use only the
published dosing tables on → 12-13 and the label; never guess.

**Reference books on paper**
- A real first-aid manual. *Where There Is No Doctor* and *Where There Is No Dentist*
  (Hesperian) are widely used for exactly this situation. Buy physical copies.
- Your **family medical summary** (→ 25-09): conditions, medicines, allergies, blood types,
  vaccination dates. Written down, in this binder.

**For your household's own conditions**
{{#each members as m}}
- **{{m.label}}**: conditions {{m.conditions}}; allergies {{m.allergies}}. The supplies for
  these come from that condition's page (→ 12-11), not from this kit.
{{else}}
- No members are entered yet. Add them in settings so this list fills in.
{{/each}}
- Life-critical medicines (epinephrine, insulin, glucagon, rescue inhalers, seizure
  medicines) stay in their own known place. → 12-11 lists every condition page.

## The mistakes to avoid

- **Buying a boxed kit and calling it done.** A "300-piece" kit is mostly adhesive bandages. It
  is a restock source, not a plan.
- **Skipping the training.** Supplies without skills is the most common failure.
- **Burying the trauma kit in a closet.** Serious bleeding is a minutes problem. The kit has
  to be where the injury happens.
- **Nothing in the vehicle or the go-bag.**
- **Ignoring expiry dates.** Sterile packaging degrades; medicines lose strength. Count
  everything twice a year (→ 22-04).
{{#if has.child}}- **No children's sizes.** Small bandages, a child-suitable thermometer,
  children's medicine strengths and an oral dosing syringe. A one-year-old and a four-year-old
  need different everything.
{{else}}- **No children's sizes.** Even without children at home, you may be caring for
  someone else's child. Keep a few small bandages and children's medicine strengths.
{{/if}}- **Latex.** Use nitrile.

## Two things that prevent more harm than any kit treats

1. **Handwashing and clean water** (CDC, About Hygiene; → 13-02). Preventing infection is far
   cheaper than treating it when there are no antibiotics (→ 12-04).
2. **Not getting hurt.** Sharp tools used carefully (→ 16-02), traction on ice (→ 11-06), fire
   discipline (→ 10-02){{#if has.child}} and children kept away from the stove (→ 20-02){{/if}}
   prevent more harm than any amount of gauze fixes.

## Buy first: the life-saving core

Write what you own in the second column. Anything blank is the first thing to buy (also on
→ 22-07).

| Item | Owned (count) | Why it is first |
|---|---|---|
| **Genuine tourniquets ×2**, plus one for practice | ____ | The only fix for a limb bleed that pressure cannot hold (→ 12-02) |
| **Hemostatic gauze ×2** plus compressed gauze | ____ | Wounds in the groin, armpit and neck; packing |
| **Pressure bandages ×2** | ____ | One-handed and fast |
| **Oral rehydration salts (ORS) packets**, enough for at least 20 litres | ____ | Dehydration from diarrhoea is one of the biggest killers when water is unsafe (→ 12-05) |
| **Children's acetaminophen and ibuprofen in the strengths the published tables use, plus two oral dosing syringes** | ____ | The tables on → 12-13 are useless without the bottles and syringes |
| **CPR pocket mask**, adult and child sizes | ____ | → 12-18 |

## Build toward this

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Stop the Bleed course plus first-aid and CPR course** | Worth more than the whole kit | Every adult; refresh every few years |
| Genuine tourniquets ×2 to 3 | Copies fail under load | Train with a practice one |
| Hemostatic gauze ×2 to 4 | Bleeding pressure alone will not stop | Check expiry |
| Pressure bandages ×2 to 4 | One-handed use | |
| **Gauze pads and rolls by the box** | Highest-volume item by far | Assorted sizes |
| Nitrile gloves by the box | Protects the caregiver; no latex | Several sizes |
| Moldable splints ×2 plus elastic bandages | Falls and broken bones (→ 12-09) | Reusable |
| Trauma shears, fine tweezers, irrigation syringe | The three most-used tools | |
| Antiseptics (iodine, chlorhexidine) | Wound cleaning | Bulk |
| Non-adherent burn dressings plus cling film | Burns are a top-three likely injury | → 12-03 |
| Thermometers ×2 to 3 plus batteries | Fever is a critical signal (→ 12-04) | {{#if has.child}}Include one suited to small children{{else}}One spare{{/if}} |
| Blood pressure cuff, pulse oximeter | Checking a patient with no clinic | Batteries |
| *Where There Is No Doctor* and *Where There Is No Dentist* on paper | The reference that matters | Physical copies |
| Family medical summary, printed | Conditions, medicines, allergies, blood types | → 25-09 |
| Labeled, sealed, waterproof containers | Findable in the dark, by anyone | Contents list on the outside |

## Scavenge or substitute

- **Dressings:** clean cotton cloth, boiled and dried; clean sheets torn into strips.
  Sanitary pads and disposable diapers make good absorbent dressings: they come sealed and soak
  up a lot.
- **Washing wounds:** a clean squeeze bottle, a plastic bag with a pinhole, any syringe, and
  clean drinkable water (→ 03-04). Pressure and volume matter more than sterility.
- **Splints:** cardboard, magazines, sticks, foam pads, rolled newspaper (→ 12-09).
- **Tape:** duct tape or electrical tape over gauze, not directly on skin.
- **Slings and triangular bandages:** a T-shirt, a pillowcase, a scarf.
- **Cold packs:** snow, ice, a bag of anything frozen.
- **Tourniquet:** improvised tourniquets often fail. Buy real ones. If you must improvise, it
  needs a wide strap and a rigid stick to twist. Read → 12-02 first.
- **From other houses (→ 22-02):** medicine cabinets, veterinary supplies, first-aid stations
  in workplaces and vehicles, school and church kits.

## When it runs out

- **Gauze, tape and gloves run out fastest.** One significant wound with dressing changes for
  two weeks uses an astonishing amount. Stock in bulk and list it on → 23-02.
- **Count dressing changes, not packets.** One wound, changed twice a day for ten days, is
  twenty dressings, for one injury.
- **Ration:** wash and reuse cloth dressings, boiled, dried and stored clean. This is how it
  was done for most of history and it works. Keep sterile commercial dressings for fresh, deep
  or dirty wounds.
- **Resupply:** scavenging (above) and trade. Medical supplies are among the most valuable
  trade goods there are (→ 18-02). That cuts both ways: you can get them, and people will want
  yours. Think about what you tell others (→ 14-03).
- **Substitute:** clean cloth for gauze, boiled water for saline, honey as a wound dressing
  (→ 12-02), soap and water for antiseptic. **Cleanliness substitutes for almost everything;
  nothing substitutes for cleanliness.**
- **What cannot be substituted:** epinephrine, insulin and the other life-critical medicines
  on the condition pages (→ 12-11). Everything else on this page has a workaround.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** all three tiers set up. Everyday kit in the kitchen, trauma kits at the
  work area and in the vehicle, bulk stock stored and counted. Take the courses now.
- **B (moving):** a compact kit per adult: tourniquet, pressure bandage, gauze, tape, gloves,
  blister care, pain relief, **and each person's life-critical medicines first** (→ 22-03,
  → 01-07). Blisters and cold injury are the realistic problems on the move.
- **C (resettled):** further from help, more dangerous work (axes, animals, building), so you
  need more capability, not less. A trauma kit at every work site, a real supply store, and
  ideally someone in the group with real medical training (→ 18-03).

pages.title: Bleeding control and wound care
pages.body:
# Bleeding control and wound care

**What this page is for.** Stopping serious bleeding in the first minutes, then cleaning and
caring for a wound over the following weeks so it does not become infected. It is a reminder
card for people who have taken a hands-on course, not the course itself.

> **SAFETY**
> - **Reading this page does not make you able to do this.** Bleeding control is a physical
>   skill. **Take a Stop the Bleed course now**, while classes exist. It takes about an hour.
> - **Never loosen a tourniquet once placed; mark the time.** Re-bleeding and clot release
>   kill. This is one of the binder's floors (→ 30-01): it is not offered as a choice.
> - **Severe bleeding kills in minutes.** That is why the trauma kit lives where the work
>   happens (→ 12-01, → 12-08).
> - **Infection is the bigger long-term killer** when there is no clinic (→ 12-04). A wound
>   you survive in the first hour can still kill in the second week. Cleaning matters as much
>   as stopping the bleeding.

## Do this now: serious bleeding

1. **Make the scene safe.** Stop the chainsaw, step off the ice. A second casualty helps
   nobody.
2. **Find the bleeding.** Cut or pull clothing away. Blood soaks into dark cloth unseen.
3. **Press hard** on the wound with gauze or cloth and a gloved hand. **Do not lift to check.**
4. **Arm or leg still bleeding through pressure? Tourniquet:** 2 to 3 inches above the
   wound, never over a joint. Tighten until the bleeding stops **and** there is no pulse
   below it. Still bleeding? A second tourniquet above the first. **Write the time on it.
   Never loosen it.**
5. **Groin, armpit or neck?** Pack the wound with gauze and press hard.
   **Chest or belly?** Do **not** pack. Cover and press.
6. **Keep them warm and lying flat.** Watch breathing. Then read → 12-16.

{{figure fig-tourniquet-placement}}

## Do this now: preparation

- **Take the Stop the Bleed course.** Every adult who might respond. Then buy genuine
  tourniquets and a practice one, and drill putting one on yourself, one-handed, in the dark,
  with gloves on.
- **Put a trauma kit where wood is cut.** Axe and saw injuries to the leg and foot are among
  the most likely serious bleeding events in a long emergency (→ 16-06). Until you have
  counted tourniquets, hemostatic gauze and pressure bandages on → 22-04, assume you do not
  have them (→ 12-01, "buy first").
- **Check tetanus vaccination dates for everyone** while clinics are open (→ 12-04, → 25-09).
- **Stock gauze in bulk.** One serious wound managed for two weeks uses far more dressing
  than any commercial kit contains.

## The order of operations for serious bleeding

This is the framework taught by Stop the Bleed (American College of Surgeons). Learn it in a
class; use this page as the reminder.

1. **Your own safety first.** Falling wood, a running saw, a fire, thin ice.
2. **Find the bleeding.** Look and feel. Use trauma shears to cut clothing away.
3. **Firm, direct pressure** with a gloved hand and gauze or cloth, **hard**, and **do not
   lift to check.** Most bleeding stops with steady direct pressure. It is the single most
   effective action and it needs no equipment.
4. **On an arm or leg, if pressure is not controlling it, use a tourniquet** (Stop the Bleed):
   - **2 to 3 inches above the wound, on the limb, never over a joint.** The bone of the
     knee or elbow stops the strap from squeezing the artery. If the wound is at or just below
     a joint, go above the joint.
   - **Tighten until the bleeding stops and there is no pulse below it**, then lock the
     windlass (the twisting handle) in its clip.
   - **If it still bleeds, put a second tourniquet above the first.**
   - **Write the time on it**: on the strap, the skin, the forehead, anywhere it will be seen.
   - It will hurt a great deal. That is expected.
   - **Small children:** a windlass tourniquet closes down on most children from about 2 years
     old. On an infant's or toddler's thinner limb it may not. Use direct pressure and packing
     instead.{{#if has.young_child}} You have a young child: practise direct pressure and
     packing on a pillow, not only the tourniquet.{{/if}}
5. **Junctional wounds** (groin, armpit, neck, where a tourniquet cannot go): **pack the wound**
   with hemostatic or plain gauze, pushing it in firmly until the wound is filled, and hold
   hard pressure. Packing is exactly what the course teaches. **Never pack a wound in the
   chest or abdomen** (Stop the Bleed): packing there pushes into the organs. Cover it and hold
   firm pressure. That is an injury to move toward whatever care exists (→ 12-16).
6. **Keep them warm** (→ 08-05), **lying flat**, and watch them. Blood loss plus cold is a
   dangerous combination{{#if is.cold_winters}}, and in your winters "keep them warm" is not
   an afterthought{{/if}}.

{{figure fig-wound-packing}}

### Once a tourniquet is on

**Never loosen a tourniquet once placed; mark the time.** Loosening lets the wound bleed again
and can release clots into the blood, and both kill. This is a floor (→ 30-01).

Be honest about what this means with no hospital. A tourniquet left on for many hours costs
the limb below it. That is the price of the life. Keep the person warm, keep them lying down,
give fluids by mouth if they are awake and can swallow, and move toward any care that exists
(→ 12-16).

**Myths that persist anyway:** a tourniquet does **not** automatically cost the limb when care
arrives within a few hours; pressing "pressure points" and raising the limb are **not**
substitutes for direct pressure; and **improvised tourniquets often fail** because they are too
narrow or lack a rigid windlass. Buy real ones.

## Cleaning a wound: the part that decides the outcome

With no clinic and possibly no antibiotics (→ 12-04), **cleaning the wound is your infection
control.**

- **Wash your hands first** (CDC, About Hygiene) and put on gloves. Every time.
- **Irrigate (flush) with lots of clean drinkable water.** This is the core of it. **Volume and
  pressure matter more than sterility.** A large syringe, a squeeze bottle, or a plastic bag
  with a pinhole gives the pressure. Use far more water than feels necessary.
- **Remove dirt and debris**: grit, splinters, gravel, bark, cloth. Anything left in the wound
  becomes an abscess (a pocket of pus) later. Use fine tweezers and good light (→ 10-01).
- **Antiseptics** (iodine, chlorhexidine) are for the **skin around** the wound. Strong
  antiseptics poured into a wound damage healthy tissue as well as germs. Clean water is the
  workhorse.
- **Dress it:** a non-stick layer against the wound, absorbent gauze over it, secured.
- **Change the dressing regularly and look at the wound every time.** This is how you catch
  infection early (→ 12-04).

## When not to close a wound

**Read → 12-14 before closing anything.** In brief: **closing a dirty wound traps the infection
inside.** Wounds that are dirty, deep, punctures, bites, more than several hours old, or from an
axe or chainsaw in a dirty place should generally **be left open**, packed lightly, and allowed
to heal from the bottom up. It is slower and uglier, and far safer without a surgeon and
antibiotics.

## The wounds a long emergency produces

| Wound | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Axe or hatchet to the foot or shin** | The classic wood-splitting injury. Deep, dirty, often bleeds hard. Sharp tools and a correctly placed chopping block prevent it (→ 16-06) |
| **Chainsaw** | Ragged, very dirty, severe. Chaps and protective gear are the answer; treatment without a surgeon is poor |
| **Knife, from butchering and cooking** | Frequent, usually clean, often deep in the hand (→ 05-09) |
| **Splinters and punctures** | Small and easy to dismiss, and the classic route to tetanus and abscesses |
| **Animal bites and scratches** | Always treated as dirty. Never close. High infection risk (→ 20-09, → 05-15) |
| **Burns** | Handled differently; see → 12-03 |
| **Crush injuries** | Falling wood, vehicles, machinery. Damage inside may be worse than what shows |
{{#if has.child}}| **Children's cuts and scrapes** | Constant. Clean well, cover, watch. Most are trivial; a few are not |
{{/if}}

## Eye injuries: shield, flush, or dark rest

Wood chips, wire ends, sunlight off snow. The three responses are very different, and mixing
them up is what costs sight.

- **Something stuck in or through the eye: shield it. Never remove it, never press**
  (MedlinePlus, Eye emergencies). Use rigid protection that rests on the bone around the eye,
  not on the eye: **a clean paper cup, or half a foam cup, taped over the eye socket.** Cover
  the other eye too if the person can bear it, because the eyes move together and movement
  grinds the object. No rubbing, no rinsing around it. **Nothing to eat or drink** (it may need
  surgery). Move toward whatever care exists (→ 12-16). The shield's job is to change nothing
  on the way.
- **Loose grit, eyelash or sawdust:** blinking and tears clear most of it. Help with a **gentle
  flush of clean water** (MedlinePlus). Never fingers or tweezers on the eyeball, and **never
  rub.**
- **Scratched eye (corneal abrasion):** the grit is out but it still feels like glass:
  scratchy pain, tears, light hurts. Flush once, then **stop touching it.** MedlinePlus says
  the discomfort of a minor scratch settles within a day or two. If pain gets worse, redness
  spreads, there is discharge, or sight gets worse instead of better, treat it as an infection
  (→ 12-04). Tight patching is no longer routine; do not press or rub an injured eye. Dark
  glasses for comfort are fine.
- **Snow blindness:** hours on snow or water glare, then that evening both eyes burn, water,
  and cannot stand light (American Academy of Ophthalmology, What Is Photokeratitis). It is a
  sunburn of the clear front of the eye. **It heals by itself, gradually, in about a day or
  two.** Treatment is dark rest: contact lenses out, a dim room or covered eyes, a cool cloth
  over closed lids, comfort measures from → 12-13. **Prevention is the real medicine:
  UV-blocking sunglasses or goggles on every snow and ice day (→ 11-08).** The field
  improvisation works: cardboard, bark or cloth with two narrow horizontal slits, tied on.
  Both eyes at once plus a day of glare means snow blindness; one eye, or no glare, means look
  for the other causes above.
- **Chemical splash in the eye** is covered on → 12-03 and → 12-17: flush with lukewarm water
  for 15 to 20 minutes, from the nose side outward, lids held open, starting now. It is more
  urgent than anything else in this list.

## Watching for infection: the second-week killer

Check at every dressing change and know the signs (→ 12-04; CDC, About Sepsis):
- Redness, swelling, warmth and pain that **increase after day two or three.** Normal healing
  gets less uncomfortable, not more.
- **Red streaks** spreading from the wound.
- **Pus or a foul smell.**
- **Fever, chills, feeling unwell all over.**
- **Confusion, fast breathing, fast heartbeat, extreme discomfort**: signs of **sepsis**, the
  body's overwhelming reaction to infection, a life-threatening emergency.

**Tetanus** (lockjaw, a germ from soil that causes muscle spasms) is a real risk with punctures
and dirty wounds. Early signs are jaw stiffness and muscle spasms. **There is no home treatment
once it starts.** The defence is the vaccine. After any wound, ask whether a booster is due now.
The CDC wound rule (CDC, About Tetanus; full table on → 12-04): **a clean minor wound needs a
booster if the last dose was 10 or more years ago; any other wound (dirty, puncture, bite,
burn, crush, frostbite) needs one if it was 5 or more years ago, ideally within 48 to 72
hours; fewer than 3 lifetime doses plus a dirty wound also calls for tetanus immune globulin**,
which only a clinic has. Everyone's dates belong on → 25-09.

## Honest limits

With no clinic, some injuries are beyond what a household can manage: bleeding inside the body
you cannot reach, deep chest or belly wounds, broken bones that cut off blood to a limb, severe
head injuries, and infections that outrun what you have. **→ 12-16 covers those decisions.**
Knowing your limits in advance is part of the plan. Prevention (→ 16-02 sharp tools, → 16-06
safe technique, → 11-06 traction) does more than any treatment page.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Stop the Bleed training** | The skill, not the gear, saves the life | Every adult; refresh |
| Genuine tourniquets ×2 to 3, plus a practice one | Copies fail | Count on → 22-04 |
| Hemostatic gauze ×2 to 4 | Wounds you cannot put a tourniquet on | Check expiry |
| Compressed and roller gauze, **in bulk** | The volume item | Boxes |
| Pressure bandages ×2 to 4 | One-handed, fast | |
| **Large irrigation syringe (20 to 60 mL)** | Flushing pressure is the infection control | Cheap; get several |
| Nitrile gloves by the box | Protects you and the wound | Not latex |
| Fine tweezers, magnifier, headlamp | Splinters and debris | Good light matters |
| Trauma shears | Cut clothing away fast | |
| Antiseptic (iodine, chlorhexidine) | Skin around the wound | Bulk |
| Non-stick dressings, abdominal pads, tape | Weeks of dressing changes | Quantity |
| Medical-grade honey (or plain honey) | Traditional wound dressing with real evidence | See below |
| A trauma kit at the work area and in the vehicle | Minutes matter | → 12-08 |
| Chainsaw chaps, safety glasses, cut-resistant gloves | **Prevention beats all of it** | → 16-06 |
| UV-blocking sunglasses or goggles for each person; a rigid eye shield (or clean paper cups) | Snow blindness; shielding a stuck object | → 11-08 |
| *Where There Is No Doctor* on paper | The reference | → 12-01 |

## Scavenge or substitute

- **Dressings:** clean cotton cloth, boiled and dried; **sanitary pads and diapers** (sealed,
  very absorbent, excellent for this); clean torn sheets.
- **Flushing:** any squeeze bottle, a plastic bag with a pinhole, a turkey baster, and clean
  drinkable water (→ 03-04).
- **Honey** on clean wounds and burns has traditional and evidence-supported use: it fights
  germs and keeps the wound moist. **Not for deep punctures, and never for a baby under 12
  months** (risk of infant botulism, a rare paralysing illness).
- **Sugar packing** of infected wounds is another traditional method with real history.
- **Tape:** duct tape over gauze, not directly on skin; cloth strips tied.
- **Sterilising instruments:** boiling for a sustained time; flame for metal.
- **What you cannot improvise well:** a tourniquet, hemostatic gauze, and the training. Get all
  three now.

## When it runs out

- **Dressings go fastest.** One significant wound dressed twice a day for two weeks is dozens
  of dressings. Count in dressing changes, not packets (→ 23-02).
- **Ration:** wash and reuse cloth dressings, boiled, dried, stored clean. Keep sterile
  commercial dressings for fresh, deep or dirty wounds and for the first days.
- **Resupply:** medicine cabinets and workplace kits (→ 22-02); trade (→ 18-02); cloth, which is
  plentiful (→ 11-05).
- **Substitute:** clean cloth for gauze; boiled water for saline; soap, water and flushing for
  antiseptic; honey or sugar for antibiotic ointment on suitable wounds.
- **What cannot be substituted is cleanliness** (→ 13-02). Clean hands, clean water and clean
  cloth at every dressing change prevent far more harm than any supply here treats. When
  supplies run low, be more careful, not less.
- **The real answer is prevention.** Sharp tools that cut instead of glancing off (→ 16-02), a
  proper stance, chaps, gloves, not swinging an axe when exhausted or cold, traction on ice
  (→ 11-06). The wound you do not get costs nothing to treat.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** trauma kit at the work area and in the kitchen. Wood splitting and cooking
  are where the injuries are. Use clean water for flushing generously while you have it.
- **B (moving):** a tourniquet and a pressure bandage for each adult, reachable with one hand.
  Water for flushing is scarce on the move, so wound cleaning gets worse exactly when dirt goes
  up. Clean thoroughly at the next stop with real water.
- **C (resettled):** more axe work, more animals, more building, further from help. More
  capability, not less. A trauma kit at every work site, and protective gear treated as
  required.

pages.title: Burns (high risk around fire)
pages.body:
# Burns (high risk around fire)

**What this page is for.** Preventing burns, giving first aid in the first minutes, judging
how serious a burn is, and caring for it afterwards when no hospital is reachable.

> **SAFETY**
> - **Burns are one of the three most likely serious injuries in a long emergency**, and the
>   risk rises sharply once a household heats with fire, cooks over flame and lights with
>   lamps{{#if has.young_child}}, especially with young children in the same warm room{{/if}}.
> - **A large burn without a hospital is very serious.** Large burns lose a great deal of body
>   fluid and get infected easily. Burn care is one of the clearest limits of home medicine
>   (→ 12-16). **Prevention is worth far more than treatment here.**
> - **Any large burn; any burn to the face, hands, feet, genitals or across a joint; any burn
>   that goes all the way around a limb; any electrical or chemical burn; and any burn on an
>   infant or small child needs professional care wherever it exists.**
> - **Never ice or snow on a burn.** Ice deepens the injury (WHO, Burns fact sheet).

## Do this now: someone is burned

1. **Stop the burning.** Away from the heat. Smother flames (stop, drop, roll, or a fire
   blanket). Take off hot clothing that is not stuck. **Never pull off clothing melted into
   the skin.**
2. **Cool it with cool running water for at least 15 minutes by the clock** (American Red
   Cross); up to 20 is fine. **No ice, no snow.**
3. **Keep the rest of the person warm** while you cool the burn.
4. **Take off rings, watches and tight items** before swelling starts.
5. **Cover** with a non-stick dressing or **clean cling film laid on, not wrapped tight.**
6. **No butter, oil, toothpaste or ointment. Do not break blisters.**
7. **Size it with their own palm** (below). Big, deep, or in a high-risk place: move toward
   care. Start drinking fluids (→ 12-05).

**Chemical on the skin or in the eye:** dry powder, brush it off first, then flush 15 to 20
minutes. Liquid, flush at once. Details below.

## Do this now: preparation

- **Put a physical barrier around every heat source before the cold season.** A hearth gate,
  a stove guard, a fixed screen.{{#if has.young_child}} A toddler walks into things; a
  preschooler reaches over them.{{/if}} This is the single highest-value action on this page.
- **Set a "hot zone" rule and teach it**: a marked line on the floor that children do not
  cross when the stove or fire is going (→ 20-02, → 20-04). Practise it before you need it.
- **A fire extinguisher and a fire blanket in every room with a heat source**, plus pot lids
  in the kitchen. Learn to use them (→ 29-12).
- **Stock burn dressings and cling film.** Clean cling film is a recommended burn covering: it
  does not stick, it is clean off the roll, and you already have it.
- **Wool, not fleece, for fire work** (→ 11-05). Synthetic fabric melts onto skin and turns a
  minor burn into a severe one.

## Where burns actually come from

| Source | Who | Prevention |
|---|---|---|
| **Wood stove and stovepipe surfaces** | **Children, constantly** | Physical barrier; the hot-zone rule |
| **Scalds from hot water, soup, boiling water for purification** | **Children and adults** | Pot handles turned in; never carry hot liquid past a child; children out of the cooking area |
| Cooking over an open fire | Adults | Long tools, gloves, stable pot supports (→ 07-01) |
| Grabbing hot cast iron | Adults | Dedicated hot pads that live with the cookware (→ 07-04) |
| Fuel flare-up (refilling a lamp, priming a stove) | Adults | Never refuel anything hot or lit (→ 10-02, → 06-06) |
| Synthetic clothing melting | Anyone near fire | **Wool, not fleece** (→ 11-05) |
| Chemicals (lye for soap, battery acid, pool chlorine) | Adults | Gloves and eye protection (→ 13-09, → 09-03, → 29-05) |
| Sunburn | Everyone in summer | → 11-08 |
| **House fire** | Everyone | Alarms, extinguishers, escape plan (→ 00-04) |

**Scalds are the most common burn in small children.** A household boiling water for drinking
and cooking over fire has a lot of hot liquid moving around. Set up the kitchen so **hot
liquids never travel through the space where children are.**

## First aid in the first minutes

This is standard first-aid practice. Learn it in a hands-on course.

1. **Stop the burning.** Remove the person from the heat. Smother flames: stop, drop and roll,
   or a fire blanket. **Remove smouldering or hot clothing that is not stuck**, but **never
   pull off clothing that has melted into the skin.**
2. **Cool the burn with cool (not ice-cold) running water for at least 15 minutes by the clock
   (American Red Cross); up to 20 is fine.** This is the single most effective thing you can
   do, and it still helps if you start some minutes late. **Do not use ice**: the World Health
   Organization is explicit that ice deepens the injury. Do not run cooling far past 20
   minutes on a large burn or a small child, because of hypothermia (dangerous body cooling;
   WHO).
3. **Watch for hypothermia while cooling**{{#if is.cold_winters}}, a real tension in your
   winters{{/if}}, and it matters most with a small child. Cool the burn; keep the **rest** of
   the person warm.
4. **Remove rings, watches and tight items** before swelling starts. Easy to forget and hard
   to undo.
5. **Cover** with a sterile non-stick dressing or **clean cling film laid on (not wrapped
   tight).** Covering reduces pain and dirt.
6. **Do not** put butter, oil, grease, toothpaste or ointment on a fresh burn. **Do not** break
   blisters. Both are traditional and both are wrong. **A burn that is white, leathery or
   painless in the centre is deeper than it looks**: the nerve endings are destroyed. Count it
   as full-thickness (through all layers of skin), not as "not that bad".
7. **Fluids.** Burns lose a lot of fluid. Someone with a significant burn needs to drink
   (→ 12-05). See the fluid note below for big burns.
8. **Pain.** See → 12-13. Follow the label for adults; for children use only the published
   tables printed there.

## Sizing the burn: the palm rule and when to seek care

**The person's own palm, fingers included, is about 1% of their body surface** (American Burn
Association, Burn Center Referral Criteria). Count palms of the burned person: an adult's palm
on a toddler measures nothing. Redness alone does not count; count blistered or worse.

{{figure fig-burn-palm-rule}}

**Move toward whatever care exists (→ 01-02, → 12-16) for any of these** (American Burn
Association referral criteria unless noted):
- **Adult: burned area bigger than about 10 of their own palms (more than 10% of the body).**
- **Child:** the American Burn Association says burned children should be treated where
  there is staff and equipment for children's burn care. The World Health Organization calls
  10% or more a major burn in a child. Children lose fluid faster than adults, so with no
  hospital, treat any child's burn larger than a few of their own palms as serious.
- **Any full-thickness burn** (white, leathery or charred; painless in the centre).
- **Face, hands, feet, genitals, the area between the legs, or across a joint**, any size.
- **Burns that go all the way around** a limb, finger or the chest. Swelling turns them into a
  tourniquet.
- **Any electrical or chemical burn; any sign of breathing in hot smoke** (burned in a closed
  space, singed nose hair, soot in the mouth, hoarse voice, cough).
- **Any burn on an infant.** A baby's skin is thinner; the same heat burns deeper.
{{#if has.infant}}  Your household has an infant: keep this line in mind every time water
  boils.{{/if}}

## Fluids for a big burn when there is no IV

Large burns kill early through fluid loss. A hospital would use IV fluid (fluid dripped into a
vein), which a household will not have. **The World Health Organization's 2024 guidance for
burns in mass-casualty situations covers exactly this gap: where IV fluid is unavailable, use
fluids by mouth: safe drinking water plus oral rehydration salts (ORS)** (→ 12-05 has the
packets and the published recipe). In practice: for any burn at or past the thresholds above,
start ORS early, in steady small amounts, write down what goes in (→ 25-05), and keep it going
while you move toward care. Vomiting or a drowsy patient is where this method stops working.
**It replaces nothing when a hospital is reachable; it is the bridge for when one is not.**

## Why burns are so dangerous with no clinic: infection

A burn destroys a patch of skin, and skin is what keeps germs out. **Burns get infected easily,
and infection is the main cause of death in burns people would otherwise survive.** With
little or no antibiotics (→ 12-04), your defences are:
- **Strict cleanliness** at every dressing change: handwashing, gloves, clean materials (CDC,
  About Hygiene).
- **Clean, non-stick dressings, changed regularly.**
- **Watching for the signs**: pain and redness that increase after the first days, spreading
  redness, pus, foul smell, fever, and the signs of **sepsis** (the body's overwhelming
  reaction to infection; CDC, About Sepsis; → 12-04).
- **Honey** has traditional and evidence-supported use as a burn dressing on suitable burns: it
  fights germs and does not stick. **Never for a baby under 12 months** (infant botulism), and
  not a substitute for professional care.
- **Tetanus status matters for burns too** (CDC, About Tetanus; → 12-04).

## Chemical splashes: skin and especially eyes

Lye from soap-making (→ 13-09), pool chlorine (→ 29-05), fuels, drain cleaner.
**The treatment is water, at once and in quantity, with one step first for dry chemicals.**

- **Dry powder or granules** (pool shock, lye flakes, garden lime): **brush off every visible
  grain first** with a gloved hand or a dry cloth, **take off the dusted clothing, then flush
  for 20 minutes.** A little water on a pile of dry chemical concentrates the heat on the skin
  (American Red Cross; MedlinePlus, Chemical burn or reaction).
- **Liquids:** flush at once.
- **Skin:** strip contaminated clothing and rinse under running water **15 to 20 minutes by the
  clock.** A splash and a wipe is not a rinse.
- **Eye:** flush with lukewarm clean water for 15 to 20 minutes, lids held open, pouring from
  the nose side outward so the runoff misses the other eye. Take out contact lenses.
- **Never add a "neutralising" chemical** to skin or eye. The reaction adds heat.

A lye or acid splash in the eye is one of the most time-critical injuries in this binder.
Seconds of delay cost sight. The saline in the medicine kit (→ 12-07) is only the start; clean
water in volume is the treatment (→ 12-17).

## The honest limits

**A large burn is beyond household care.** Large burns need IV fluids, surgery and infection
control that cannot be improvised. **Burns to the airway from breathing hot smoke can close the
airway and kill quickly.** Electrical burns damage the inside of the body far beyond what
shows. Knowing this changes behaviour: **it makes prevention the priority and the fire-safety
rules non-negotiable.** → 12-16 covers decisions when treatment is not possible.

## Fire prevention is burn prevention

- **Smoke alarms on every level, tested, with spare batteries** (→ 10-02, → 29-12).
- **Carbon monoxide alarms**: a different hazard, the same principle (→ 08-02, → 29-03).
- **Extinguishers** in the kitchen, near the stove, near lamps.
- **An escape plan, practised**{{#if has.child}}, including exactly who carries out which
  child{{/if}} (→ 00-04). A house fire in a grid-down winter with no fire department is a
  catastrophe: you lose the shelter, the supplies and the medicines at once.
- **Never leave a fire, lamp or candle unattended.** Use flashlights, not candles, when the
  power is out (US Fire Administration, Candle Fire Safety; → 10-02).
- **Nothing that can burn near the stove**, including clothes drying (→ 11-03). Near, never on.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Hearth gate or stove guard** | A physical barrier between children and heat | The highest-value item here |
| Fire extinguishers (several) plus a fire blanket | Stop the burn at the source | Every room with a heat source |
| **Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms on every level** | Prevents the catastrophic version | Battery; test monthly |
| Sterile non-stick burn dressings | Will not stick to the wound | Several sizes |
| **Cling film (plastic wrap)** | Clean off the roll; good burn covering | Stock several rolls for this |
| Clean water in quantity for cooling | The most effective first aid there is | → 03-02 |
| ORS packets | Fluids for a big burn | → 12-05 |
| Long-handled fire tools, heavy leather gloves | Cooking over fire from a distance | → 07-01 |
| Hot pads that stay with the cast iron | The pot is as hot as the fire | → 07-04 |
| Wool outer layers for fire work | Synthetics melt onto skin | → 11-05 |
| Non-stick dressings, gauze, tape in bulk | Burns need frequent changes | Quantity |
| Raw or medical-grade honey | Traditional, evidence-supported dressing | **Never under 12 months** |
| *Where There Is No Doctor* on paper | Burn assessment guidance | → 12-01 |
| Tape line on the floor for the hot zone | Makes a rule concrete for children | → 20-04 |

## Scavenge or substitute

- **Cooling:** any clean cool water. **Never snow or ice directly on a burn**: snow in a cold
  snap is ice, and ice deepens the injury (WHO), the same reason → 12-09 and → 12-19 say wrap
  cold packs. **In winter, melt snow into cool (not icy) water first**, or use stored
  room-temperature water. Pour or run it over the burn for 15 to 20 minutes and keep the rest
  of the person warm.
- **Coverings:** clean cling film, clean plastic bags, clean cotton cloth (boiled and dried),
  sanitary pads for absorbency over a non-stick layer.
- **Non-stick layer:** cling film, a clean plastic sheet, or cloth with a thin layer of clean
  petroleum jelly or honey so it does not bond to the wound.
- **Fire blanket:** a wool blanket (wool chars instead of melting; **not a synthetic throw**).
- **Instead of an extinguisher:** a pot lid, baking soda on a grease fire, sand. **Never water
  on a grease or fat fire** (→ 10-04).
- **What you cannot improvise:** the IV fluids and surgery a large burn needs. That is why the
  barrier around the stove matters.

## When it runs out

- **Burn dressings go fast.** A significant burn needs dressing changes daily or more, for
  weeks. One serious burn can use up your whole dressing stock. Stock in bulk and list it on
  → 23-02.
- **Ration:** boil and reuse clean cloth for the outer absorbent layers; keep commercial
  non-stick dressings for direct contact with the burn, where sticking matters.
- **Substitute:** honey or clean petroleum jelly on cloth makes a non-stick layer; cling film is
  cheap and keeps for years.
- **The permanent substitute is prevention.** Barriers, hot-zone rules, wool, long tools, and
  never carrying hot liquid past a child. When a serious burn may not be survivable,
  prevention is the treatment plan.
- **Fire risk grows over time.** The more a household relies on flame for heat, cooking and
  light, the more burns it risks. Re-check the barriers and rules every time the setup changes:
  a new stove position, a new lamp, a child who just learned to climb.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** the highest-exposure phase: cooking over fire, heating one room with fire,
  perhaps lighting with flame, all in a small warm room. **Barriers and rules first, kit
  second.**
- **B (moving):** camp stoves, fires in unfamiliar places, cooking while exhausted, everyone in
  a small space. Cook away from where children are. Carry burn dressings and cling film; they
  weigh nothing.
- **C (resettled):** more fire, more hot work, further from help. Build the fire and cooking
  areas **with barriers designed in**, not added later.

pages.title: Infection, fever and antibiotics
pages.body:
# Infection, fever and antibiotics

**What this page is for.** Spotting infection early, recognising sepsis, knowing when a wound
needs a tetanus booster, and what a household can do when antibiotics are scarce or absent.
It is written for people with no doctor in the house.

> **SAFETY**
> - **Infection is the most likely way a survivable injury becomes a fatal one when there is
>   no clinic.** Before antibiotics, ordinary wounds routinely killed healthy adults.
> - **This page does not tell you which antibiotic to use or how much.** The right drug depends
>   on what the infection is, the germ, the person, their allergies and their other medicines.
>   **Getting it wrong causes harm and breeds resistance** (CDC, Antibiotic Use). This binder
>   never calculates or suggests a dose.
> - **Sepsis is a medical emergency.** Know its signs by heart (below).

## Do this now: is this wound infected?

1. **Look at the wound at every dressing change.** Healing wounds get *less* red, swollen and
   painful after day two or three.
2. **Worse instead of better, red streaks, pus or a foul smell:** it is infected. Open the
   dressing, flush it again with lots of clean water (→ 12-02), keep it open, keep it clean.
3. **Take the temperature and write it down with the time** (→ 25-05).
4. **Confusion, fast breathing, fast heartbeat, clammy skin, extreme pain:** this may be
   sepsis. If any care exists, go now. If not, → 12-16.
5. **Check the tetanus table below** for every wound.

## Do this now: preparation

- **Get everyone's tetanus vaccination up to date and write the dates on → 25-09.** Puncture
  wounds are common in a long emergency and there is no home treatment for tetanus (CDC, About
  Tetanus). **A booster six years old is not enough for an axe wound** (table below).
- **Write down every household member's drug allergies now** (→ 25-09). Any medicine you ever
  give will be checked against that list.
- **Build the hygiene system: it is the real defence** (→ 13-02). Soap, clean water,
  handwashing, clean dressings. Prevention is not the consolation prize here; it is the main
  strategy.
- **Learn the sepsis signs and post them** where everyone can see them.

> **Before the collapse:** talk to a clinician about emergency preparedness while you can. It is
> an ordinary conversation and clinicians have it regularly. Ask about tetanus status for
> everyone, about each person's long-term conditions (→ 12-11), and whether they would
> prescribe anything for your situation, with written instructions for when and how to use it.
> Write the answers here, with the clinician's name and the date:
>
> ____________________________________________________________________
>
> ____________________________________________________________________

## Recognising infection early

A healing wound gets **less** painful, **less** red and **less** swollen after the first day
or two. Anything moving the other way is a warning.

**Infection in the wound:**
- Redness, swelling, warmth and pain that **increase** after day 2 or 3
- Pus, cloudy fluid, or a foul smell
- **Red streaks spreading** from the wound toward the body
- The wound reopening, or a hard, tender, swollen lump (an **abscess**, a closed pocket of pus)

**Infection spreading through the body:**
- **Fever, chills, shaking**
- Feeling clearly, unmistakably unwell
- Loss of appetite, weakness

**Sepsis: a life-threatening emergency** (the body's overwhelming reaction to infection; CDC,
About Sepsis):
- **Confusion or disorientation**
- **Fast breathing; fast heartbeat**
- Extreme pain or discomfort
- Clammy or sweaty skin
- **Shortness of breath**

**Confusion in someone with an infection is the sign that changes everything.** When care
exists, that is an immediate trip to a hospital. Without it, → 12-16.

## Fever: a signal, not the disease

Fever is the body fighting infection. It is useful information, which is why the kit list has
several thermometers.
- **Track it.** Write temperatures down with the time (→ 25-05). A trend tells you far more
  than one reading.
- **Treating a fever** with over-the-counter medicine makes the person more comfortable and
  helps them drink and rest (→ 12-13). Adults follow the label. For children, use only the
  published tables printed on → 12-13 and the label.
- **Fever plus dehydration is the dangerous combination in small children** (→ 12-05).
- **Fever in a baby is different and more urgent** than fever in an adult. The American Academy
  of Pediatrics' fever guidance on → 12-13 says when it is an emergency.{{#if has.infant}} Your
  household has an infant: read that section before you need it.{{/if}}
- **Some conditions change the rules when illness hits.** Diabetes (→ 02-01, → 02-02, → 02-05,
  → 02-06), adrenal insufficiency (→ 02-20) and a weakened immune system (→ 02-18) each have
  their own sick-day steps. Read that condition's page as soon as fever starts.
{{#each members as m}}
  - {{m.label}}: conditions {{m.conditions}}
{{/each}}

## Tetanus: the after-a-wound booster rule

Tetanus (lockjaw) is caused by a germ found in soil and manure. There is no home treatment once
it starts. The whole defence is the vaccine, and after any wound the question is **whether a
booster is due now.** The CDC wound rule (CDC, Tetanus clinical guidance: wound management):

| Wound | Last dose **under 5 years** ago | **5 to 10 years** | **10 years or more**, or **fewer than 3 lifetime doses, or unknown** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Clean and minor** | nothing | nothing | **Td or Tdap booster** |
| **Everything else**: dirty, soil or manure, puncture, bite, burn, crush, frostbite, anything hours old | nothing | **Td or Tdap booster** | **Td or Tdap booster** |

- **Get the booster as soon as possible, ideally within 48 to 72 hours** of the wound. While
  pharmacies and urgent care work, a wound turns straight into that errand.
- **Fewer than 3 documented lifetime doses (or unknown) plus any wound that is not clean and
  minor calls for tetanus immune globulin (TIG) as well as the vaccine.** TIG is a clinic item.
  That makes it a wound to take toward care while any clinic functions.
- **Adults who cannot remember their last booster count as "unknown".**

## Prevention: the actual plan

Antibiotics may be unavailable, scarce, or wrong for the germ. **The household's infection
strategy is prevention, and it has to be taken seriously.**

1. **Handwashing** with soap and clean water, properly: before food, before wound care, after
   the toilet, after animals (CDC, About Hygiene). **This is the most powerful medical step a
   household with no clinic can take.** It needs soap (→ 13-09) and water (→ 03-01), so budget
   both.
2. **Clean water** for drinking, cooking and washing wounds (→ 03-04).
3. **Sanitation**: human waste handled properly, away from water and food (→ 13-01, → 13-07).
   Historically, sanitation failures kill more people than injuries do.
4. **Food safety**: cooking temperatures, no cross-contamination (→ 04-17, → 05-16). For
   households with food allergies, the same kitchen discipline protects them (→ 02-04).
5. **Wound care**: flushing, cleanliness, and **not closing dirty wounds** (→ 12-02, → 12-14).
6. **Not getting hurt**: sharp tools, safe technique, traction on ice.
7. **Keeping sick people apart** within the household where you can (→ 13-11).
8. **Tetanus vaccination**, current, for everyone (CDC).

## Antibiotics: the honest discussion

People ask about this constantly, so here is the straight answer.
- **Antibiotics are prescription medicines for good reasons.** The right drug depends on the
  diagnosis. The wrong one does not work, delays the right treatment, causes side effects and
  breeds resistance (CDC, Antibiotic Use).
- **Most infections a household sees do not need antibiotics at all**, and most coughs and
  colds are viral, where antibiotics do nothing (CDC). Using them wrongly wastes something you
  cannot replace.
- **The safest route to a contingency supply is a clinician**, with **written instructions**
  for when and how to use it, while clinics still exist.
- **Any antibiotic must be checked against the patient's allergies and other medicines** before
  use (→ 25-09).
- **Take an antibiotic exactly as the prescription or written plan directs**: the right drug,
  dose and length, not improvised and not stopped early because someone "feels better" on day
  two. Current guidance has moved from "always finish the bottle" to "exactly as prescribed":
  many modern courses are deliberately short. The point is that the plan decides, not the
  patient halfway through.

### Two trade-offs your household decides

**Antibiotics without a prescription.** Some households keep veterinary, aquarium or leftover
antibiotics as a last resort for a life-threatening infection when nothing else exists. Those
products are not checked for human use, their labels do not translate to people, and using
any antibiotic without a diagnosis risks the wrong drug, an allergic reaction, a delay and
resistance. Card DC-16 explains the risk and the options; children are excluded from every
option.
Your household's choice: {{choice DC-16}} (→ 30-17)

**Giving someone else's prescription.** A bottle prescribed for one person may be the only one
in reach for another. The risks are the wrong drug for this illness, a dose set for a different
body, allergies and interactions, and leaving the owner without their own medicine. Card DC-15
sets out the options.
Your household's choice: {{choice DC-15}} (→ 30-16)

Whatever you choose, a small antibiotic supply is irreplaceable and expires. If you have one,
it is for a genuinely life-threatening infection, not for a cold, a scrape or "just in case".

## What you can do without antibiotics

- **Flush and clean, thoroughly and repeatedly** (→ 12-02).
- **Opening and draining an abscess** is the historical standard treatment for a closed pocket
  of pus. **It is also a procedure** with real risks depending on where the abscess is. Read
  → 12-14 and a real medical reference in advance, and learn it on a course if you can.
- **Do not close dirty wounds** (→ 12-14). Trapping infection is worse than an open wound.
- **Warm compresses, raising the infected part, and rest.**
- **Honey and sugar dressings** both have traditional and evidence-supported use on suitable
  wounds. **Never honey for a baby under 12 months** (infant botulism), and neither replaces
  care.
- **Support the person:** fluids (→ 12-05), food, warmth, sleep. A well-fed, well-watered,
  rested person fights infection much better than a cold, dehydrated, exhausted one. That makes
  water, food and heat medical supplies too.
- **Recognise when it is beyond you** (→ 12-16), and if any medical care is within reach,
  **go**. "There is no hospital" is often less absolute than people assume.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Current tetanus vaccination for everyone** | No home treatment exists | Before the collapse |
| **A conversation with a clinician, now** | The safest route to any contingency plan | Write the answers in the box above |
| Thermometers ×2 to 3 plus spare batteries | Fever is the main whole-body signal | {{#if has.child}}Include one suited to children{{else}}One spare{{/if}} |
| **Soap in large quantity** | The most powerful medical supply you can own | Plus → 13-09 to make more |
| Water purification | Clean water underlies everything | → 03-04 |
| Nitrile gloves by the box | Stops germs passing either way | |
| Wound flushing supplies | Mechanical cleaning stands in for antibiotics | → 12-02 |
| Povidone-iodine, chlorhexidine | Cleaning skin | Bulk |
| Raw or medical-grade honey | Traditional dressing with real support | **Never under 12 months** |
| Written allergy and medicine list for everyone | Prevents a preventable disaster | → 25-09 |
| *Where There Is No Doctor* on paper | Real guidance on infection and abscesses | → 12-01 |
| Fever and symptom log sheets | Trends matter more than one reading | → 25-05 |

## Scavenge or substitute

- **Soap** can be made (→ 13-09) and is the thing most worth making.
- **Clean water** by boiling or filtering (→ 03-04).
- **Dressings** from boiled clean cloth (→ 12-02).
- **Antiseptics:** diluted bleach has documented uses for **surfaces** (→ 29-05); alcohol for
  skin and instruments. **Do not improvise antiseptic strengths for use inside wounds.**
  Flushing with clean water is safer and works.
- **What you cannot scavenge or improvise:** a diagnosis or a clinician. That is why prevention
  carries the weight here.

## When it runs out

- **Soap and clean water matter most** for infection control, more than any dressing. Budget
  them as medical supplies, not household ones (→ 23-02), and learn to make soap (→ 13-09).
- **A household's ability to treat serious infection is limited and shrinks over time.** That
  should change how you weigh risk for good. Tool safety (→ 16-02), fire safety (→ 12-03),
  sanitation (→ 13-01) and water treatment (→ 03-04) become medical priorities, not chores.
- **Substitute:** cleanliness, drainage, rest, fluids, food and time. That is what people had
  before antibiotics, and it worked more often than people assume, though not always. That is
  what → 12-16 is for.
- **The best long-term move is a person, not a supply.** Finding and supporting someone with
  real medical training in your community is worth more than any stockpile (→ 18-01, → 18-03).

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** clean water and soap are available, and pharmacies may work for a while.
  **Use the early period to settle tetanus status, talk to a clinician and build the hygiene
  system.** Early is when medical problems can still be solved.
- **B (moving):** hygiene gets worse exactly when wound risk rises. Carry soap and hand
  sanitiser, clean thoroughly at each stop with real water, and treat any wound from the road as
  dirty (→ 12-02).
- **C (resettled):** further from care, more injuries, and animals in the picture, which adds
  bites, scratches and diseases caught from animals (→ 05-04, → 05-15). **Where you put the
  latrine matters enormously at a new site** (→ 13-07): getting waste and water apart on day one
  prevents the illness that would otherwise arrive in month two.

pages.title: Common illness, diarrhoea and dehydration
pages.body:
# Common illness, diarrhoea and dehydration

**What this page is for.** Recognising dehydration, treating it with oral rehydration
solution, knowing when it is beyond home care, and the other common illnesses of a long
emergency.

> **SAFETY**
> - **Diarrhoeal illness is one of the most likely and most dangerous things that will happen
>   to a household in a long emergency.** Worse sanitation, doubtful water, food kept without
>   a fridge and less handwashing all arrive at once. **Worldwide, dehydration from diarrhoea is
>   a leading killer of small children**, and **oral rehydration therapy fixes the large
>   majority of it** (WHO, Diarrhoea). A baby or toddler can become dangerously dehydrated in
>   hours.
> - **Some conditions make it worse.** Vomiting and diarrhoea in someone with diabetes is a
>   sick-day emergency risk (CDC, Managing Sick Days; → 02-01, → 02-05). Kidney disease, adrenal
>   insufficiency and some heart and blood-pressure medicines also change the rules (→ 12-11).
> - **This page prints one recipe: the World Health Organization's home oral rehydration
>   solution.** Commercial packets, mixed as their label says, come first. The printed recipe is
>   the backstop, and its safety rules (level spoons, measured litre, taste check) are part of
>   the recipe.
> - **Nothing by mouth** to anyone unconscious, too drowsy to swallow safely, or unable to
>   swallow.

## Do this now: someone has diarrhoea or vomiting

1. **Start oral rehydration solution (ORS)** from a packet, mixed with safe water exactly as the
   label says. No packets? Use the printed recipe below.
2. **Small sips every few minutes, for hours.** Keep going through vomiting.
3. **Keep feeding** if they can eat. Babies keep nursing or taking formula.
4. **Check for dehydration signs** (below), and write down what goes in and comes out
   (→ 25-05).
5. **Anyone with diabetes or another condition on → 12-11:** open that condition's page now.
6. **Blood in the stool, a drowsy child, nothing staying down for hours:** that is the line for
   moving toward care (→ 12-16).
7. **Keep the sick person's waste, cloths and dishes apart** and wash hands every time
   (→ 13-11).

## Do this now: preparation

- **Buy commercial oral rehydration salts or children's electrolyte solution in quantity, now,
  and rotate it.** Packets are light, cheap and keep for years, and for a household with small
  children they may be the most life-saving item in this section. Stock far more than seems
  reasonable. Write your count on → 22-04.
- **Tape one used ORS packet label to this page.** The label carries its own mixing ratio.
- **Mark a 1-litre container** and keep it with level measuring spoons in the medical kit.
- **Fix the prevention chain first:** water treatment (→ 03-04), handwashing and soap
  (→ 13-02), and human waste handled well away from water and food (→ 13-01, → 13-07). **This
  is a sanitation problem before it is a medical one.**

> **Before the collapse:** for anyone with a long-term condition, ask their prescriber now for
> written sick-day instructions (what to do with each medicine during vomiting, diarrhoea or
> fever) and put them on that person's condition page and in the "my meds" table (→ 12-07).

## Why this is the illness to plan for

Diarrhoeal illness spreads when traces of stool reach the mouth: through dirty water, dirty
food and unwashed hands. Every one of those gets worse when the grid goes down: toilets that do
not flush (→ 13-01), untreated water (→ 03-04), food kept without a fridge (→ 04-17), less
washing because water is rationed{{#if has.toddler}}, and a toddler who puts everything in their
mouth{{/if}}.

**One outbreak can put the whole household down at once.** That is dangerous when someone still
has to haul water, keep the fire going and look after the sickest person.

## Recognising dehydration
