pages.body:
# Carbon monoxide, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** Every winter power outage kills families who brought a generator,
grill or stove inside to stay warm. They die from carbon monoxide. This page says what it is,
where it comes from, why your senses will not warn you, what an alarm does and does not do, and
what to do if you suspect it.

> **SAFETY — the floor that applies (→ 30-01).** **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any
> engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open window.** Carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no
> warning; alarms fail; there is no mitigation that works every time.

## What it is

**Carbon monoxide (CO)** is a gas made whenever a fuel burns: gasoline, diesel, kerosene,
propane, natural gas, wood, charcoal (→ 29-01). It has **no colour, no smell and no taste**
(CDC). When you breathe it, it takes the place of oxygen in your blood, so the body slowly
starves of oxygen. More than 400 Americans die each year from CO poisoning that is not caused
by fire, and more than 100,000 go to an emergency room (CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: Basics).

## Where it comes from in a house

Furnaces, water heaters, gas ranges, fireplaces and wood stoves, portable generators, charcoal
grills, camp stoves, kerosene and propane heaters, and cars. A properly vented appliance sends
its CO up a flue or chimney. **Trouble starts when the exhaust stays in the room**: a generator
or grill brought inside, a camp stove used indoors, a blocked chimney, or a vent buried by snow.

## Why you will not notice it

The first symptoms feel like flu: **headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting,
chest pain, confusion** (CDC). People feel tired, lie down, and do not wake up. **People who are
asleep or drunk can die from CO before they have any symptoms** (CDC). Infants, older adults, and
people with heart or lung disease or anaemia are hurt first and worst (CDC). A clue: several
people, or the pets, feel ill at the same time and feel better outdoors.

## What a CO alarm does and does not do

An alarm measures CO in **parts per million (ppm)**: how many CO molecules there are in every
million molecules of air. Alarms are designed to stay **silent at low levels** so they do not
go off constantly (CPSC, citing the UL 2034 alarm standard):

| CO level | What the alarm standard requires |
|---|---|
| Below 30 ppm | No alarm, even for 30 days |
| 70 ppm | Alarm within 1 to 4 hours |
| 150 ppm | Alarm within 10 to 50 minutes |
| 400 ppm | Alarm within 4 to 15 minutes |

For comparison, the outdoor air standard is 9 ppm averaged over 8 hours (EPA). So **a quiet
alarm is not proof the air is clean**, and a reading that sits above zero means something is
making CO. An alarm with a number display tells you more than one that only beeps.

- **Where:** on every level of the home and outside each sleeping area (CPSC). In a room where
  people sleep near a heater, at the height of sleeping heads, on the wall away from the heater,
  not in a dead-air corner, not next to an open window. The alarm's own manual gives the height.
- **Power:** battery or battery backup (CDC). A plug-in alarm with no battery does nothing in an
  outage.
- **Replace** the alarm at the end-of-life date printed on it, and at once if it chirps that it
  has reached end of life.
- **An alarm is a backup, not permission.** It can fail, have a dead battery, or be in the wrong
  room. It does not make a generator in the garage safe.

## If you suspect CO

1. **Get everyone outside into fresh air now**, pets included. Do not stop to open windows or
   look for the cause.
2. **Call 911** if it works. CO poisoning needs medical care; some effects show up later.
3. **Count heads.** Confusion is a symptom; someone may not follow you out.
4. **Nobody goes back in** until the source is found and shut off and the house is aired out.
5. **No 911:** fresh air is the treatment. Keep everyone outside, warm and resting, for hours,
   with someone watching anyone who was confused, vomiting or passed out. The full offline
   procedure is on → 08-02.

## Rules that follow from this

- Generators run **outdoors only, at least 20 feet from the house**, exhaust pointed away
  (CPSC, Portable Generator Safety). Never in a garage, even with the door open.
- **Never** burn charcoal indoors. **Never** heat the house with a gas oven or range. **Never**
  use a portable camp stove indoors (CDC).
- **After heavy snow**, clear the snow from furnace, water-heater and dryer vents.

## Decisions on this page

- An unvented heater running while people sleep: {{choice DC-01}} → 30-02
- A propane cylinder larger than 1 lb inside: {{choice DC-02}} → 30-03
- Open-flame cooking or candles indoors: {{choice DC-20}} → 30-21

## This household

CO alarms on hand: {{ gear.co_alarms }}.
{{#if has.unvented_heater}}You have a portable heater that vents into the room. Install and test
the alarms before it is lit the first time. → 08-01{{/if}}
{{#if has.generator}}You have a generator. Mark its outdoor spot now, at least 20 feet out. → 09-04{{/if}}

{{photo co-alarm-spot}}

pages.title: Electricity in the house: the panel, breakers, transfer switches and backfeeding

photo_slots.caption: Our electrical panel with the main breaker marked

pages.body:
# Electricity in the house, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** In an outage you may want to shut the power off, run a generator, or
power the furnace. Each of those touches the house wiring, where mistakes kill. This page names
the parts, explains backfeeding (the mistake that kills line workers), and says what a safe
generator connection looks like.

> **SAFETY — the floor that applies (→ 30-01).** **Never connect a generator to house wiring
> without a transfer switch, interlock, or a cord-and-plug conversion with the main breaker
> locked off. Never backfeed through an outlet.** Electrocutes line workers and neighbours;
> fire.

## The parts

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Service** | The wires from the utility pole or underground line to your meter. They carry power **both ways**: whatever is on your side can flow out to the street |
| **Meter** | Measures what you use. Belongs to the utility |
| **Panel** (breaker box) | The metal box where the incoming power is split into **circuits**, each feeding a group of outlets, lights or one big appliance |
| **Main breaker** | The large switch at the top of the panel. Off = the whole house is cut off from the utility line. Learn where it is now (FEMA, Utility Shut-off and Safety) |
| **Breaker** | One switch per circuit. It trips (shuts off) by itself if the circuit draws too much current, which protects the wiring from overheating |
| **GFCI** | An outlet or breaker that shuts off in a fraction of a second if current leaks to ground, for example through a person. Required near water: kitchen, bathroom, outdoors |
| **Transfer switch** | A switch installed by an electrician next to the panel. It connects the chosen circuits **either** to the utility **or** to a generator inlet, never both at once |
| **Interlock** | A metal plate fitted to the panel so the main breaker and a generator breaker cannot both be on at the same time. Same job as a transfer switch, done inside the panel |
| **Inlet** | A recessed, outdoor-rated plug on the house wall that a generator cord plugs into. Used with a transfer switch or interlock |

Most US household outlets are 120 volts; large appliances such as dryers, ranges, central air
and many well pumps run on 240 volts. Your generator or power station label says which it can
supply. → 29-02, → 28-03

{{figure fig-panel-transfer-switch-interlock}}

## Backfeeding: why it kills

**Backfeeding** means pushing power from a generator into the house wiring in a way that lets it
flow out through the service to the street. The usual way people do it is a homemade cord with a
plug on both ends, pushed into a wall outlet. The power goes backward through your meter, up to
the transformer, which raises it to the high voltage of the street line, and **can electrocute a utility worker
repairing a line they believe is dead**, or a neighbour near a downed wire. It can also start a
fire in your walls and destroy the generator when the grid comes back (OSHA, Portable Generator
Safety).

OSHA's rule: **never attach a generator directly to a building's electrical system unless it
has a properly installed transfer switch**, because of the electrocution risk to utility
workers. A cord with two plug ends is never used for anything.

## The safe ways to use a generator

1. **Extension cords to individual appliances.** Plug the appliance into a cord, the cord into
   the generator. Nothing touches the house wiring. This is always allowed.
2. **A transfer switch or interlock with an inlet**, installed by an electrician. You then power
   chosen circuits through the panel with no path to the street.
3. **A cord-and-plug conversion** of one hard-wired appliance (such as a furnace) so it can be
   unplugged from the house and plugged into a generator cord, with the main breaker locked off.
   Whether you do this yourself or have an electrician do it is a choice: {{choice DC-07}} → 30-08

Generators run outdoors, at least 20 feet from the house (CPSC). → 29-03

## Extension cords

- **Gauge** is the thickness of the wire inside. **A lower gauge number means a thicker wire**
  that carries more current without overheating: 12-gauge is thicker than 16-gauge.
- Use **heavy-duty, outdoor-rated, grounded (3-prong) cords** with no damage (OSHA, Portable
  Generator Safety). The cord's tag gives its rating; it must be at least the total of what is
  plugged into it.
- **Unroll the whole cord.** A coiled cord under load heats up.
- **Never chain cords together or plug power strips into each other.**
- Do not run a cord through a door or window that then has to stay open: exhaust gets in.

## Shutting the power off

To switch off the whole house, turn the **main breaker** off (FEMA, Utility Shut-off and
Safety). Stand on a dry surface. If there is water near the panel, or you smell burning, or see
scorching, stay away and get help. Any work inside the panel, any permanent wiring, any
connection to house circuits: a qualified electrician (OSHA, Electrical).

## This household

{{#if has.generator}}Your generator connects to the house by: {{ gear.house_connection }}.
{{#if has.house_connection}}Before you ever use it, check that the main breaker is off, or the
transfer switch is set to generator, every single time. → 09-04{{else}}Use extension cords to
individual appliances only. → 09-04{{/if}}{{else}}No generator is listed. Extension cords from a
power station follow the same cord rules. → 09-03{{/if}}

{{photo main-breaker}}

photo_slots.caption: Where our bleach and pool shock are kept, apart from fuel and acids

pages.body:
# Chlorine products, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** Chlorine kills germs in water and on surfaces, and a household may
have it in three or four forms. They differ in strength by hundreds of times, and two of them
together can make a poison gas. This page says what each one is, what "ppm" means, and how to use
the published tables without guessing.

> **SAFETY — the floors that apply (→ 30-01).**
> - **Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners.** Chlorine gas.
> - **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products.** Fixed in
>   every source.
>
> Water contaminated with fuel or toxic chemicals **cannot be made safe** by chlorine or boiling
> (CDC). Swallowed chlorine product: **Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222**, → 12-17.

## The forms you will meet

| Product | What it is | Strength | Keeps | Drinking water? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Household bleach** | Liquid **sodium hypochlorite** in water | Regular unscented bleach is 5 to 9% (CDC); the % is on the label | Loses strength over months; a year-old bottle is weaker than the tables assume. Mixed solutions lose strength in about a day | **Yes**, unscented only, using the table below |
| **Pool shock (cal-hypo)** | Granular **calcium hypochlorite** | Usually 65 to 73% | Years, sealed and dry | **Yes**, only if the label shows calcium hypochlorite with **no** algaecides, clarifiers or stabilisers, using EPA's two-step method (→ 03-04) |
| **Pool tablets (trichlor, dichlor)** | Slow-dissolving chlorine compounds for pools | Strong | Years, dry | **No** — pool use only. Never stored with cal-hypo: together they can catch fire or release chlorine gas |
| **Chlorine dioxide tablets** | A different chemical sold for drinking water | Per label | Per label | **Yes**, following the label's times exactly; the one chemical that handles *Cryptosporidium* (CDC) |

Scented, "splashless", gel or "multi-action" products are **not** used for water or disinfection:
they are weaker or carry additives.

## What ppm means

**ppm** is **parts per million**. In water, 1 ppm is 1 milligram of chlorine in each litre
(mg/L). It is how strengths are compared:

- **Drinking water** gets the lowest strength: just enough to leave a faint chlorine smell after
  30 minutes.
- **Surface disinfection** uses 1,000 to 5,000 ppm for the hardest jobs (CDC, norovirus
  cleanup).
- A **cal-hypo stock solution** made by EPA's method is about 500 ppm (500 mg/L), and is then
  diluted 1 part to 100 parts water for drinking. The stock itself is a poison: labelled, lidded
  and kept from children.

Surface strength in drinking water is poisoning. Drinking strength on a vomit spill does
nothing. **Never mix up the two tables. An unlabelled jug of mixed bleach is surface solution:
pour it out.**

## Drinking water with bleach (CDC; EPA)

Clear cloudy water first (let it settle, pour off, filter through cloth). Then:

| Water | 5 to 9% bleach | 1% bleach |
|---|---|---|
| 1 quart or litre | 2 drops | 10 drops |
| 1 gallon | 8 drops (0.5 mL) | 40 drops (2.5 mL) |
| 5 gallons | 40 drops (2.5 mL, 1/2 tsp) | 200 drops (12.5 mL) |

Stir, wait **at least 30 minutes**. **Double the dose** if the water is cloudy, coloured or very
cold. If the label gives drinking-water directions, follow the label. Full method: → 03-04.

## Surfaces and dishes (CDC)

| Job | Recipe, per gallon of room-temperature water, 5 to 9% bleach | Contact |
|---|---|---|
| Sanitising washed dishes | 1 tablespoon | At least 1 minute, then air dry |
| General surface disinfection | 1/3 cup (5 tablespoons) | At least 1 minute, visibly wet |
| Vomit or diarrhoea (norovirus) | 5 to 25 tablespoons; the strong end for the spill itself | At least 5 minutes |

Clean first, then disinfect: bleach does not work on visible dirt. Make it fresh every day.
Rinse food surfaces with safe water afterward. Ventilate. → 13-10, → 13-11

## Storing chlorine safely (CDC/ATSDR)

Cal-hypo is an **oxidiser**: it feeds a fire, releases chlorine gas when wet or heated, and its
dust burns skin and lungs. Keep it sealed and dry in its original container, off the floor,
away from fuel, acids, ammonia, trichlor or dichlor, and anything that gets wet. Add granules to
water, never water to granules. Bleach goes up high, away from ammonia cleaners and acids.

## Decisions on this page

- Drinking water from a pool, hot tub or untreated surface source: {{choice DC-13}} → 30-14
- Chlorinating beyond label strength when water is very dirty: {{choice DC-23}} → 30-24

{{#if has.pool}}You have a pool: its chemicals belong on this page's storage rules. → 03-03, → 03-08{{/if}}

{{photo chlorine-store}}

pages.title: Water words: boil, filter, micron, germs, turbidity, potable
pages.body:
# Water words, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** Water treatment advice uses a handful of words that sound alike but
mean different jobs. Mixing them up is how people drink water they thought was safe. This page
defines them.

> **SAFETY.** **Clear is not clean.** Water can look perfect and carry enough germs to cause
> days of diarrhoea, which in a small child, an elder or someone with diabetes is a medical
> emergency. And **no boiling, filtering or chlorine makes water safe if it may contain fuel,
> toxic chemicals or radioactive material** (CDC). Find another source.

## Three different jobs

| Job | What it does | How |
|---|---|---|
| **Clarifying** | Removes dirt and particles so the water is clear | Settle and pour off; strain through cloth or a coffee filter |
| **Disinfecting** | Kills or removes germs | Boiling, chlorine (→ 29-05), a fine enough filter plus chlorine, UV |
| **Distilling** | Removes salts and many chemicals by boiling water and collecting the steam | A still (→ 03-03). Needed for salt water and pool water with salts |

Boiling and chlorine disinfect. **They do not remove salt or chemicals.** A filter removes some
germs but, on its own, not all of them.

## The words

- **Potable** — safe to drink. Tap water from a working public system is potable; after a main
  break or a boil-water notice it is not, until the utility says so.
- **Boil** — a **rolling boil**: big bubbles that keep rolling when stirred, not the first small
  bubbles. Hold it **1 minute**; above 5,000 ft (EPA) or 6,500 ft (CDC) hold it **3 minutes**.
  Boiling is the most reliable way to kill germs (CDC).
  {{#if is.high_altitude}}Your home is above 5,000 ft: boil 3 minutes.{{/if}}
- **Germs** come in three kinds that behave differently:
  - **Bacteria** — single cells, such as *E. coli*. Killed by boiling and chlorine; removed by a
    filter of 0.3 micron or finer.
  - **Parasites** (protozoa), such as *Giardia* and *Cryptosporidium*. Larger. Killed by
    boiling; removed by a filter of 1 micron or finer. **Chlorine works poorly on them, and
    iodine does not kill *Cryptosporidium*** (CDC).
  - **Viruses** — far smaller than either. Killed by boiling and chlorine. **No common portable
    filter removes viruses**, so filtered water still needs chlorine or boiling (CDC).
- **Micron** — one millionth of a metre. A filter's **absolute** pore size is the largest gap it
  lets through; a "nominal" size is an average and promises less. Read which one the package
  states (→ 28-06).
- **Turbidity** — cloudiness. Cloudy water shields germs from chlorine and UV and uses up the
  chlorine, so it is cleared first and dosed double (CDC; → 29-05).
- **Residual** — the chlorine left over after it has done its work. A faint smell after 30
  minutes means some remains; no smell means the dose was used up, so treat again.
- **UV** — ultraviolet light from a pen-style device or the sun. Works on small amounts of clear
  water only. Sunlight method: clear plastic bottles of 2 litres or less, 6 hours in full sun or
  2 days if cloudy (CDC) (→ 03-04).
- **Contaminated vs. dirty** — dirty water has mud and germs and can be treated. Contaminated
  water has fuel, chemicals, sewage overflow or floodwater from industrial areas; treat it as
  unusable unless distilled, and even then not if fuel or solvents are the problem.

{{figure fig-micron-scale-germs}}

## Stored water

Store water in clean, food-grade containers, sealed, cool and dark, and replace stored tap water
every 6 months (CDC, Creating and Storing an Emergency Water Supply). → 03-02

## Wells and testing

A private well is not tested by anyone but you. Test it for bacteria at least once a year and
after a flood (CDC, Guidelines for Testing Well Water).
{{#if has.well}}Your home has a well: → 03-07 and → 03-10.{{/if}}

## Decisions on this page

- Drinking water from a pool, hot tub or untreated surface source: {{choice DC-13}} → 30-14

pages.title: Refrigerated medicines: the cold chain without power

photo_slots.caption: Our cooler or medical fridge, with the thermometer inside

pages.body:
# Refrigerated medicines, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** Some medicines, insulin above all, lose strength if they get too warm
and are ruined if they freeze. When the power goes, the kitchen fridge stops protecting them.
This page explains the "cold chain", how to read a storage label, and the order of things to try
when there is no working fridge. It gives no doses.

> **SAFETY — the floor that applies (→ 30-01).** **A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is
> discarded.** Loss of potency with no way to tell; the published guidance is unanimous.
>
> **No derived dosing.** Never change a dose because a medicine got warm. Your prescriber's plan
> and the condition page govern (→ 02-01, → 02-03).

## What "cold chain" means

The **cold chain** is the unbroken run of correct temperatures from the factory to the moment of
use. Every link counts: pharmacy, car, home fridge, cooler, pocket. A break is called an
**excursion**. **Heat is a slope**: the warmer and longer, the more strength is lost, usually
without any visible change. **Freezing is a cliff**: one freeze can ruin the medicine.

## Reading a storage label

The box and the package insert say how to store the product. The words mean:

| Label says | Means |
|---|---|
| "Store refrigerated, 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C)" | Fridge temperature, never the freezer, never against the cooling plate |
| "Do not freeze" / "Discard if frozen" | One freeze ends it, even if it thaws and looks normal |
| "Store at room temperature, 68°F to 77°F (20°C to 25°C); excursions permitted 59°F to 86°F (15°C to 30°C)" | The usual range, and the short swings the maker tested and allows |
| "Once opened (in use), may be kept at room temperature up to N days" | A countdown starts when the vial or pen is first used or taken out of the fridge. Write the date on it |
| "Protect from light" | Keep it in its box |
| "Inspect before use; do not use if cloudy, discoloured or contains particles" | The look-test the maker allows. A normal look does not prove full strength |

Two examples, as published:
- **Insulin:** unopened, in the fridge at 36°F to 46°F. In an emergency, insulin can be kept
  unrefrigerated at 59°F to 86°F for up to 28 days (FDA, Insulin Storage in an Emergency;
  American Diabetes Association). Never frozen. Each product's own label gives its in-use days.
- **Epinephrine auto-injector:** room temperature, 68°F to 77°F, with excursions to 59°F to 86°F
  allowed; **do not refrigerate**; protect from freezing and light; replace if the liquid is
  discoloured or has particles (FDA, EpiPen prescribing information).

Expiry dates and lot numbers: → 29-14.

## The fridge-without-power ladder

Try these in order. **At every step, a thermometer decides, not a guess.** A min/max thermometer
(it records the highest and lowest temperature since you last reset it) in each place medicine is
kept, read and written down morning and evening.

1. **A powered fridge kept running.** A small 12-volt medical or travel fridge on a power station
   or generator-charged battery is the most reliable cold chain (→ 09-10, → 29-02). Some go cold
   enough to freeze: set it and check it with the thermometer, not the display.
2. **A cooler with ice or cold packs**, with a towel or box between the ice and the medicine so
   it **cannot freeze**. Keep it shut; add ice before it is gone.
3. **The coolest stable place in the house**: a basement, an interior closet, a cooler set on a
   concrete floor. More stable than living space, but measure it.
4. **An evaporative cooling pouch or clay-pot cooler** for warm weather: water evaporating from
   its surface cools what is inside below the air temperature, but not to fridge cold. The
   pouch maker's instructions set how to soak it and how long it lasts (→ 12-21).
5. **Winter cold, carefully.** An unheated room or porch may sit at fridge temperature, but it
   swings below freezing. Only inside an insulated cooler as a buffer, with the min/max
   thermometer, never below 36°F.

## Decisions on this page

- Using insulin or other refrigerated medicine after a heat excursion: {{choice DC-08}} → 30-09
- Using expired or heat-exposed epinephrine or other expired medicine: {{choice DC-04}} → 30-05

## This household

{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}Medicines in your profile, with whether each is marked refrigerated:

| Person | Medicine | Refrigerated |
|---|---|---|
{{#each meds as m}}| {{m.member}} | {{m.name}} | {{m.refrigerated}} |
{{/each}}

Put a thermometer with each refrigerated one today.{{else}}No refrigerated medicine is listed in
your profile. If that changes, add it in settings and regenerate.{{/if}}

{{photo med-cooler}}

pages.title: Canning words: acid, pH, pressure canner, headspace, the seal, botulism
pages.body:
# Canning words, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** Home canning keeps food for years without power, and done wrong it
makes a poison you cannot see, smell or taste. Every canning rule comes from a few words. This
page explains them so the tested recipes in the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning make sense.
It does not give process times: those come only from a tested recipe (→ 04-04, → 04-05).

> **SAFETY — the floor that applies (→ 30-01).** **Low-acid foods are pressure-canned to the
> published time and pressure, or not canned.** Botulism has no field treatment and the food
> looks and smells normal.

## Botulism in one paragraph

*Clostridium botulinum* is a germ that lives in soil and on vegetables as tough **spores** that
survive boiling. In a sealed jar with no air, little acid and room temperature, the spores wake
up and make **botulinum toxin**, one of the most poisonous substances known. It causes paralysis
that starts with the eyes, face and swallowing and can stop breathing. **The jar can look, smell
and taste normal** (USDA; CDC). Acid stops the spores growing; very high heat kills them; heat
also destroys the toxin. That is the whole logic of canning.

## The words

- **pH** — a scale of how acidic something is, from 0 to 14. **Lower is more acidic**; 7 is
  neutral (plain water). Lemon juice and vinegar are low; meat and most vegetables are near
  neutral.
- **High-acid food** — pH **4.6 or lower**: most fruit, pickles, jams, and tomatoes **with added
  lemon juice or citric acid**. Botulism spores cannot grow, so a **boiling-water canner** is
  enough (USDA, Principles of Home Canning).
- **Low-acid food** — pH **above 4.6**: vegetables, beans, meat, poultry, fish, soups, and plain
  tomatoes with nothing added. These **must** be processed in a **pressure canner** (USDA).
- **Boiling-water canner** (water bath) — a big pot with a rack; jars covered by boiling water.
  Water cannot get hotter than boiling: **212°F at sea level**, and lower the higher you live.
- **Pressure canner** — a heavy pot with a locking lid, a vent, and a **gauge**. Holding steam
  under pressure raises the temperature to **about 240°F to 250°F**, which kills botulism spores
  in the tested time (NCHFP, Using Pressure Canners). USDA processes for low-acid vegetables have
  used pressure only since 1943.
- **Pressure cooker vs. pressure canner** — a pressure cooker cooks dinner. **Many pressure
  cookers and electric multi-cookers are not tested for canning** and may not hold the
  temperature for long enough. Use equipment the maker states is for canning.
- **Dial gauge vs. weighted gauge** — a **dial gauge** shows pressure on a needle and must be
  tested yearly; one that reads more than 2 psi off is replaced. A **weighted gauge** rocks or
  jiggles at its set pressure and needs no testing (NCHFP).
- **psi** — pounds per square inch, the unit of pressure on the gauge.
- **Altitude adjustment** — because water boils cooler up high, recipes add time (water bath) or
  pressure (pressure canner) above 1,000 ft. **The recipe's altitude table governs.**
  {{#if is.high_altitude}}Your home is above 5,000 ft: every recipe needs its altitude row.{{else}}Your home elevation is about {{ region.home.elevation_ft }} ft; find that row in every recipe.{{/if}}
- **Venting** — letting steam pour out of a pressure canner for the time the recipe says before
  closing the vent, to push out the air. Trapped air means a lower temperature.
- **Headspace** — the empty space between the food and the top of the jar, set by the recipe.
  Too little and food bubbles out and the lid fails; too much and air stays in.
- **Hot pack / raw pack** — filling jars with hot, cooked food or with raw food. The recipe's
  time is tested for one or the other, not both.
- **The seal** — as the jar cools, a vacuum pulls the lid down. A sealed lid is concave and does
  not flex or pop when pressed in the centre. **Unsealed after 24 hours:** refrigerate and eat, or
  reprocess with a new lid.
- **Tested recipe** — a recipe whose time, pressure, jar size and pack were measured in a
  laboratory. USDA and the National Center for Home Food Preservation publish them. **A family
  recipe card is not a tested recipe.**

{{figure fig-jar-headspace-and-seal}}

## Before eating home-canned low-acid food

CDC's backstop: boil it hard in an open pan **10 minutes, plus 1 minute for every 1,000 ft of
elevation**, liquid included, before eating (CDC, Botulism Prevention). This destroys the toxin.
It does not rescue a jar that is **bulging, leaking, spurting, mouldy or foul-smelling**: those
are thrown out unopened, where children and animals cannot reach them.

## Decisions on this page

- Eating food past its date, from dented cans or a failed freezer: {{choice DC-14}} → 30-15
  (Bulging, leaking or spurting cans are not a choice: discard.)

{{#if has.pressure_canner}}You have a pressure canner: check what kind of gauge it has.{{/if}}

pages.title: Radios: FRS, GMRS, CB, MURS, ham and NOAA Weather Radio
pages.body:
# Radios, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** When phones are down, radios are how a family stays in touch and how
you hear warnings. The radios on sale use different "services" with different rules, power and
reach. This page says what each one is, what range to honestly expect, what a repeater is, and
how NOAA Weather Radio works.

## Words first

- **Handheld** — a walkie-talkie. **Mobile** — mounted in a vehicle. **Base** — at home with an
  outside antenna.
- **Watts** — transmit power. More power helps a little; **antenna height helps far more**.
- **Line of sight** — the radios these services use travel roughly in straight lines. Hills,
  buildings and the curve of the earth block them. Two people on rooftops talk much farther than
  two people in basements.
- **Repeater** — a radio on a tall tower or building that receives you on one frequency and
  re-transmits on another at once, so two handhelds that cannot reach each other can both reach
  it. GMRS repeaters listen 5 MHz above the frequency they transmit on (47 CFR Part 95).
- **"Privacy codes"** (CTCSS/DCS tones) only stop **your** radio from playing other people's
  traffic. **Everyone can still hear you.** Nothing on these radios is private.
- **Simplex** — radio to radio directly, no repeater.

{{figure fig-line-of-sight-and-repeater}}

## The services

| Service | Licence | Power (47 CFR Parts 95 and 97) | Honest everyday range | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **FRS** (Family Radio Service) | None | 2 W on channels 1–7 and 15–22; 0.5 W on 8–14; fixed antenna | A few hundred yards to about a mile in town | The yard, the block, a campsite |
| **GMRS** (General Mobile Radio Service) | Yes; **no exam**; one licence covers the family | Up to 5 W on 1–7, 50 W on 15–22; removable antennas; repeaters allowed | 1 to 5 miles handheld; more with a repeater or a roof antenna | Family coordination around a town |
| **MURS** | None | 2 W, 5 channels near 151–154 MHz; external antennas allowed | 1 to 3 miles | A quiet alternative to FRS |
| **CB** (Citizens Band) | None | 4 W AM, 12 W single-sideband; 40 channels near 27 MHz | 1 to 5 miles; occasionally very far | Road and traffic information from truckers |
| **Amateur ("ham")** | Yes; **exam** | Depends on licence class and band | Across town to across the world, depending on band and antenna | Real distance; organised emergency nets |
| **Scanner / receiver** | None to listen | — | — | Hearing what is going on without being heard |

FRS and GMRS share the same 22 channels, so FRS and GMRS radios can talk to each other on them.
The "35-mile" figure on a blister pack is a mountaintop-to-mountaintop number; expect the
everyday column. **Test your own:** one person walks or drives away calling every block until
contact is lost, and you write that distance down (→ 15-06).

> **Before the collapse:** transmitting on GMRS or amateur bands requires an FCC licence while
> the FCC operates; GMRS needs no exam, amateur radio does (47 CFR Parts 95 and 97). A licence
> you hold and a radio you have practised on now are worth far more than one you are guessing at
> later. Listening needs no licence. → 15-05

## NOAA Weather Radio

The National Weather Service runs a network of transmitters that broadcast forecasts and warnings
around the clock. It does not depend on the internet, cell towers or your house power, only on
the transmitter and your radio's batteries. **Every transmitter in the country uses one of seven
frequencies: 162.400, 162.425, 162.450, 162.475, 162.500, 162.525 and 162.550 MHz** (NWS). Any
radio that tunes those finds the local one by stepping through seven channels.

**SAME** (Specific Area Message Encoding) is a code for each county. A weather radio with SAME,
programmed with your county's code, stays silent until an alert for that county arrives, then
sounds an alarm. Program the counties around yours too: storms arrive from neighbouring counties
first. What the alerts mean: → 29-10.

Your home transmitters (from the region appendix):

| Call sign | Frequency (MHz) | SAME code |
|---|---|---|
{{#each region.home.nwr as t}}| {{t.call}} | {{t.freq}} | {{t.same}} |
{{/each}}

{{#if has.noaa_radio}}You have a weather radio: program the SAME code above and test it.{{else}}A weather radio with SAME and battery backup is one of the cheapest life-saving purchases there is. → 15-01{{/if}}
{{#if has.gmrs}} You have FRS or GMRS radios: agree a family channel and practise. → 15-03{{/if}}
{{#if has.ham}} Someone in the household is licensed or has a ham radio. → 15-05{{/if}}

pages.title: Weather alert words: watch, warning, advisory, wind chill, heat index
pages.body:
# Weather alert words, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** A weather alert is only useful if everyone in the house knows what
the words mean and what to do at once. This page explains the three alert levels, the two
"feels like" numbers, and the hazard ratings printed for your region.

## Watch, warning, advisory

| Word | What it means | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| **Watch** | Conditions are right for the hazard to develop. It has not happened yet. Watches cover large areas and last hours | Get ready. Charge things, check the plan, know where everyone is, shoes on |
| **Warning** | The hazard is happening, or is about to, where you are | **Act now.** For a tornado warning: to the shelter spot, immediately |
| **Advisory** | Less serious, but still a hazard that can hurt people who ignore it | Take care; change plans for travel or outdoor work |

**Tornado warning** means a tornado has been seen or shown by radar: the warning time is minutes
(NWS, Tornado Safety). A **severe thunderstorm warning** means damaging wind or large hail, and
tornadoes can form from these storms with little extra warning. → 17-02, → 17-06

Other alerts you will hear:
- **Flood or flash flood warning** — water is rising or about to. Never drive or walk into
  moving water: 6 inches can knock an adult down and 12 inches can carry away most cars (NWS,
  Turn Around Don't Drown). → 17-03
- **Red flag warning** — warm, dry, windy weather in which any fire spreads fast. No outdoor
  burning (NWS Glossary). → 17-05
- **Winter storm, ice storm, blizzard warning** — travel becomes dangerous and power loss is
  likely. → 17-01
- **Extreme cold warning** and **extreme heat warning** — dangerous cold or heat. Older radios
  and pages may say "wind chill warning" or "excessive heat warning"; treat them the same.

Each NWS office sets its own trigger numbers for its area, so the same word can start at a
different temperature in different states. Your office: {{ region.home.nws_office }}.

## The two "feels like" numbers

**Wind chill** is how cold it feels on bare skin when wind is added to cold air, because wind
strips heat away faster. It is the number that predicts **frostbite**. The NWS wind chill chart
shows, for each air temperature and wind speed, whether bare skin freezes in 30, 10 or 5 minutes
(NWS, Wind Chill Chart). Use the chart, not a feeling. → 08-05

**Heat index** is how hot it feels when humidity is added to heat, because damp air stops sweat
from cooling you. The NWS categories (NWS, Heat Index):

| Heat index | Category | What can happen with long exposure or work |
|---|---|---|
| 80°F to 90°F | Caution | Tiredness |
| 90°F to 103°F | Extreme caution | Heat cramps and heat exhaustion possible |
| 103°F to 124°F | Danger | Cramps and exhaustion likely; heat stroke possible |
| 125°F and up | Extreme danger | Heat stroke imminent |

The published heat index assumes shade and a light wind. **Full sun can add up to 15°F** (NWS).
→ 17-04

{{figure fig-wind-chill-chart}}

{{figure fig-heat-index-chart}}

## The hazard ratings in your region pages

The region appendix rates each natural hazard for every county on a scale of **1 to 3**: 1 is
lower, 3 is higher, and each rating is printed with its words. The rating says how much a hazard
deserves planning where you live; it does not predict any single day. Your home county:

| Hazard | Rating | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
{{#each region.home.hazards as h}}| {{h.name}} | {{h.rating}} | {{h.rating_text}} |
{{/each}}

Pages for the hazards rated 2 or 3 are moved to the front of their sections in your binder.

## Hearing the alert

The alert only helps if it reaches you at 3 a.m. with the power and phones out: a NOAA Weather
Radio with SAME and fresh batteries (→ 29-09). When to leave home altogether is a decision your
household writes down in advance: {{choice DC-19}} → 30-20

photo_slots.caption: Where the caliber is stamped on each of our firearms

pages.body:
# Firearms basics, for someone who does not shoot

**What this page is for.** This page is for the person in the house who does not use guns but
may one day have to move one, store one, or keep children away from one. It covers the four
safety rules, how to tell in general terms whether a gun is loaded, how to match ammunition to a
gun, and safe storage. It does not teach shooting or tactics. The page is in every binder,
whether or not the household owns a firearm, because guns turn up in other people's homes.

> **SAFETY — the floor that applies (→ 30-01).** **Children do not have access to firearms,
> fuel, medications or chlorine products.** Fixed in every source.

## The four rules

These are the same in every safety course (NSSF, Firearm Safety). Every accident breaks at least
one of them.

1. **Treat every gun as if it is loaded.** Always, including one someone just told you is empty.
2. **Never point a gun at anything you are not willing to destroy.** Keep the muzzle (the open
   end of the barrel) pointed in a safe direction: usually at the floor, away from people, or at
   something that would stop a bullet.
3. **Keep your finger off the trigger** and outside the trigger guard, resting along the side of
   the gun, unless you are about to shoot.
4. **Know your target and what is beyond it.** Bullets go through walls, doors and people.

## Words you will hear

- **Muzzle** — the open end the bullet comes out of. **Barrel** — the tube.
- **Chamber** — where the cartridge sits, ready to fire, at the back of the barrel.
- **Action** — the moving parts that load, fire and unload. Opening the action shows the chamber.
- **Magazine** — a removable box (or a fixed tube) that holds cartridges and feeds them in.
  Removing the magazine does **not** empty the chamber.
- **Cylinder** — the turning drum on a revolver, with several chambers.
- **Safety** — a switch that blocks firing on some guns. It is a mechanical part and can fail.
  It never replaces the four rules.
- **Cartridge** (round) — one unit of ammunition. **Caliber** (or gauge, for shotguns) — the size
  and type of cartridge a gun is made for.

## Is it loaded? (general terms)

If you do not know how a particular gun opens, **do not experiment**. Leave it where it is,
pointed in a safe direction, keep others away, and get the person who knows it. If you must
check one you know how to open:

1. Muzzle in a safe direction, finger outside the trigger guard, the whole time.
2. **Remove the magazine first**, if it has a removable one. Then open the action.
3. **Look into the chamber, and feel it with a finger**: dim light fools eyes. On a revolver,
   open the cylinder and look at every chamber. On a gun with a tube magazine under the barrel,
   the tube may still hold cartridges.
4. If you closed it or put it down, it is **loaded again in your mind**: rule 1.

## Matching ammunition to the gun

Use only the ammunition the gun's maker designates. **The caliber is stamped on the barrel**, or
sometimes on the frame or receiver. The **headstamp** is the lettering on the flat base of each
cartridge. **The headstamp must match the marking on the gun** (SAAMI, Generally Accepted
Firearms and Ammunition Interchangeability). Some cartridges, such as rimfire and some military
rounds, have no caliber on the headstamp: then the original box must say, and if it does not,
the ammunition is not used until a knowledgeable person identifies it. **A cartridge that fits
is not proof it is safe**: the wrong one can burst the gun. SAAMI lists a few accepted
alternatives (for example, a gun marked 357 Magnum may fire 38 Special, not the reverse); the
gun's manual is the authority.

{{figure fig-barrel-marking-and-headstamp}}

## Safe storage

- The safest storage is **unloaded, locked, with ammunition locked separately** (American Academy
  of Pediatrics, Guns in the Home). Locks include cable locks through the action, lock boxes and
  gun safes (CPSC; NSSF Project ChildSafe). Keys and combinations are kept from children.
- **Teach children:** if you see a gun, do not touch it, leave the area, and tell an adult
  (AAP). Ask about guns at homes where children visit.
- **Ammunition:** in its original box, cool and dry, away from fuel and pool chemicals; avoid
  temperatures over 150°F (SAAMI).
- **Lead:** handling ammunition and cleaning guns leaves lead on the hands. Wash hands before
  eating or touching children; no cleaning on the kitchen table (CDC, Childhood Lead Poisoning
  Prevention). → 14-05

## Decisions on this page

- Firing on your own property for practice: {{choice DC-11}} → 30-12

## This household

{{#if has.firearms}}Your profile says there are firearms in the home. {{#if has.safe}}They have
a safe: write who holds the key or combination on → 14-14.{{else}}No safe is listed: a lock for
each firearm is the first purchase. → 14-14{{/if}}{{else}}No firearms are listed in your profile.
This page still applies at other people's homes.{{/if}}
{{#if has.child}} There are children in the house: storage rules above are not optional. → 20-02{{/if}}

{{photo barrel-marking}}

photo_slots.caption: Where our extinguishers hang, and the class on each label

pages.body:
# Fire extinguishers, fire blankets and alarms, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** In an outage, a household burns more things indoors (heaters, lamps,
candles, stoves) and the fire department may not come. This page explains the alarm that wakes
you, the extinguisher that stops a small fire, the blanket that smothers one, and the moment to
stop fighting and leave.

> **SAFETY.** **People first, then the fire.** A home fire can fill a house with smoke very
> fast. If the fire is bigger than a wastebasket, spreading, or between you and the exit, **get
> everyone out, stay out, and call 911 from outside** (USFA, Choosing and Using Fire
> Extinguishers). Young children and older adults should not use extinguishers (USFA).

## Smoke alarms

- **Where:** inside each bedroom, outside each sleeping area, and on every level including the
  basement (USFA, Smoke Alarms).
- **Test monthly** with the test button. Replace 9-volt batteries yearly; hard-wired alarms need
  their backup battery replaced yearly. **Replace the whole alarm 10 years from the manufacture
  date** printed on it (USFA).
- **Two kinds of sensor:** ionization (quicker to flaming fires) and photoelectric (quicker to
  smouldering fires). Because you cannot predict the fire, have both kinds or dual-sensor alarms
  (USFA).
- **Smoke alarms do not detect carbon monoxide.** A combination alarm does both; otherwise you
  need separate CO alarms. → 29-03

## Fire classes

An extinguisher's label shows the letters of the fires it is for (USFA):

| Class | Fire in | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Ordinary materials | Wood, paper, cloth, bedding |
| **B** | Flammable liquids | Gasoline, oil, grease, oil-based paint |
| **C** | Electrical equipment that is plugged in | Appliances, tools, power strips |
| **D** | Burning metals | Workshop and industrial metals |
| **K** | Cooking oils and fats in cooking appliances | Deep fryers |

A household **"ABC"** extinguisher covers the first three. The numbers before the letters rate
its size: on "1A:10B:C", the 1A matches 1.25 gallons of water on a class A fire and the 10B
covers a liquid fire of about 10 square feet (USFA). A bigger number is a bigger fire.

## Using an extinguisher: PASS

Use it **only if** everyone else is out or leaving, 911 has been called, the fire is small and
not spreading, you are not breathing smoke, and **your back is to a clear exit** (USFA). Then:

1. **Pull** the pin, nozzle pointing away from you.
2. **Aim** low, at the base of the fire, not the flames.
3. **Squeeze** the lever slowly and evenly.
4. **Sweep** side to side across the base until it is out.

Small extinguishers empty in seconds. If it is not out when the extinguisher is empty, leave.
Watch the spot afterwards: fires can re-light. Check that the gauge needle is in the green; some types need shaking monthly and pressure testing every few years (USFA).

{{figure fig-extinguisher-pass}}

## Fire blankets

A fire blanket is a sheet of fire-resistant fabric in a quick-pull pouch. It smothers a small
fire by cutting off air: laid over a burning pan (heat off, leave it covered until cold), or
wrapped around a person whose clothes are burning after they **stop, drop and roll**. Read its
pouch now, before you need it. **Never throw water on burning fat or oil.** Put a lid or the
blanket on it and turn off the heat. A wool blanket can stand in; synthetic blankets melt. → 12-03

## When to leave instead

- The fire is spreading, or bigger than you can cover with one extinguisher.
- Smoke is filling the room, or you cannot see the exit.
- It is a **lithium battery** fire (power station, e-bike, tool pack): it burns fiercely, makes
  toxic smoke and can re-light. Get out and call for help (NFPA, Lithium-Ion Batteries). → 29-02
- Fuel is involved and the fire is near more fuel. → 29-01

**Plan two ways out of every room** and a meeting place outside, and practise it. Close doors
behind you: a closed door slows fire and smoke.

## In an outage

Flashlights, not candles (USFA, Candle Fire Safety). Every heater gets 3 feet of clear space
around it (NFPA, Heating Fire Safety). Open flame indoors is a decision your household makes:
{{choice DC-20}} → 30-21

## This household

Smoke alarms: {{ gear.smoke_alarms }}. Extinguishers: {{ gear.extinguishers }}.
Hang an extinguisher near each room with a heat source, by the exit, not beside the stove or
heater, so you never reach through the fire to get it.

{{photo extinguisher-spots}}

pages.title: Measuring things without instruments: volume, weight, temperature, distance, time
pages.body:
# Measuring without instruments, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** Many survival jobs depend on a measurement: how much water is left,
how much bleach goes in, whether the freezer is still cold, how far the next town is. When the
scale's battery is dead and the phone is off, you can still measure, by **calibrating** ordinary
things against something whose size you know. Do the calibrating now, while you still have
instruments, and write the results on this page. Unit conversions are on → 25-02.

> **Where a number keeps someone safe** (a bleach dose, a cooking temperature, a canning time),
> measure it properly or use the published method that needs no instrument: a rolling boil
> (→ 03-04), drops from a dropper (→ 29-05), a tested recipe (→ 29-08). Do not estimate those.

## The idea: one known thing

Every method below works the same way. You find **one thing whose size is known**, compare the
unknown thing to it, and count. Then you write the answer down so nobody has to do it twice.

## Volume

- **Mark a bucket.** Pour in a known measure (a 1-gallon jug, a 1-litre bottle) one at a time
  and draw a line at each level with a marker. That bucket now measures water, feed and fuel.
- **Labels carry volumes:** water jugs, milk jugs, soda bottles, paint cans, the water heater's
  data plate ({{ dwelling.water_heater_gallons }} gal for yours).
- **A box of known size:** volume = length × width × height. One cubic foot holds about 7.5
  gallons (→ 25-02).
- **Firewood:** a cord is a stack 4 ft high, 4 ft deep and 8 ft long, 128 cubic feet
  (University of Missouri Extension, Wood Fuel for Heating). A tape measure is the scale.
- **Small amounts:** a medicine dropper or syringe from a first-aid kit is your most accurate
  small measure. Kitchen spoons vary; check one against the dropper's marks.

## Weight

- **Water is the reference weight:** a gallon of water weighs about 8.34 lb (→ 25-02). Two
  full gallon jugs are close to 17 lb.
- **A balance:** a board over a round log or pipe, the unknown on one end, jugs of water on the
  other, slid until it balances. Count the jugs.
- **A bathroom scale for heavy things:** weigh yourself holding it, then without it, and
  subtract.
- **Count what is packed:** cans and bags carry their weight on the label; a pantry can be
  weighed by counting labels.

## Temperature

- **Check a thermometer** in a glass packed with ice and a little water, stirred: it should read
  32°F. In boiling water it reads 212°F at sea level, less the higher you live.
- **The fridge and freezer:** a refrigerator should be at 40°F or below and a freezer at 0°F or
  below. With the door shut, a fridge keeps food safe about 4 hours without power and a full
  freezer about 48 hours (FoodSafety.gov, Food Safety During a Power Outage). Ice crystals still
  in frozen food are a useful sign; a cheap appliance thermometer is the real answer.
- **Hand feel is not a thermometer.** Cooked meat is safe at the temperature on the published
  chart, not by colour (FoodSafety.gov, Safe Minimum Internal Temperatures). Keep one probe
  thermometer with spare batteries, and a min/max thermometer for medicine (→ 29-07).

## Distance

- **Your pace.** Walk a measured 100 feet (along a tape, or a known length such as a lot line
  from your deed) and count your steps. Do it on rough ground and with a pack too. Write it down:
  _____ steps per 100 ft.
- **Time it.** Walk for 15 minutes on a road whose length you know and work out your own walking
  speed, then your speed carrying a load and with children. Write both down. → 24-04
- **Maps** have a scale bar: mark its length on a strip of paper and step it along the route.
- **Vehicles:** the odometer, while the car still runs.

## Time

- **A wind-up or battery wall clock** outlasts phones. Keep one, with batteries.
- **Count seconds** ("one-one-thousand, two-one-thousand") against a clock now, until your count
  matches; then you can time a minute without one.
- **Measure what burns:** light a candle or an oil lamp with a full tank and note how many hours
  it lasts. That tells you hours of light per candle or per fill.
- **The sun** is highest at local noon, when shadows are shortest. A stick in the ground makes a
  rough clock.

## Your calibrations (fill in once, in pen)

| Thing | My number |
|---|---|
| Steps per 100 ft, flat / rough / loaded | _____ / _____ / _____ |
| Walking speed, alone / with children | _____ / _____ |
| Marked bucket: lines at | _____ |
| Hours per candle / per lamp fill | _____ / _____ |
| Drops per mL from our dropper | _____ |
| Wood burned per day in a blackout weekend | _____ |

pages.title: Reading a label: data plates, fuel cans, cylinders, medicines, dates and lot numbers

photo_slots.caption: The data plates of our generator, power station and heaters

pages.body:
# Reading a label, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** Almost every limit that keeps you safe is printed on the thing
itself: how much power an appliance draws, what fuel a can held, when a cylinder must be
retired, how a medicine is stored, when food stops being good. This page shows where to look
and what the abbreviations mean. Photograph your own labels into the app now: labels fade, peel
and get lost. → 28-07

## Appliance and gear data plates

A **data plate** (or rating label) is the sticker or metal plate on the back or bottom of an
appliance, generator, power station or heater.

| Mark | Means |
|---|---|
| **V** (volts) | The electrical "pressure" it needs or supplies: 120 V household, 12 V car-style |
| **A** (amps) | The current it draws or can supply |
| **W** (watts) | Power while running. Watts = volts × amps. "Rated" or "running" watts is what it does all day; "surge", "peak" or "starting" watts is a short burst for motors starting |
| **Wh / kWh** | Stored or used energy (power stations, batteries) |
| **Ah** | Battery capacity; × volts = Wh |
| **Hz** | Mains frequency; US is 60 Hz |
| **Input / PV input** | What can charge it: a voltage range and a maximum current or watts. Stay inside it |
| **BTU/h** | Heat output (or gas burned) per hour on heaters and stoves. 1 kWh of electricity = 3,412 BTU (DOE, Fuel Properties) |
| **"For indoor use" / "outdoor use only"** | Where the maker allows it to run. An outdoor-only heater, stove or generator is never brought inside → 29-03 |
| **Model / serial number** | What to quote for a manual or part |

Meaning of the electrical words: → 29-02.

{{figure fig-data-plate-example}}

## Fuel cans

- **What was in it:** the printed or written label, not the colour (→ 29-01). Write the fuel and
  the fill date on every can.
- **Safety features by date:** gasoline cans have had child-resistant closures since 2009;
  kerosene and diesel containers since December 2022; and portable fuel containers made since
  July 2023 must carry a **flame mitigation device**, a mesh that stops flame jetting into the can
  (CPSC, Fuel Container Safety). Older cans lack them; they are worth replacing.

## Propane cylinders

The collar or foot ring of a cylinder is stamped. On a refillable 1-lb cylinder you will find the
**DOT specification**, **TW (tare weight)**, the weight of the empty cylinder, and the **date of
manufacture**; the cylinder has a 12-year requalification requirement (Flame King, 1-lb Refillable
LP Cylinder; YSN/Flame King, Training Program 1A). Filling by weight uses TW: the published fill
stops at TW plus 1.0 lb. A cylinder that hisses, is dented or rusted, or has a bent or stiff
valve is retired. Refilling 1-lb cylinders at home is a decision card: {{choice DC-03}} → 30-04

## Chlorine products

Look for the **% sodium hypochlorite** (bleach) or **% calcium hypochlorite** (pool shock), the
words unscented or regular, and any **drinking-water directions**; if the label gives them,
follow the label (CDC). Additives (scents, algaecides, clarifiers, stabilisers) rule a product
out for water. → 29-05

## Medicines

**Over-the-counter medicines** carry a **Drug Facts** box in the same order on every package
(FDA, OTC Drug Facts Label):

1. **Active ingredient** and the amount in each tablet or dose. Two products with the same active
   ingredient must not be taken together.
2. **Purpose** (for example, pain reliever, antihistamine).
3. **Uses**.
4. **Warnings**: who should not take it, when to stop, when to ask a doctor.
5. **Directions**: the dose by age, as published. **Follow it as printed; never work out a
   dose of your own.**
6. **Other information**: how to store it.
7. **Inactive ingredients**: what matters for allergies.

**Prescription labels** show the patient's name, the drug and strength, directions, the pharmacy,
the prescription number and refills. The package insert gives storage (→ 29-07).

**Expiry date ("EXP")** is the date the maker guarantees full strength under the stated storage.
**Lot number ("LOT")** identifies the batch: recalls are announced by lot, so keep the box or
write the lot down. Using a medicine past its date is a decision card: {{choice DC-04}} → 30-05

## Food dates

USDA explains the phrases (FSIS, Food Product Dating). **"Best if used by"** is about flavour and
quality, not safety. **"Sell by"** tells the store how long to display it. **"Use by"** is the last
date recommended for peak quality. **"Freeze by"** says when to freeze it. Except for infant
formula, these dates are not required by federal law and are not safety dates. Cans may also
carry a packing code instead of a readable date. Spoilage signs and dented cans: {{choice DC-14}}
→ 30-15. **Bulging, leaking or spurting cans are thrown out, unopened.**

{{photo data-plates}}

pages.title: How this binder was made, and what to trust
pages.body:
# How this binder was made, and what to trust

**What this page is for.** Before you rely on a reference in an emergency, you should know who
wrote it, how it was checked, and where its limits are. This page explains how
{{ household.name }}'s binder was put together, what the stamp on every page means, and how to
change or rebuild it later.

## Built in layers

| Layer | What it is | Who wrote it |
|---|---|---|
| **Core** | Method and fact that are true everywhere: water, food, fire and fuel, heat, power, first aid, sanitation, tools, communications. Plus these explainers (Section 29) and the decision cards (Section 30) | Written once from a fact-checked family binder, with that family's details removed, then frozen. Every household gets the same text |
| **Region** | Climate, hazards, plants, trees, weather offices and radio codes for every state and DC (Section 32). Your home base is moved to the front; the rest stays one tap away, because you may have to cross the country | Built from public datasets, not from memory |
| **Household** | Your people, contacts, meeting places, destinations, house, gear and supply lists | Filled in by the AI from your answers in settings. Every number on these pages traces to something you typed or to a dataset |
| **Condition library** | Modules for common medical conditions (Section 02). The whole library is in every binder; the ones you ticked are moved to the front | Written once and frozen. No doses are worked out for anyone; published tables are printed as published |
| **Gear library** | How to read and run common classes of gear (Section 28) | Written once; your models are filled in from your answers |

Your copy was made at the **{{#if experience.new}}"new to all of this"{{/if}}{{#if experience.some}}"some experience"{{/if}}{{#if experience.experienced}}"experienced"{{/if}}**
level you chose: that sets whether these explainers sit at the front of each section or in the
back.

## "AI-reviewed, not human-verified": what the stamp means

Every page carries this stamp. It means exactly what it says. **No doctor, engineer,
electrician or other professional has checked your copy.** After your binder was generated, an
AI ran automatic review passes over it:

- every fill-in slot was checked against your answers;
- every page was compared with every other, so one rule, one number and one name are used
  throughout;
- every number on a page marked critical was traced back to a named source, your answers, or a
  dataset;
- the binder was scanned for anything left over from the family whose binder the core came from;
- the text was checked for plain language.

Anything the review could not fix is listed on the **review notes** page. **The known limit:**
if every public source is wrong in the same way, an AI review will not catch it. Where this
binder and a professional disagree, **the professional is right**. While normal services work,
use them.

## Sources, and why there are no links

There is no internet in the situation this binder is for, so it never prints a web address.
Each fact names its source by title, publisher and date in the sentence, preferring US federal
agencies (CDC, EPA, FDA, USDA, NWS, FEMA, CPSC, OSHA, FCC), then national societies and
manufacturers, then university Extension services. **Laws, licences and codes** appear only in
boxes marked **Before the collapse**: they are true while government works, and they never
decide a survival procedure.

## Decision cards and floors

Some choices have no single right answer: running a heater overnight, keeping fuel in the
garage, using an expired medicine. For each, a **decision card** (Section 30) explains the
hazard, why the maker or agency set its rule, how people actually get hurt, what makes it safer,
and the options. **Your household chooses**; your answer is printed wherever the subject comes
up, or "not decided yet". The choice, and the responsibility for it, are yours.

A few things are **floors**, not choices: where there is no mitigation and the failure is death
or permanent injury without warning, such as an engine running indoors or mixing bleach with
ammonia. They are stated as rules with the reason, the same words every time, and no options
box. → 30-01

## Small and Large

{{#if size.large}}**This is the Large copy.**{{else}}**This is the Small copy.**{{/if}}

- **Small** has every page, explainer, card, condition and gear module, the national region
  appendix and all plant plates. Each citation shows title, publisher and date. It carries only
  this kit's own text and public-domain material.
- **Large** is the same, plus the full text of every cited document bound behind the page that
  cites it, fetched for your household when you downloaded, and topographic maps for your home
  and route counties. Some publishers refuse automatic fetching: those are listed on the
  **sources not captured** page with the binder's own summary in their place, so you can save
  them yourself while the internet works.
- A Small copy can be upgraded to Large later from your saved profile file, without rewriting
  the pages.

## Changing it later

- **Your answers are never stored by us.** If you chose to save them, they are in a file called
  `profile.json` on your own device. Keep a copy somewhere safe.
- **To add a medical condition, a person, a pet or new gear:** open the settings page, load your
  `profile.json`, change the answer, and generate again. The whole condition library stays in the
  app, so a condition added later gets its full module. A condition that is not in the library
  has its own page: → 02-27.
- **To rebuild from scratch** (a new phone, a lost file): load `profile.json` and generate.
  Without the file, you answer the questions again.
- **Photos you add** to pages stay in your copy on your device and are never sent anywhere.

## This file is your private copy

{{#if size.large}}Your copy contains the full text of documents written by other people and
organisations, fetched for your personal use when you downloaded it. Those documents are
copyrighted by their publishers. **Giving this file to someone else copies their work without
permission and breaks copyright. Keep it within your household.**{{else}}Your Small copy carries
only this kit's own text and public-domain material, but it is still built from your household's
private answers. **Keep it within your household.**{{/if}} If a friend wants a binder, send them
to the settings page so they can make their own. → 00-09
