pages.title: DC-11. Firing weapons on your own property for practice, pests or zeroing

options.label: Never on our property
options.summary: No shots fired on or from the property for practice, pests or sighting in. Practice is dry (unloaded) at home; pests are trapped; live fire happens only at a proper range or open land with a real backstop elsewhere.

options.label: Only into a known backstop, nobody downrange
options.summary: Shots only into an earth bank or backstop that will stop that ammunition, never toward a house, road or path, never at a target above the horizon, never at night, nobody downrange, neighbours told beforehand.

pages.settings_summary: In a long emergency, ranges close, and households may want to practise, sight in a rifle or deal with pests at home. Every firearms safety rule says be sure of your target and what is beyond it: a bullet that misses or passes through keeps going, far past any yard or rural lot, and can ricochet off water, rock or frozen ground. In town, what is beyond is a neighbour's house. Shots also tell everyone nearby that the house is armed and occupied, and damage hearing. What helps most: no live fire at home, dry practice and traps instead (removes it); only into a solid earth backstop, never toward houses or roads, never at a target above the horizon, nobody downrange, neighbours told (reduces it a lot).
pages.body:
# DC-11. Firing weapons on your own property for practice, pests or zeroing

**What this page is for.** When ranges are closed and gunsmiths are gone, a household may want
to fire on its own land: to practise, to "zero" (sight in) a rifle, or to kill pests. This card
explains what is beyond the target, why every safety rule is built around it, and what the
household decides.

> **SAFETY.** Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products
> (floor, → 30-01). New to firearms? Read → 29-11 before this card.

## 1. The thing, in plain words

A **backstop** is whatever stops the bullet after it passes the target: a thick earth bank, a
hillside, a purpose-built berm. A fence, a wooden shed, a tree or a snowbank is not a backstop.
**Downrange** means the direction the gun points, all the way to where the bullet could land.
A **ricochet** is a bullet bouncing off a hard or flat surface (water, rock, frozen ground,
metal) in a direction nobody planned. **Zeroing** means adjusting a sight so the bullet hits
where you aim.

{{#if has.firearms}}Your household has firearms. Home setting: {{ home.setting }}.{{/if}}

## 2. The rule, and why it was set

- The universal firearms safety rules include **be sure of your target and what is beyond
  it** (NSSF, Firearm safety: rules for safe gun handling).
- Shooting ranges are built with berms and baffles and set distances from houses for this
  reason. Many towns ban discharge inside limits.

**Why:** a bullet does not stop because it missed. A bullet from an ordinary rifle or handgun
can carry far past any yard and many rural property lines, and it can pass through a target,
an animal or a wall (SAAMI, Small Arms Ammunition). The shooter rarely sees where it lands.

> **Before the collapse:** your town and state set rules on where firearms may be discharged.
> Look them up while they are enforced. The backstop physics below does not change with the
> law.

## 3. How it actually hurts people

- **A miss or a pass-through** travels into a neighbour's wall, a car on the road or someone
  walking a field you cannot see.
- **A shot at a target above the horizon** (a squirrel in a tree, a bird on a roof) has no
  backstop at all; the bullet comes down somewhere far away.
- **A ricochet** off a frozen yard, a pond or a rock goes sideways or back toward people.
- **Noise**: gunshots are loud enough to damage hearing permanently with even a few exposures
  (CDC/NIOSH, About Noise and Hearing Loss).
- **Signalling**: in a tense neighbourhood, a shot says "this house is armed and occupied". It
  can start fear, rumours, or a response you did not want.

## 4. What makes it safer

**Removes the risk**
- **No live fire at home.** Practise dry, with an unloaded gun and no ammunition in the room
  (→ 14-15). Trap pests instead (→ 05-15). Zero and train at a real range or on open land
  with a proper backstop, away from houses.

**Reduces it a lot**
- **A known, solid earth backstop** that will stop the ammunition you use, high enough that a
  miss still hits it.
- **Never toward a house, road, path or livestock**, whatever the backstop.
- **Never at a target above the horizon**, and never over water or frozen ground.
- **Nobody downrange.** Check before every string of shots.
- **Daylight only.**
- **Tell the neighbours beforehand** when and where you will shoot.

**Reduces it a little**
- Low-power, small-calibre ammunition for pests at short range.
- Hearing and eye protection for everyone nearby.
- Children kept well back and supervised by an adult who is not shooting.

## 5. The options

**`never`: Never on our property.**
You give up: practice, zeroing and pest control by firearm at home. You accept: less live-fire
practice and more reliance on traps and dry practice.

**`with-backstop-rule`: Only into a known backstop, nobody downrange, neighbours told.**
You give up: freedom to shoot where it is convenient. You accept: that the backstop and the
rules above are all that stand between a missed shot and a neighbour, and that every shot is
heard.

## 6. Our choice

{{card DC-11}}

pages.title: DC-12. Defensive use of force: our household rule

options.label: Write our own rule
options.summary: The adults read this page together and write the household's use-of-force rule in their own words on the worksheet, sign and date it, and rehearse it.

pages.settings_summary: This card has no multiple choice. Every household that keeps any means of defence, firearm or not, needs a rule written in calm advance about when force may be used against another person. Without courts or police, nobody else will draw that line. The traditional tests are: the threat is happening now; nothing less will stop it; the force matches the threat; and a calm person would see it the same way. Mistakes cannot be undone: a bullet passes through walls into neighbours' homes, people are shot by family members who misidentified them in the dark, and with no surgeon any wound may be fatal. The neighbourhood remembers. Read the page, then write the rule in your own words on the worksheet.
pages.body:
# DC-12. Defensive use of force: our household rule

**What this page is for.** This card is a worksheet, not a multiple choice. It gives the adults
the facts and the questions; they write the household's own rule, in their own words, now,
while they are calm. A rule written in advance is worth more than any judgement made at 3 a.m.

> **SAFETY.** Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products
> (floor, → 30-01). This page is not legal advice.

> **Before the collapse:** {{ home.state_name }} has its own self-defence laws, and they differ
> from state to state. Read them while they are available and enforced, and write the section
> numbers here: ______________. Nothing in this binder summarises them.

## 1. The thing, in plain words

**Use of force** is any physical action to stop another person: a shove, a locked door held
shut, pepper spray, a weapon. **Deadly force** is force likely to kill or cause serious injury,
which includes firing a gun at someone. **De-escalation** means calming or ending a
confrontation without force: a locked door, distance, light, a calm voice (→ 14-13).

## 2. The rule as lawful self-defence has always stated it, and why

Across traditions of lawful self-defence the test has four parts:
- **Imminence**: the threat is happening now, not feared, threatened or over.
- **Necessity**: nothing less would stop it (a door, a light, a warning, leaving).
- **Proportionality**: the force matches the threat. Deadly force answers only a threat of
  death or serious injury **to a person**.
- **Reasonableness**: a calm adult in the same place would have believed the same.

**Why these tests persist without anyone enforcing them:** a shot cannot be taken back, and
the people who live around you will still be there tomorrow.

## 3. How it actually hurts people

- **Misidentification.** A family member or neighbour coming in at night is shot because nobody
  identified them first.
- **Through the wall.** Bullets from ordinary rifles, shotguns and handguns can pass through
  interior and exterior walls into other rooms and other houses (NSSF: know what is beyond your
  target).
- **No surgeon.** With no hospital, a gunshot wound, to the other person or to you if it goes
  wrong, is likely fatal. Bleeding control buys time, not a cure (→ 12-02).
- **Over property.** A household that shoots someone over a fuel can or a generator becomes the
  household the neighbourhood fears and turns against (→ 18-01).
- **Children watching.** What children see at the door stays with them (CDC, Helping Children
  Cope During and After a Disaster; → 21-03).

## 4. What makes it safer

**Removes most confrontations**
- Locked, hardened doors and lights (→ 14-02). Not looking like the best-stocked house on the
  street (→ 14-03). Good relations with neighbours (→ 18-01).

**Reduces harm a lot**
- **Avoid, then de-escalate**: stay behind a locked door, use a light and a loud, calm voice,
  let a thief leave (→ 14-13).
- **Identify before anything else.** A light and a challenge word the family knows.
- **Know the safe directions** in your house: where a shot would go toward the fewest people.
- **Less-lethal tools** for lesser threats; pepper spray stops many people, though not all
  (National Institute of Justice, The Effectiveness and Safety of Pepper Spray).

**Reduces harm a little**
- Rehearse the rule out loud with every adult who may hold a weapon.
- A trauma kit and the training to use it, for anyone hurt (→ 12-02).

## 5. The worksheet: write our rule

Answer every line in your own words. Both or all adults agree, sign and date.

1. We use deadly force only when: _____________________________________________
   ______________________________________________________________________________
2. When someone takes or damages property (generator, fuel, food, car) but threatens no
   person, we: __________________________________________________________________
3. A person in the yard or on the road who is not threatening a person is: (challenged / lit /
   watched / left alone) ______________________________________________________
4. Inside the house, before anyone fires, we identify the person this way: _____________
   ______________________________________________________________________________
5. Our challenge word or phrase for family and trusted neighbours: _____________________
6. The adults who may use a firearm in defence: ______________________________________
7. The safe directions in our house (the way a shot would go toward the fewest people):
   ______________________________________________________________________________
8. What we try first, in order (lock, light, voice, leave, pepper spray, other):
   ______________________________________________________________________________
9. Afterwards: weapons secured, children kept away, first aid for anyone hurt (including the
   other person if safe), what we write down: _______________________________________
10. Anything else we agree: _________________________________________________________

Signed: ______________________ ______________________ Date: __________

## 6. Our choice

{{card DC-12}}

pages.title: DC-13. Drinking water from a pool, hot tub or untreated surface source

options.label: Distil before drinking
options.summary: Water from a pool, hot tub or untreated stream, pond or lake is drunk only after distilling (boil it and collect the steam). Undistilled, it is used for flushing, washing and cleaning only.

options.label: Fresh pools: filter and chlorinate
options.summary: A freshwater (not salt) pool known to hold no algaecide or other additive may be drunk after settling, filtering and disinfecting by the published method. Salt pools and hot tubs still need distilling; surface water still needs distilling.

options.label: Surface water through the treatment ladder
options.summary: Streams, ponds and lakes away from obvious fuel, chemical or farm runoff are drunk after the full ladder: settle, filter, then boil or disinfect by the published method. Pools follow the two options above.

pages.settings_summary: A swimming pool or a nearby stream can look like a large water supply. Germs in water (bacteria, viruses, parasites) are killed by boiling or by chlorine used as CDC and EPA describe. Chemicals are not. Pool water holds chlorine, stabilizer, often algaecide, and in a salt pool, salt that no boiling or filter removes. Hot tubs hold bromine and body oils. Streams and ponds can carry fuel, farm or industrial runoff. CDC says water that may contain fuel or toxic chemicals cannot be made safe by boiling or disinfecting. Only distillation (boil and catch the steam) removes salt and most chemicals, and it is slow and uses fuel. What helps most: use pool and hot-tub water for flushing and washing, saving stored water for drinking (removes most of it); distil what you drink from them (reduces it a lot).
pages.body:
# DC-13. Drinking water from a pool, hot tub or untreated surface source

**What this page is for.** When stored water runs low, a pool, hot tub or nearby stream can
look like the answer. This card separates the germ problem, which boiling and chlorine solve,
from the chemical problem, which they do not, and asks the household to decide which sources it
will drink and how.

> **SAFETY.** Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners
> (floor, → 30-01). **Salt water is never drunk unless distilled**: boiling, chlorine and
> ordinary filters leave the salt in, and salt water makes dehydration worse. Water that may
> hold fuel or toxic chemicals cannot be made safe by boiling or disinfecting (CDC).

## 1. The thing, in plain words

Read → 29-06 for the water words.
- **Pool water** has chlorine (or salt that a machine turns into chlorine), a stabilizer called
  cyanuric acid, acid or base to adjust pH, and often an **algaecide** (some contain copper).
- **Hot-tub water** is hot and full of skin oils, and usually treated with bromine.
- **Surface water** is any stream, pond, lake or ditch.
- **Boiling** and **disinfecting** (bleach, pool shock dissolved by the published method,
  → 29-05) kill germs. **Filtering** removes dirt, parasites and most bacteria, not viruses.
  **Distilling** means boiling water and collecting the steam, which leaves salt and most
  chemicals behind in the pot.

{{#if has.pool}}Your pool holds about {{ dwelling.pool_gallons }} gallons.{{#if has.saltwater_pool}} It is a salt pool: drinking it always needs distilling.{{/if}}{{/if}}

## 2. The rule, and why it was set

- CDC's emergency guidance: boil water, or disinfect it with unscented bleach at the published
  dose after letting cloudy water settle and filtering it; and **water contaminated with fuel or
  toxic chemicals will not be made safe by boiling or disinfection** (CDC, How to Make Water Safe
  in an Emergency; EPA, Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water).
- CDC treats pool and hot-tub water in an emergency as water for **washing and flushing, not
  drinking** (CDC, Guidelines for Personal Hygiene During an Emergency).
- Distillation removes germs, salts, heavy metals and most other chemicals (CDC; AWWA, distillation
  in an emergency).

**Why:** pool chemicals are made for swimming water, not for drinking water. Surface water's germs are well understood and handled by the
methods above; its chemicals depend on what lies upstream, which you usually cannot know.

## 3. How it actually hurts people

- **Germs from untreated surface water**: diarrhoea and vomiting from bacteria, viruses and
  parasites such as Giardia and Cryptosporidium. In a baby, an elder or someone with diabetes,
  diarrhoea quickly becomes dangerous dehydration (CDC Yellow Book, Travelers' Diarrhea; → 12-05).
- **Salt**: drinking salt-pool water pulls water out of the body; thirst gets worse, not better.
- **Chemicals**: copper algaecide, stabilizer, and fuel or farm chemicals in runoff are not removed
  by boiling or chlorine; some build up over weeks. A child, smaller and drinking more for its
  size, gets the larger share.
- **Cryptosporidium** resists ordinary chlorine; boiling or a fine filter is needed (CDC Yellow
  Book, Water Disinfection for Travelers).

## 4. What makes it safer

**Removes most of the risk**
- **Use pool and hot-tub water for flushing, washing and cleaning**, and keep stored, rain or snow
  water for drinking (→ 03-05). This alone can stretch drinking water a long way.
- **Distil** pool, hot-tub or suspect surface water before drinking (→ 03-03).

**Reduces it a lot**
- **Choose the cleanest source**: rain and snow first; flowing water upstream of roads, farms and
  buildings; never water with a fuel sheen or chemical smell.
- **The treatment ladder** for surface water: let it settle, pour off the clear part, filter
  through cloth then a 1-micron-or-finer filter, then **boil** (1 minute at a rolling boil, 3
  minutes above 6,500 feet, CDC) or **disinfect** by the published bleach dose and wait 30 minutes
  (CDC; → 03-04).
- For a freshwater pool: know exactly what has been added. No algaecide, no "multi-action"
  products.

**Reduces it a little**
- Activated carbon filters reduce some chemicals and taste.
- Test strips for chlorine and pH, if you have them (→ 03-07).

## 5. The options

**`distill-only`: Distil before drinking.**
You give up: easy volume; distilling is slow and burns fuel (→ 03-03). You accept: needing more
stored, rain and snow water.

**`filter-and-chlorinate`: Fresh pools: filter and chlorinate.**
You give up: certainty about what is in the water. You accept: drinking pool chemicals at low
levels for as long as the outage lasts. Salt pools, hot tubs and surface water are not covered.

**`drink-treated-surface-water`: Surface water through the treatment ladder.**
You give up: protection from chemicals upstream. You accept: that boiling or chlorine handles the
germs but not fuel or farm runoff, so source choice matters.

## 6. Our choice

{{card DC-13}}

pages.title: DC-14. Food past its date, dented or rusted cans, or food from a failed freezer

options.label: Follow the label and the published rules strictly
options.summary: Food past its date is discarded; dented, rusted or swollen cans are discarded; anything from the fridge or freezer above 40 °F for 2 hours or more is discarded, as USDA advises.

options.label: Inspect and eat, with the rules for each case
options.summary: Shelf-stable food past its quality date is eaten if the package is intact and it looks and smells normal; lightly dented cans with sound seams are eaten; thawed food still holding ice crystals is cooked or refrozen; the floor lines still apply.

pages.settings_summary: In a long emergency a household will have food past its printed date, dented or rusty cans, and fridges and freezers that have warmed. Most dates on food mark best quality, not safety; infant formula is the exception. Canned food stays safe for years if the can is sound and was not frozen or overheated. The dangers are a can whose seal has failed, which can carry botulism, a toxin that paralyses and looks, smells and tastes normal, and perishable food held warm, which grows bacteria that cause severe vomiting and diarrhoea. USDA says discard perishables above 40 °F for 2 hours. What helps most: rotate stock and check freezers with a thermometer (removes much of it); inspect every can and package, discard any bulging, leaking or spurting can (floor), and cook thoroughly (reduces it a lot).
pages.body:
# DC-14. Food past its date, dented or rusted cans, or food from a failed freezer

**What this page is for.** Throwing out food that might be fine is a real loss when no more is
coming. Eating food that is not fine can put a child or an elder in serious danger with no
hospital. This card sets out what the published rules say, which parts are about quality and
which about safety, and what the household decides.

> **SAFETY.** Low-acid foods are pressure-canned to the published time and pressure, or not
> canned (floor, → 30-01). **Any can or jar that is bulging, leaking, spurting liquid or foam
> when opened, or smells bad, is thrown away without tasting.** Never taste food to find out if
> it is safe.

## 1. The thing, in plain words

- **Date labels** ("best by", "use by", "sell by") are mostly set by the maker for best taste
  and texture, not safety. Infant formula is the exception: its use-by date matters
  (USDA FSIS, Food Product Dating; → 29-14).
- **Shelf-stable food** is food sealed so it keeps without a fridge: cans, jars, dry goods.
- **Perishable food** is meat, fish, eggs, dairy, cooked leftovers: food that needs the cold.
- **Botulism** is poisoning by a toxin that bacteria make in sealed, airless, low-acid food. It
  paralyses muscles, including the breathing muscles (→ 29-08).

## 2. The rule, and why it was set

- USDA: canned foods are safe indefinitely if not exposed to freezing or to temperatures above
  90 °F and the cans are in good condition; **discard cans that are dented, leaking, bulging or
  rusted** (USDA FSIS, Shelf-Stable Food Safety).
- In a power outage: a closed fridge keeps food safe about **4 hours**; a full freezer about
  **48 hours**, a half-full one about **24 hours**; **discard perishable food above 40 °F for 2
  hours or more**; and **never taste food to decide** (FoodSafety.gov, Food Safety During a Power
  Outage).
- CDC: throw out containers that are leaking, bulging or swollen, look damaged, cracked or
  abnormal, spurt when opened, or smell or look bad (CDC, Botulism Prevention).

**Why:** a sharp dent on a seam can break the seal invisibly and let bacteria in; deep rust can
eat through the metal. Between 40 and 140 °F bacteria multiply fast in perishable food, and some
make toxins that cooking does not destroy. The agencies draw simple lines because no one can see
or smell most of these dangers.

## 3. How it actually hurts people

- **Botulism from a failed can**: blurred or double vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech,
  difficulty swallowing, then weakness spreading down to the breathing muscles, hours to days
  after eating (CDC). Without a hospital and a breathing machine, it can kill.
- **Spoiled perishables**: vomiting and diarrhoea within hours. In a baby, an elder or someone
  with diabetes, the dehydration that follows is a medical emergency (→ 12-05).
- **Old but sealed dry goods**: usually just stale taste, rancid fat or lost vitamins. Rarely
  dangerous.

## 4. What makes it safer

**Removes much of the risk**
- **Rotate**: eat oldest first so little ever goes past date (→ 04-10).
- **Thermometers in the fridge and freezer**, so you know what actually happened during an outage
  rather than guessing. Keep doors shut (→ 04-17).
- Cook and eat perishables first in an outage, then freezer food as it thaws, then the pantry.

**Reduces it a lot**
- **Inspect every can**: discard if bulging, leaking, deeply rusted, or sharply dented on the top
  or side seam. A small smooth dent on the body, seams intact, is a quality issue.
- **Inspect every package**: discard if torn, wet, mouldy, infested or smelling wrong.
- **Thawed freezer food** that still has ice crystals or was kept at 40 °F or below can be cooked
  or refrozen; fully warm is a discard (FoodSafety.gov).
- **Cook to safe internal temperatures** with a thermometer (FoodSafety.gov, Cook to a Safe
  Minimum Internal Temperature).

**Reduces it a little**
- Boil home-canned low-acid food 10 minutes (plus 1 minute per 1,000 feet of altitude) before
  tasting, as CDC advises; this destroys the toxin but not a spoiled can's other problems.
- Feed questionable food to adults before children, never to infants.

## 5. The options

**`label-strict`: Follow the label and the published rules strictly.**
You give up: food that is probably fine. You accept: a smaller food supply and running out
sooner.

**`inspect-and-eat`: Inspect and eat, with the rules for each case.**
You give up: the simple bright lines. You accept: that a judgement call will sometimes be wrong
and someone may get sick, and that bulging, leaking or spurting cans and jars stay on the
discard side regardless.

## 6. Our choice

{{card DC-14}}

pages.title: DC-15. Giving someone else's prescription medication

options.label: Never
options.summary: Each prescription medicine is taken only by the person it was prescribed for. If someone runs out, the household looks for a clinician, pharmacy or the same prescription elsewhere.

options.label: Same drug and strength, already prescribed to them
options.summary: Only when the person was already prescribed the same drug at the same strength and has run out: they take it as their own label said, after checking allergies and their other medicines. Never a new drug for a new problem; never to a child from an adult's supply.

pages.settings_summary: When pharmacies close, one person may run out of a medicine that someone else in the house or the neighbourhood still has. Prescriptions are written for one person because the right drug and dose depend on the illness, allergies, other medicines, kidney and liver function, weight and age. Shared medicine can cause an allergic reaction, a dangerous interaction, a dose far too strong (for example a painkiller or sleeping medicine that stops the breathing of someone not used to it), or the wrong insulin causing severe low blood sugar. What helps most: get each person's own supply and a written plan from their clinician now (removes most of it); share only the same drug at the same strength the person already takes, after an allergy and interaction check (reduces it a lot).
pages.body:
# DC-15. Giving someone else's prescription medication

**What this page is for.** When a person runs out of a medicine and nobody can write a new
prescription, the bottle on the next shelf is tempting. This card explains why prescriptions
are personal, what goes wrong when they are shared, and what the household decides. It never
tells you which drug or dose to give.

> **SAFETY.** Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products
> (floor, → 30-01). If someone has taken a medicine not meant for them and becomes very sleepy,
> confused or is breathing slowly, treat it as a poisoning: → 12-17.

## 1. The thing, in plain words

A **prescription medicine** is one a clinician chose for a particular person, at a particular
strength (the milligrams or units on the label), on a particular schedule. **Sharing** means
anyone else taking it. The label on the bottle (→ 29-14) gives the name, strength, the person
it was for and the directions.

## 2. The rule, and why it was set

- Pharmacists and clinicians say take prescription medicine only as prescribed for you, and never
  share it. CDC says this specifically for antibiotics (CDC, Antibiotic Use).
- For insulin in disasters, FDA and the American Diabetes Association explain that insulins
  differ in how fast and how long they work, so switching between them needs care and
  monitoring (FDA, Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products in an Emergency; ADA, Switching
  Between Insulin Products in Disaster Response Situations).

**Why:** the right drug and dose depend on what is actually wrong, the person's allergies,
everything else they take, their kidney and liver function, their weight and age. A medicine
that is safe for one person can be dangerous for another.

**The strongest case for sharing** is an emergency drug given once: for example, epinephrine
from another person's auto-injector in anaphylaxis, which allergy plans treat as life-saving
(AAAAI, Anaphylaxis Emergency Action Plan; → 02-03). This card is about regular prescriptions.

## 3. How it actually hurts people

- **Allergy**: a person allergic to a drug family (penicillin is the common one) takes a shared
  pill and has a severe reaction.
- **Interaction**: a shared painkiller or antibiotic interacts with a blood thinner, a heart
  medicine or a seizure medicine the person already takes.
- **Too strong**: a strong painkiller or a sleeping or anxiety medicine that one person
  tolerates can stop the breathing of someone who has never taken it, especially a child, an
  elder, or anyone who has also had alcohol (MedlinePlus, Poisoning first aid).
- **Wrong insulin**: a fast-acting insulin taken as if it were a long-acting one, or a different
  strength, causes severe low blood sugar: shaking, confusion, seizures, unconsciousness.
- **Wrong diagnosis**: treating a problem with the wrong medicine hides it while it gets worse.

## 4. What makes it safer

**Removes most of the risk**
- **Each person's own supply, and a written plan**: ask every clinician now for extra supply
  where allowed and for written instructions on what to do if a medicine runs out (→ 12-07).
- **A written list** of every household member's medicines, strengths and allergies
  (→ 25-09).

**Reduces it a lot**
- **Same drug, same strength, already prescribed to that person**: they take it as their own
  prescription said, nothing else changes.
- **Check allergies and every other medicine** they take before the first dose.
- **Never** give a child a medicine from an adult's supply, and never give a new drug for a new
  problem.

**Reduces it a little**
- Watch the person closely for the first hours after the first dose.
- Write down who took what and when.

## 5. The options

**`never`: Never.**
You give up: the chance to bridge a gap with medicine that is in the house. You accept: that
someone may go without their medicine until a source is found.

**`same-drug-same-strength-only`: Same drug and strength, already prescribed to them.**
You give up: the pharmacist's check. You accept: the risk of an unchecked allergy or
interaction and of a label misread, controlled by matching drug and strength exactly and
checking the person's allergy and medicine list.

## 6. Our choice

{{card DC-15}}

pages.title: DC-16. Antibiotics without a prescription (stockpiled or veterinary)

options.label: Never without a clinician
options.summary: Antibiotics are taken only when a clinician prescribed them for that person and that illness, or wrote a plan in advance. No stockpiled, shared, veterinary or aquarium antibiotics are used on a guess.

options.label: Last resort for adults, with the infection page
options.summary: Only for an adult showing the signs of a spreading or serious bacterial infection on the infection page, with no clinician reachable: a human antibiotic, with the drug and dose taken from a clinician's written plan or a published adult table printed as published. Never for children.

pages.settings_summary: Before antibiotics, ordinary wounds and infections killed healthy adults, so many preppers stockpile them, sometimes as fish or farm-animal products. Antibiotics are prescription drugs because the right one depends on the infection, the person's allergies and other medicines, and the dose depends on weight and kidney function. Most coughs, colds and stomach bugs are viral, and antibiotics do nothing for them. The wrong antibiotic can cause a severe allergic reaction or severe diarrhoea, hide a worsening infection, and breed resistant bacteria. Products sold for animals are not made or checked for human use. What helps most: ask a clinician now for a written plan and supply (removes most of it); use only for adults with clear signs of a serious bacterial infection, by a written or published adult table, never for children (reduces it a lot).
pages.body:
# DC-16. Antibiotics without a prescription (stockpiled or veterinary)

**What this page is for.** An infected wound or a serious infection with no doctor is one of
the most likely ways a survivable injury becomes fatal. This card explains what antibiotics can
and cannot do, why they need a prescriber, what goes wrong when they are used on a guess, and
what the household decides. It does not choose a drug or a dose.

> **SAFETY.** Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products
> (floor, → 30-01). **Sepsis** (the body's runaway reaction to infection) is an emergency: a
> person with infection plus confusion, fast breathing, a racing heart, clammy skin or severe
> pain needs the best care that can be reached, now (CDC, About Sepsis; → 12-04).

## 1. The thing, in plain words

An **antibiotic** is a medicine that kills bacteria or stops them growing. It does nothing to
**viruses** (colds, flu, most coughs and sore throats, most stomach bugs). Different antibiotics
work on different bacteria; no single one covers everything. **Resistance** means bacteria that
survive a course and multiply, so the drug stops working for that person and for others.
**Veterinary** and **aquarium** antibiotics are sold for animals and fish.

## 2. The rule, and why it was set

- CDC: antibiotics should be used only when needed, for bacterial infections, the right drug at
  the right dose for the right time; they do not work on viruses; and taking them when not
  needed causes side effects and drives resistance (CDC, Antibiotic Use).
- Antibiotics are prescription-only in the US. Products sold for animals are made and labelled
  for animals.

**Why:** choosing an antibiotic means knowing the likely bacteria, the site of infection, the
person's allergies, other medicines, pregnancy, age, weight and kidney function. Getting any of
those wrong can harm the person or fail to treat them while the infection spreads.

## 3. How it actually hurts people

- **Allergic reaction**: penicillin-family and other antibiotics cause rashes, swelling and
  sometimes anaphylaxis.
- **Severe diarrhoea**: antibiotics can kill the gut's normal bacteria and let a harmful one take
  over (CDC, Antibiotic Use); with no clinic, the dehydration is dangerous (→ 12-05).
- **The wrong drug**: the infection keeps spreading while everyone believes it is being treated.
  A wound that needed cleaning, draining or a tetanus booster gets pills instead (CDC, Tetanus
  wound management; → 12-02).
- **Animal products**: strength, purity and fillers are not made or checked for human use, and
  the labels do not translate to human doses.
- **Resistance**: a half course or the wrong drug leaves tougher bacteria behind in the family.

## 4. What makes it safer

**Removes most of the risk**
- **Ask a clinician now**, while you can, for a written plan: which signs mean "start", which
  antibiotic, what dose for whom, for how long, and what not to use with each person's allergies.
  Get any supply through them (→ 12-04).
- **Prevent infection**: clean wounds early and well, hand-washing, tetanus up to date (→ 12-02).

**Reduces it a lot**
- **Adults only, with clear signs** of a spreading or serious bacterial infection on → 12-04
  (spreading redness, pus, fever with a wound, red streaks), not a cold or a cough.
- **Human antibiotics only**, in intact original packaging, stored cool and dry. Intact tablets
  and capsules often keep strength past their date (Lyon and others, 2006); liquids do not
  (→ 30-05).
- **Drug and dose from a written source**: the clinician's plan or a published adult table
  printed as published with its publisher named. Never worked out or adjusted by the household.
- **Check every allergy and medicine** on the family list first (→ 25-09).

**Reduces it a little**
- Take it exactly as the plan says: same times, the full planned course.
- Write down who took what, when, and how they responded.

## 5. The options

**`never`: Never without a clinician.**
You give up: a possible treatment when no clinician exists. You accept: that some bacterial
infections that antibiotics would have cured may become severe.

**`last-resort`: Last resort for adults, with the infection page.**
You give up: diagnosis and a prescriber's choice of drug. You accept: the risks of allergy,
side effects, the wrong drug and resistance, limited by clear signs, human antibiotics, a
written or published adult source and the allergy check. Children are not included.

## 6. Our choice

{{card DC-16}}

pages.title: DC-17. Old kerosene, diesel or gasoline in a heater or engine

options.label: Fresh fuel only, on a rotation schedule
options.summary: Every can is dated. Gasoline is stabilised when bought and rotated into vehicles on a schedule; kerosene and diesel are used and replaced on a schedule. Fuel past the household's age limit is not burned in heaters or the generator.

options.label: Jar-test old fuel and use it if it passes
options.summary: Old fuel may be used if a sample in a clear jar, left to stand, is clear and bright with no water layer, cloudiness, sludge or colour change, and it smells like the right fuel. Any doubt, or an unlabelled can, and it is not used.

pages.settings_summary: Fuel ages. Gasoline loses the parts that help it start, can absorb water and leaves gum that blocks small-engine carburettors. Kerosene and diesel take up water from the air in part-full cans and can grow sludge. One common wick-heater maker says never use kerosene stored from one season to the next. The real danger is in heaters: old or wet kerosene fouls the wick, so the flame burns badly and makes more smoke and carbon monoxide (CO) indoors. Old gasoline in a generator mostly means it will not start when needed. What helps most: date, stabilise and rotate (removes most of it); store full, sealed, cool and dark, and jar-test before every fill (reduces it a lot). An unlabelled or unknown can is never poured.
pages.body:
# DC-17. Old kerosene, diesel or gasoline in a heater or engine

**What this page is for.** Stored fuel gets old. Throwing it out when no more is coming costs
heat and power; burning it can foul a heater indoors or leave a generator dead. This card
explains what ageing does to each fuel, what the makers say, and what the household decides.

> **SAFETY.** Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance
> (floor, → 30-01). **Gasoline is never put in a kerosene heater**: that causes a fire or
> explosion (heater maker's manual). A can with a missing or unreadable label is not poured
> into anything. If a heater smokes, smells strongly or a CO alarm sounds: off, everyone out,
> → 08-02.

## 1. The thing, in plain words

Read → 29-01 for what each fuel is.
- **Gasoline** is a blend that evaporates easily. With age the lightest parts evaporate (it gets
  harder to start an engine), it can take up water (especially blends with ethanol), and it
  leaves gum and varnish in small engines.
- **Kerosene** is a heavier fuel for wick heaters and lamps. **K-1** (also written 1-K) is the
  clear, low-sulfur grade made for indoor heaters (MU Extension). Kerosene does not "go off"
  quickly, but part-full cans breathe in damp air, collect water at the bottom, and can grow
  sludge.
- **Diesel** behaves like kerosene: water and sludge are the enemies, and they plug filters.
- **Stabiliser** is an additive put in fresh gasoline to slow ageing.
- The **jar test**: pour a sample into a clean clear glass jar and let it stand. Good fuel is
  clear and bright. Water sits as a separate layer or droplets at the bottom; contamination shows
  as cloudiness, sludge, specks or a darker colour.

{{#if has.kerosene_heater}}Your household has a wick kerosene heater. Kerosene on hand: {{ gear.fuel.kerosene_gal }} gal.{{/if}} {{#if has.generator}}Generator fuel: {{ gear.generator_fuel }}. Gasoline on hand: {{ gear.fuel.gasoline_gal }} gal.{{/if}}

## 2. The rule, and why it was set

- A common wick kerosene heater maker says use only **water-clear 1-K kerosene**, and **never use
  kerosene stored from one season to the next**, because old kerosene will not burn properly
  (GHP Group/Dyna-Glo, kerosene heater owner's manual).
- University of Missouri Extension says unvented kerosene heaters must burn only 1-K, and that
  contaminated or wrong fuel increases smoke and pollutants indoors (MU Extension, Unvented
  Portable Kerosene Heaters, G1999).
- Generator and small-engine makers call for clean, fresh gasoline and give storage steps for
  long idle periods.

**Why:** a wick heater works only when the wick soaks up clean fuel evenly. Water and sludge
clog the wick, the flame burns low and uneven, and an unvented heater then puts more carbon
monoxide and soot into the room (→ 29-03). For engines, stale gasoline is the most common reason
a stored generator will not start.

## 3. How it actually hurts people

- **Kerosene heater indoors:** wet or dirty fuel fouls the wick. The flame burns low and
  smoky; the household turns the wick down to stop the smell, which makes more CO. The family is
  sleeping in a closed room (→ 30-02). CO poisons quietly (CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning:
  Basics; CPSC, Carbon Monoxide Fact Sheet).
- **Wrong fuel in an old, faded can:** gasoline poured into a kerosene heater makes the flame run
  away: flare-up, fire, explosion.
- **Generator:** stale gasoline gums the carburettor. It will not start on the night it is
  needed, or it surges and stalls, and the insulin fridge or furnace goes without power.
- **Diesel:** water and sludge plug the fuel filter and stop the engine, often at the worst
  moment on the road.

## 4. What makes it safer

**Removes most of the risk**
- **Date every can** on a label, and keep a log (→ 26-08).
- **Rotate**: stabilise gasoline when you buy it and pour each can into a vehicle on a schedule,
  refilling fresh; burn the oldest kerosene first each winter and replace it.
- **Propane** does not go stale; where it fits, it avoids this problem for generators (→ 09-04).

**Reduces it a lot**
- **Store full, sealed, cool and dark.** A full can has little air to breathe and little room for
  water to condense.
- **Jar-test before every fill** of a heater, and before using any can older than your rotation
  limit.
- **Read the label aloud, smell, then pour.** Gasoline smells sharp and stings the eyes;
  kerosene smells oily. The usual can colours (red gasoline, yellow diesel, blue kerosene) are a
  convention, not a guarantee.

**Reduces it a little**
- Run a generator for a short time every month and drain or run it dry for long storage, as its
  manual says (→ 09-15).
- Keep spare wicks and fuel filters; a fouled wick is replaced, not turned down.

## 5. The options

**`fresh-only`: Fresh fuel only, on a rotation schedule.**
You give up: old fuel that might still have burned; you must buy, rotate and dispose of fuel
regularly. You accept: less fuel in a long emergency once fresh supply ends.

**`jar-test-and-use`: Jar-test old fuel and use it if it passes.**
You give up: the heater maker's season-to-season rule. You accept: that the jar test catches
water and sludge but not every problem, so the heater's flame and the CO alarm must be watched
more closely, and any smoky, smelly burn means off and out.

Write your household's age limit for each fuel here: gasoline ______ · kerosene ______ ·
diesel ______.

## 6. Our choice

{{card DC-17}}

pages.title: DC-18. Feeding a food-allergic person unlabeled, traded or scavenged food

options.label: Never: only food with a full, readable label
options.summary: The allergic person eats only food whose full ingredient label has been read, or food the household made itself from labelled ingredients in a clean kitchen. No traded, donated, scavenged or foraged food, ever.

options.label: Single-ingredient foods only
options.summary: Unlabelled or traded food is allowed only if it is one plain, recognisable ingredient (whole rice, dry beans, a whole vegetable or fruit, a whole cut of meat) that is not on the person's allergen list, washed and cooked in the household's own clean pots.

options.label: With epinephrine in hand, by our own line
options.summary: Unlabelled food may be tried by the household's own written line, only with in-date epinephrine in hand, an adult who knows the plan watching, the first taste small, and never alone or at night.

pages.settings_summary: When stores close, food arrives without labels: bartered, donated, scavenged, repackaged or foraged. For a person with a food allergy, a label is how you find the hidden egg, peanut, milk, sesame or soy. US law requires the nine major allergens to be declared on packaged food, but only while labels exist. Without one, a trace of the allergen, or a pot or spoon that touched it, can cause anaphylaxis: throat swelling, trouble breathing, collapse, death within minutes to hours without epinephrine. With no ambulance, epinephrine is the only treatment, and a reaction can need more than one dose. What helps most: a deep stock of verified safe food and kept labels (removes most of it); single-ingredient foods cooked in the household's own pots (reduces it a lot).
pages.body:
# DC-18. Feeding a food-allergic person unlabeled, traded or scavenged food

**What this page is for.** In a long emergency, food stops coming with labels. For someone with
a serious food allergy that is the moment the danger jumps. This card explains why, what makes
it safer, and what the household decides for each allergic person.

> **SAFETY.** In anaphylaxis, **give epinephrine first** and think second (→ 02-03).
> Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products (floor,
> → 30-01).

## 1. The thing, in plain words

A **food allergy** is the immune system reacting to a food protein as if it were a threat.
**Anaphylaxis** is the most severe reaction: swelling of the throat or tongue, trouble
breathing, wheezing, vomiting, a drop in blood pressure, collapse (CDC, Recognizing and
Responding to Anaphylaxis). **Epinephrine** is the drug that treats it, usually from an
auto-injector. **Cross-contact** means a safe food picking up traces of an allergen from a pot,
a spoon, a cutting board or hands.

{{#each allergies as a}}{{a.member}}: {{a.allergen}} ({{a.severity}}). {{else}}No allergy rows entered in settings.{{/each}}

## 2. The rule, and why it was set

- FDA: US food labels must declare the **nine major allergens**: milk, eggs, fish, crustacean
  shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame (FDA, Food Allergies).
- Allergy specialists' standard advice is **strict avoidance** of the allergen and epinephrine
  carried at all times (AAAAI, Anaphylaxis Emergency Action Plan; AAP, Allergy and Anaphylaxis
  Emergency Plan).

**Why:** the label is the only practical way to find an allergen hidden in a sauce, bread,
ration bar or seasoning. Without the label there is no way to know, and the amount that triggers
a reaction can be very small.

## 3. How it actually hurts people

A neighbour trades a loaf of bread. It looks plain; it was made with egg and brushed with
sesame. Or plain rice is cooked in a pot that just held peanut stew. The allergic child eats it.
Within minutes: itching mouth, hives, coughing, vomiting, then trouble breathing. Epinephrine is
given; the reaction comes back an hour later and needs a second dose (reactions can return,
AAAAI). With no ambulance and limited devices, each exposure uses up the stock that protects
against the next one.

Foraged food adds two problems: a new food can trigger a new allergy, and some wild plants are
simply poisonous (→ 05-06).

## 4. What makes it safer

**Removes most of the risk**
- **A deep stock of verified safe food** for the allergic person, bought by brand, labels read
  and kept (cut out and filed when food is repackaged), marked "SAFE for ______" (→ 02-04).
- **The allergic person's own food first**; trade other food, not theirs.

**Reduces it a lot**
- **Single-ingredient foods only** from outside sources: whole grains, dry beans, whole
  vegetables and fruit, whole cuts of meat or fish if those are safe for that person. Nothing
  mixed, baked, sauced or seasoned by someone else.
- **Wash it and cook it in your own clean pots**, with utensils kept only for the allergic
  person.
- **Epinephrine in date, in reach, and enough of it** (→ 02-03, → 30-05).

**Reduces it a little**
- Ask the giver exactly what is in it and how it was made; remember that answers can be wrong.
- First taste small, in daylight, with an adult who knows the plan watching, never alone.
- A written allergen card that travels with the person and goes to anyone who feeds them.

## 5. The options

**`never`: Never: only food with a full, readable label.**
You give up: food you cannot verify, which may mean a narrower diet and hunger if the safe stock
runs low. You accept: needing a larger safe stock.

**`single-ingredient-only`: Single-ingredient foods only.**
You give up: mixed, baked and prepared foods from outside. You accept: a small cross-contact risk
from how the food was grown, stored or handled before it reached you.

**`with-epinephrine-in-hand`: With epinephrine in hand, by our own line.**
You give up: avoidance as the main protection. You accept: that a reaction is possible and that
epinephrine, a watching adult and the household's own written line are the protection.
Write the line here: ____________________________________________

If more than one person has allergies, answer for each person beside the box.

## 6. Our choice

{{card DC-18}}

pages.title: DC-19. When to leave home: our triggers

options.label: Write our own rule
options.summary: The adults fill in the trigger table on this page with their own thresholds and destinations, agree it, sign and date it, and review it each year.

pages.settings_summary: This card has no multiple choice. Leaving home is the highest-stakes decision a household makes in a long emergency, and the one most often made badly: too late, in a panic, in bad weather, with children. Staying in a stocked, known home is usually safer than moving. Leaving into a storm or extreme cold kills people every winter, and the Red Cross and National Weather Service both say avoid travel in winter storms unless you must. But staying past the point where medicine, heat, water or safety runs out forces a move in the worst condition. The answer is thresholds written now, while calm, that turn a 3 a.m. judgement into a checklist. Fill in the trigger table on the page.
pages.body:
# DC-19. When to leave home: our triggers

**What this page is for.** This card is a worksheet. It explains the two ways the leave-or-stay
decision goes wrong and gives the household a table to fill in with its own triggers. A
threshold agreed in advance is worth more than any judgement made at 3 a.m. in a cold house.

> **SAFETY.** If the house is on fire, collapsing, flooding or a wildfire is coming, leave now:
> that is not a threshold question (→ 17-03, → 17-05). Never run a generator, charcoal, or any
> engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open window (floor, → 30-01); people trapped in cars
> in snow die of this too.

> **Before the collapse:** if officials order an evacuation, follow it. The triggers below are
> for when no one is giving orders.

## 1. The thing, in plain words

**Sheltering in place** means staying at home and living off what you have (→ 01-01).
**Moving** means taking the household somewhere else, by vehicle or on foot (→ 01-03). A
**trigger** is a condition written in advance that means "start moving" or "start preparing to
move". A **destination** is a named place with shelter, heat and water, where someone expects
you (→ 01-05).

{{#if has.destinations}}Your destinations: {{#each destinations as d}}{{d.name}} ({{d.state_name}}, about {{d.approximate_miles}} miles, {{d.status_text}}); {{/each}}{{else}}You have not named a destination yet. "Out of town" is not a plan.{{/if}}

## 2. The rule as agencies state it, and why

- The Red Cross and the National Weather Service say stay off the roads in winter storms and
  extreme cold unless travel is necessary, and carry a winter car kit if you must go (Red Cross,
  Winter Storm Safety; NWS, During Extremely Cold Weather).
- FEMA asks every family to make a written plan in advance: where to meet, how to reach each
  other, where to go (FEMA/Ready.gov, Create Your Family Emergency Communication Plan).

**Why:** a stocked home you know how to heat is a strong position. A vehicle on a closed road
in a blizzard, with children, is a weak one. But a home without heat, water, medicine or safety
can become worse than the road, and the agencies cannot tell you where that line is for your
family.

## 3. How it actually hurts people

1. **Leaving when you should have stayed**: the family trades a stocked house for exposure,
   unknown roads and what fits in the car. A storm, a breakdown or an empty tank strands them.
   This is the more common mistake.
2. **Staying when you should have left**: the last fuel, insulin or water is used up, and the
   family has to move anyway, now with no fuel, no daylight, sick and weak.

Both happen because the decision is made in the moment, under fear and fatigue.

## 4. What makes it safer

**Removes much of the risk**
- **Write the triggers now** (below), agree them as adults, sign and date them.
- **Name a real destination** with someone expecting you, and a route (→ 01-05).

**Reduces it a lot**
- **Answer the four questions before moving**: Where exactly are we going? Is the route
  survivable right now (weather, fuel, daylight)? What happens when we arrive? Is it truly better
  than staying? If any answer is weak, stay and fix that answer.
- **Weather first, daylight second**: do not depart into a storm or extreme cold unless the house
  is actively unsafe; leave in the morning.
- **Once decided, go early**, with fuel in the tank and people still strong.
- **Medical triggers point toward care**, not away from it: if a life-sustaining medicine is
  running out, the move may be toward a town or hospital, not the countryside.

**Reduces it a little**
- Keep the vehicle fuelled above half and the go-bags packed (→ 22-03).
- Practise the load once (→ 01-06).

## 5. The worksheet: our triggers

Fill in each row. Leave none blank: write "not applicable" if it truly is.

| Trigger | Our threshold (start preparing / move) | Go where |
|---|---|---|
| Life-sustaining medicine remaining (each one) | ______ days / ______ days | ______________ |
| Emergency medicine (e.g. epinephrine devices) remaining | ______ / ______ | ______________ |
| Heating fuel remaining, winter | ______ days / ______ days | ______________ |
| Safe drinking water we can produce per day | below ______ gal | ______________ |
| Food remaining (including any special-diet food) | ______ days / ______ days | ______________ |
| House unsafe (fire, structure, flood) | immediately | ______________ |
| Security threat we cannot manage | __________________ | ______________ |
| Neighbourhood (fire spreading, mass departure, utilities gone for good) | __________________ | ______________ |
| Medical emergency we cannot treat | __________________ | ______________ |
| Other: __________________ | __________________ | ______________ |

Your household's medicines, for the first row: {{#each meds as m}}{{m.member}}: {{m.name}}; {{else}}none entered.{{/each}}

Weather rule (when we will not depart): _______________________________________________

Who decides if the adults are apart: ___________________________________________________

If we split up, we meet at: {{ contacts.meet.out_of_town }}

Signed: ______________________ ______________________ Date: __________ Reviewed: __________

## 6. Our choice

{{card DC-19}}

pages.title: DC-20. Open-flame cooking, candles or oil lamps indoors

options.label: No open flame indoors
options.summary: Light comes from flashlights, headlamps and battery lanterns; cooking happens outdoors or on electric appliances run from stored power. No candles, oil lamps or flame cooking inside.

options.label: Indoors with extinguisher, alarms and rules
options.summary: Candles, oil lamps or stove-top flame cooking are allowed only with working smoke and CO alarms, an extinguisher within reach, 12 inches clear all round, an adult in the room, never where anyone sleeps, out when the room is left.

pages.settings_summary: In an outage, candles, oil lamps and cooking on a match-lit gas stove are the oldest answers to dark and cold food. US Fire Administration advice is to use flashlights, not candles, in a power outage, because candles cause many home fires, often when they are left burning, placed too close to something that burns, or reached by children or pets. Any flame indoors also adds carbon monoxide and uses oxygen, and CDC says never use a gas stove or oven to heat a home. Lamp oil and kerosene are poisonous if a child swallows them. What helps most: battery lights and outdoor cooking (removes it); working smoke and CO alarms, an extinguisher in reach, an adult present, nothing within 12 inches, never in sleeping areas (reduces it a lot).
pages.body:
# DC-20. Open-flame cooking, candles or oil lamps indoors

**What this page is for.** When the power goes out, the house gets dark and the electric stove
stops. Candles, oil lamps and a gas burner lit with a match are the obvious answers. This card
explains what fire agencies say, how flames indoors actually hurt people, and what the household
decides.

> **SAFETY.** Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an
> open window (floor, → 30-01). **Camp stoves, grills and charcoal are not part of this card**:
> CDC says never use them indoors, and this binder treats them under that floor. Children do not
> have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products (floor): that includes lamp oil
> and kerosene.

## 1. The thing, in plain words

This card covers:
- **Candles.**
- **Oil lamps and kerosene lamps**: a wick in a glass chimney burning liquid fuel (→ 29-01).
- **Open-flame cooking indoors**: a gas range lit with a match when the electric igniter is dead,
  or cooking on an indoor fireplace or wood stove.

It does not cover heaters (→ 30-02) or camp stoves and grills (floor).

## 2. The rule, and why it was set

- The US Fire Administration says **use flashlights, not candles, during a power outage**; keep
  candles at least 12 inches from anything that can burn; blow them out when you leave the room or
  go to sleep; and avoid using them in bedrooms and sleeping areas (USFA, Candle Fire Safety).
- CDC says **never use a gas range or oven to heat a home** (CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning:
  Basics; CDC, Winter Weather).
- NFPA advises keeping anything that can burn well away from heat sources and having working smoke
  alarms (NFPA, Heating fire safety).

**Why:** a flame is a heat source that can be knocked over, forgotten or reached by a child. In an
outage the risks pile up: more candles than usual, people tired and distracted, dark rooms, and
often no fire department coming.

## 3. How it actually hurts people

- **Fire**: a candle left burning when people fall asleep, a curtain or paper too close, a cat's
  tail, a toddler reaching up. The fire spreads before anyone wakes. With smoke alarm batteries
  removed or dead, there is no warning.
- **Carbon monoxide**: one candle makes little, but a gas burner left on for warmth, many lamps
  in a closed room, or a smoky lamp adds CO and uses oxygen (→ 29-03).
- **Poisoning**: a child drinks lamp oil or kerosene from a lamp or a bottle that looks like juice.
  A small amount breathed into the lungs causes a severe chemical pneumonia; do **not** make the
  child vomit, call Poison Control (CDC MMWR, hydrocarbon ingestion in children; Poison Control,
  1-800-222-1222; → 12-17).
- **Burns**: hot wax, a glass chimney, a pan on an unsteady flame.

## 4. What makes it safer

**Removes the risk**
- **Battery light**: flashlights, headlamps and battery lanterns, with spare batteries (→ 10-01).
- **Cook outdoors** in a sheltered spot (→ 07-01), or on electric appliances run from stored power
  (→ 07-06).

**Reduces it a lot**
- **Working smoke and CO alarms**, tested, with fresh batteries.
- **A fire extinguisher within reach** and an adult who knows how to use it (→ 29-12).
- **12 inches clear all round**, on a stable, non-flammable surface, out of reach of children and
  pets.
- **An adult in the room** the whole time; **out when you leave the room or sleep**; never in
  bedrooms or sleeping areas.
- For a gas range: cooking only, never for heat; a window cracked; burners off when the pan comes
  off.

**Reduces it a little**
- Candles in deep jars or holders; lamps with a glass chimney and a stable base.
- Lamp fuel stored locked, in its original labelled container, never in a drink bottle.
- One flame at a time.

## 5. The options

**`never-indoors`: No open flame indoors.**
You give up: candle and lamp light and match-lit stove cooking. You accept: needing enough
batteries or stored power for light, and cooking outside in all weather.

**`with-extinguisher-and-alarm`: Indoors with extinguisher, alarms and rules.**
You give up: the USFA's flashlights-only advice. You accept: a fire and CO risk controlled by
alarms, an extinguisher, clearance and an adult present at all times.

## 6. Our choice

{{card DC-20}}

pages.title: DC-21. Using a fireplace or wood stove that has not been inspected this year

options.label: Inspect first, using the chimney page
options.summary: No fire until the household has done the inspection on the chimney page (cold flue, light and mirror, scrape test, cap and blockages) or a professional has. A flue with glaze, cracks or a blockage is not used until fixed.

options.label: Use it with small hot fires and a watch
options.summary: If it cannot be inspected now: small, hot fires of dry wood only, never smouldering overnight, CO and smoke alarms in the room, an extinguisher in reach, someone checking the chimney and attic, and an inspection at the first chance.

pages.settings_summary: A fireplace or wood stove can heat a house with no power, but the chimney is part of the appliance. Wood smoke leaves a tar called creosote on the inside of the chimney; it builds up faster with damp wood and slow, smoky fires, and it burns. A chimney fire can crack the chimney and set the house alight. A chimney blocked by a nest, leaves or fallen brick sends smoke and carbon monoxide back into the room. The national fire code for chimneys (NFPA 211) and chimney safety groups say inspect at least once a year. What helps most: inspect first, by a professional or with the household's own light-and-mirror check (removes most of it); dry wood, small hot fires, alarms, an extinguisher and a watch on the chimney (reduces it a lot).
pages.body:
# DC-21. Using a fireplace or wood stove that has not been inspected this year

**What this page is for.** A fireplace or wood stove is one of the best heat sources without
power. In an emergency it may not have been checked in years, or ever. This card explains what
can be wrong with a chimney you cannot see into, and what the household decides before the first
fire.

> **SAFETY.** If you hear a roar like a freight train in the chimney, see flames or heavy sparks
> from the top, or the chimney wall is hot: everyone out, shut the stove's air or close the
> fireplace doors, wet the roof around it, do not pour water down the flue, and watch the attic
> for hours (→ 06-09). If a CO alarm sounds: everyone out, → 08-02.

## 1. The thing, in plain words

- The **firebox** is where the fire burns. The **flue** is the passage inside the chimney that
  carries smoke out. The **damper** opens and closes the flue.
- **Creosote** is a black, sticky or crusty tar from wood smoke that sticks to the flue. It burns
  very hot. Thin, flaky soot brushes off; a hard, shiny glaze does not.
- A **chimney fire** is creosote burning inside the flue.
- An **inspection** means looking up the cold flue with a strong light and a mirror, scraping the
  wall to see how thick the deposit is, and checking the cap and top for blockages (→ 06-09).

{{#if has.fireplace}}Your home has an indoor fireplace.{{/if}} {{#if has.wood_stove}}Your household has a wood stove.{{/if}} Firewood on hand: {{ gear.fuel.firewood_cords }} cords.

## 2. The rule, and why it was set

- NFPA 211, the national standard for chimneys, fireplaces and wood-burning appliances, calls for
  chimneys to be inspected **at least once a year** (NFPA 211).
- The Chimney Safety Institute of America says creosote is the main cause of chimney fires, and
  that a flue with about 1/8 inch of buildup should be swept before the next fire (CSIA, Preventing
  Chimney Fires).
- The US Fire Administration says have the chimney inspected and cleaned every year, use a
  screen, keep things that burn well away, and never leave a fire unattended (USFA, Fireplace and
  Wood Stove Safety).

**Why:** you cannot see the inside of a chimney from the room. Creosote, cracked flue tiles,
missing mortar and nests build up silently over seasons. An inspection finds them before a fire
does.

## 3. How it actually hurts people

- **Chimney fire**: a long burn, or a hot fire after weeks of slow smouldering ones, lights the
  creosote. The flue reaches very high temperatures, cracks tiles and can ignite the wood framing
  around the chimney. With no fire department coming, the house can be lost.
- **Carbon monoxide**: a bird's nest, leaves or a collapsed tile blocks the flue. Smoke and CO
  come back into the room. CO has no smell and the smoke may not be obvious overnight (CDC).
- **Sparks and embers**: no screen, a cracked stove door, or a damaged chimney cap lets embers
  reach the floor or the roof.

## 4. What makes it safer

**Removes most of the risk**
- **Inspect before the first fire**: a professional sweep now while they work, or the household's
  own cold-flue check with light, mirror and scrape test (→ 06-09). Fix or sweep what you find.

**Reduces it a lot**
- **Dry, seasoned wood only**: green or wet wood makes far more creosote (EPA Burn Wise; → 06-03).
- **Small, hot fires**, not a damped-down fire smouldering all night (EPA Burn Wise).
- **Smoke and CO alarms** in the room and on every level; an **extinguisher** in reach (→ 29-12).
- **Screen or closed doors**, and nothing that can burn near the firebox.
- **Check the chimney top and the attic** around the chimney during the first fires: smell, heat,
  sparks.

**Reduces it a little**
- Chimney-fire suppressant sticks kept beside the fireplace.
- Ashes in a metal bucket with a lid, outside, away from the house.
- Watch the smoke from outside: thick dark smoke means a cool, dirty burn.

## 5. The options

**`inspect-first`: Inspect first, using the chimney page.**
You give up: heat until the inspection is done, which may be a cold night or two. You accept:
learning to inspect, or paying for it now.

**`use-with-small-fires-and-watch`: Use it with small hot fires and a watch.**
You give up: knowing the state of the flue. You accept: the risk of a hidden blockage or deposit,
controlled by small hot fires, dry wood, alarms, an extinguisher and someone watching the
chimney.

## 6. Our choice

{{card DC-21}}

pages.title: DC-22. Potassium iodide for adults over 40

options.label: Follow FDA: over 40 only at very large exposure
options.summary: Adults over 40 take potassium iodide only if officials say a very large dose of radioactive iodine is expected, as FDA advises. Everyone younger follows the FDA table on the potassium iodide page, on official direction.

options.label: Adults over 40 take it whenever others do
options.summary: When officials direct potassium iodide for the area, adults over 40 in the household take the FDA adult dose too, after checking the FDA list of people who should not take it, accepting a higher chance of side effects.

pages.settings_summary: Potassium iodide (KI) is a tablet that fills the thyroid gland with ordinary iodine so it does not absorb radioactive iodine released by a nuclear accident or bomb. It protects only the thyroid, only from radioactive iodine, and only when taken on official direction. FDA's guidance says adults over 40 have the lowest risk of thyroid cancer from radioactive iodine and a higher chance of side effects from KI (thyroid problems and allergic reactions), so they should take it only if a very large exposure is expected. Sheltering indoors protects far more than KI does. What helps most: shelter first; know who should not take it; decide now with a clinician; take it only when officials say so.
pages.body:
# DC-22. Potassium iodide for adults over 40

**What this page is for.** Potassium iodide is often sold as an "anti-radiation pill". It is not.
This card explains what it does, why FDA treats adults over 40 differently, and what the household
decides for its older adults. The full FDA dose table and the children's measuring recipe are on
→ 27-06.

> **Caution.** Take potassium iodide only when public health officials say to. FDA: it should not
> be taken as a preventive before exposure, and taking more than directed does not give more
> protection and can cause severe illness or death (FDA, Frequently Asked Questions on Potassium
> Iodide). Sheltering protects far more than any pill (→ 27-05).

## 1. The thing, in plain words

The **thyroid** is a gland in the neck that takes up iodine from the blood. A nuclear accident or
bomb can release **radioactive iodine**, which the thyroid absorbs and which can cause thyroid
cancer years later, mostly in people exposed as children. **Potassium iodide (KI)** is a salt of
ordinary iodine. Taken at the right time, it fills the thyroid so it absorbs less of the
radioactive kind. It does **nothing** for the rest of the body or for any other radioactive
material (FDA; CDC, Radiation Emergencies).

{{#if has.elder}}Your household includes a member over 70.{{/if}}

## 2. The rule, and why it was set

- FDA's guidance sets different exposure levels at which KI is recommended by age. **Adults over
  40 should take KI only if a very large radiation dose to the thyroid is expected**, the level at
  which the main concern becomes losing thyroid function rather than cancer (FDA, Potassium Iodide
  as a Thyroid Blocking Agent in Radiation Emergencies).
- FDA lists people who should not take KI, including those with known iodine sensitivity, the skin
  disease dermatitis herpetiformis, the blood-vessel disease hypocomplementemic vasculitis, and
  nodular thyroid disease with heart disease (FDA FAQ).

**Why:** the benefit of KI falls with age, because the adult thyroid is much less likely to turn
cancerous after radioactive iodine exposure. The risks rise with age, because older adults more
often have hidden thyroid nodules or heart disease, and iodine can push an overactive or nodular
thyroid into dangerous overactivity (HHS REMM, Potassium Iodide).

## 3. How it actually hurts people

- **Taking it when not needed or not directed**: rash, stomach upset, salivary gland swelling, and
  in some people an allergic reaction (FDA FAQ). In an older person with a nodular thyroid, a racing
  or irregular heartbeat.
- **Taking extra**: more does not protect more, and overdose can cause severe illness (FDA FAQ).
- **Relying on it**: a household that takes KI and then goes outside, instead of sheltering, takes
  the full exposure to everything else in the fallout.

## 4. What makes it safer

**Removes most of the risk**
- **Shelter first**, in the most protected room; Ready.gov says stay inside for at least 24 hours
  unless told otherwise (Ready.gov, Nuclear Explosion; → 27-05).
- **Take KI only on official direction** (→ 15-01 for how you will hear it).

**Reduces it a lot**
- **Decide now with a clinician** for each adult over 40, and write it on the family medical
  summary (→ 25-09), including whether anyone has thyroid or heart disease.
- **Know FDA's do-not-take list** before the bottle is opened.

**Reduces it a little**
- Keep the FDA table and recipe from → 27-06 with the bottle.
- Record who took what and when; do not repeat doses early.

## 5. The options

**`follow-fda-table`: Follow FDA: over 40 only at very large exposure.**
You give up: KI for the older adults in all but the largest releases. You accept: a small
remaining thyroid risk for them in a moderate release.

**`take-anyway`: Adults over 40 take it whenever others do.**
You give up: FDA's age guidance. You accept: a higher chance of side effects, especially in anyone
with thyroid or heart disease, for a small added protection.

## 6. Our choice

{{card DC-22}}

pages.title: DC-23. Chlorinating very dirty water beyond the published dose

options.label: Clear it first, then the published dose
options.summary: Very dirty water is settled and filtered until it is as clear as possible, then disinfected at the published dose (doubled only if it is still cloudy, coloured or very cold, as CDC and EPA say), with the full wait.

options.label: Heavy dose and a longer wait when it cannot be cleared
options.summary: When the water cannot be settled or filtered, it gets the doubled published dose, a longer wait, and a smell check; if no chlorine smell, dose again and wait again. The household accepts strong taste and that some germs may survive.

pages.settings_summary: Household bleach and dissolved pool shock kill most germs in water at the dose CDC and EPA publish, and they say to double that dose for cloudy, coloured or very cold water. Very dirty water is the problem: mud and plant matter use up the chlorine and hide germs inside particles, so even a big dose may not disinfect it, and a parasite called Cryptosporidium survives ordinary chlorine anyway. Pouring in much more chlorine than published mostly makes water taste and smell harsh and can upset stomachs; mistakes with concentrated pool shock are dangerous. What helps most: settle and filter first, then the published dose (reduces it a lot); boiling clear water instead (removes most germ risk). Never mix chlorine with other cleaners (floor).
pages.body:
# DC-23. Chlorinating very dirty water beyond the published dose

**What this page is for.** Some emergency water is clear; some is brown. The published chlorine
doses assume you clear the water first. This card explains why, what happens when people try to
make up for dirt with more chlorine, and what the household decides. The published doses
themselves are on → 03-04.

> **SAFETY.** Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners (floor,
> → 30-01). Water that may hold fuel or toxic chemicals cannot be made safe by chlorine or boiling
> (CDC); see → 30-14. Concentrated pool-shock solution is itself a poison: label it, keep it away
> from children (floor 9).

## 1. The thing, in plain words

Read → 29-05 and → 29-06 first if these words are new.
- **Chlorine disinfection** means adding household bleach, or a solution made from pool shock, to
  water, then waiting so the chlorine kills germs.
- **Turbidity** is cloudiness: mud, silt, plant bits floating in the water.
- **Chlorine demand** is the chlorine the dirt uses up before any is left to kill germs.
- **Residual** is chlorine left over after the wait; you can smell it. No smell can mean the dirt
  used it all.

## 2. The rule, and why it was set

- CDC and EPA: if water is cloudy, **let it settle and filter it** through cloth, paper towel or a
  coffee filter first; then add the published dose of unscented bleach; **double the dose if the
  water is still cloudy, coloured or very cold**; stir and wait 30 minutes. EPA adds: the water
  should have a slight chlorine smell; if not, repeat the dose and wait another 15 minutes (CDC, How
  to Make Water Safe in an Emergency; EPA, Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water).
- Follow the bleach label if it gives drinking-water directions.

**Why:** chlorine works on what it can reach. Germs inside or behind dirt particles are shielded,
and dirt reacts with chlorine and uses it up. Clearing the water first is what lets the published
dose work.

## 3. How it actually hurts people

- **Under-disinfection**: muddy water gets a big dose, smells of chlorine for a while, and is
  drunk, but germs inside particles survived. Diarrhoea follows; in a baby, an elder or someone with
  diabetes, dehydration becomes an emergency (→ 12-05).
- **Parasites**: Cryptosporidium survives ordinary chlorine doses; boiling or a fine filter is
  needed (CDC Yellow Book, Water Disinfection for Travelers).
- **Too much chlorine**: water that tastes and smells harsh, which people then avoid drinking, and
  stomach upset. Large mistakes with concentrated pool-shock solution burn the mouth and stomach
  (CDC/ATSDR, Calcium Hypochlorite).

## 4. What makes it safer

**Removes most of the germ risk**
- **Boil** water that has been settled and filtered (CDC), when fuel allows.
- **Choose cleaner water**: rain, snow, or the clearest source available (→ 30-14).

**Reduces it a lot**
- **Settle, then filter**: let a bucket stand for hours, pour off the clear top, run it through
  cloth and then a fine filter (→ 03-09).
- **Then the published dose**, doubled only if still cloudy, coloured or very cold, with the full
  wait and the smell check (→ 03-04).
- **Measure**: a dropper or measuring spoon, not a guess; write the bleach strength on the bottle.

**Reduces it a little**
- Pour treated water between two clean containers, or let it stand uncovered a few hours, to soften
  the taste.
- Chlorine test strips, if you have them (→ 03-07).

## 5. The options

**`label-dose-and-filter-first`: Clear it first, then the published dose.**
You give up: time and filter material; settling takes hours. You accept: a slower supply.

**`double-dose-and-wait`: Heavy dose and a longer wait when it cannot be cleared.**
You give up: the clearing step. You accept: harsh-tasting water and the risk that germs hidden in
the dirt, and Cryptosporidium, survive.

## 6. Our choice

{{card DC-23}}

pages.title: DC-24. Children doing dangerous jobs because hands are short

options.label: Write our own rule
options.summary: The adults fill in the job table on this page with the age, training and supervision each child needs for each dangerous job, agree it, sign and date it, and review it on each child's birthday.

pages.settings_summary: This card has no multiple choice. In a long emergency there is more work than adults to do it, and children want and need real jobs. But fire, fuel, cutting tools, chainsaws, large animals and open water injure and kill children every year on farms, where the same jobs are done. The US farm-safety programme at NIOSH matches each job to a child's age, size, strength and judgement, and stresses training and adult supervision. The answer is a rule written in advance: for each job, the age to start learning, the training, the supervision, and the habit a child must show before doing it alone. Fill in the table on the page. Locked storage of firearms, fuel, medicines and chlorine stays a floor.
pages.body:
# DC-24. Children doing dangerous jobs because hands are short

**What this page is for.** This card is a worksheet. Children with real jobs are calmer, braver and
safer, and in a long emergency their help matters (→ 20-07). Some jobs can kill or maim a child.
The household writes, in advance, which jobs each child may do, at what age, with what training
and supervision.

> **SAFETY.** Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products
> (floor, → 30-01). That stays true whatever this table says: storage is locked, and any work a
