cards.title: DC-08. Using insulin or other refrigerated medication after a heat excursion

options.label: Follow the published window exactly
options.summary: Insulin out of the fridge is used only inside the published room-temperature window (FDA emergency guidance: 59 to 86 °F for up to 28 days) or the product label; after that, or after heat above it, it is replaced.

options.label: Use beyond the window if nothing else; watch closely
options.summary: If no properly stored supply exists, heat-exposed or out-of-window insulin is used rather than none, with more frequent glucose checks and ketone checks, expecting it may work less well. Replaced as soon as possible.

cards.settings_summary: Insulin and some other medicines are stored in the fridge. Without power, FDA's emergency guidance says insulin can be kept at 59 to 86 °F for up to 28 days. Above that, or for longer, it slowly loses strength, and you cannot see the loss. Weaker insulin means higher blood sugar and, for type 1 diabetes, a risk of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), which can kill. But no insulin at all causes DKA for certain. FDA says that in an emergency you may still need to use insulin stored above 86 °F until proper supply returns. What helps most: keep it in the band with a powered fridge or cooler and a thermometer (removes it); evaporative pouches, cool spots, rotation (reduces it a lot). Frozen insulin is never used (floor).

cards.title: DC-09. An infant or toddler sharing a bed with adults for warmth

options.label: Own firm sleep surface beside the adults
options.summary: The child sleeps on a separate firm, flat surface (crib, play yard, firm mat on the floor) next to the adults in the warm room, dressed in layers and a sleep sack, checked by touch. Never in the adult bed.

options.label: Bed-share on cold nights, over 12 months only, with rules
options.summary: Only for a child over 12 months: firm mattress (on the floor if the bed is high), no pillows or heavy covers near the child, sleep sack instead, sober and unsedated adults, no older child beside them, nothing hot in the bed.

cards.settings_summary: In a cold house, sharing a bed keeps a small child warm with body heat. The American Academy of Pediatrics says babies under 1 year should sleep in the parents' room but on their own firm, flat surface, never in an adult bed, because about 3,500 US babies die each year from sleep-related causes, including suffocation in soft bedding and being lain on. The risk is highest under 4 months, with soft bedding, sofas, smoking, or an adult who has had alcohol or sedating medicine. Cold is a real risk too: CDC lists infants in cold bedrooms among those most at risk of hypothermia. What helps most: own firm surface next to the adults, warm room, layers and a sleep sack (removes most of it). Bed-sharing on this card is only offered for children over 12 months.

cards.title: DC-10. Pets when food, water or movement makes keeping them impossible

options.label: Keep them at all costs
options.summary: The pets stay with the household and share its food and water, and travel with it. Their needs are counted in every supply plan, and the household accepts going without to keep them.

options.label: Release with food and water left out
options.summary: If they cannot stay or come along, the pets are left or released with as much food and water as can be spared, a way in and out of shelter, and an ID tag, accepting that many will not survive.

options.label: A humane end, by the method page
options.summary: If the pets cannot be kept, carried or rehomed, a calm adult ends their lives humanely using only the method described on the pets page, not an improvised one, away from the children.

cards.settings_summary: Pets need food, water and room in the vehicle. In a long emergency a household may not be able to feed them, or may have to leave on foot or with no space. FEMA's advice while help exists is to plan to take your pets with you. When that is not possible, the choices are hard: keep them and share scarce food and water; release them, knowing most house pets do not survive long alone outdoors; or end their lives humanely, which the American Veterinary Medical Association says must be done by a method that causes no fear or pain. What helps most: plan pet food, water and carriers now, and find someone who could take them (removes most of it); decide in advance, calmly, so the decision is not made in panic.

cards.title: DC-11. Firing weapons on your own property for practice, pests or zeroing

options.label: Never on our property
options.summary: No shots fired on or from the property for practice, pests or sighting in. Practice is dry (unloaded) at home; pests are trapped; live fire happens only at a proper range or open land with a real backstop elsewhere.

options.label: Only into a known backstop, nobody downrange
options.summary: Shots only into an earth bank or backstop that will stop that ammunition, never toward a house, road or path, never at a target above the horizon, never at night, nobody downrange, neighbours told beforehand.

cards.settings_summary: In a long emergency, ranges close, and households may want to practise, sight in a rifle or deal with pests at home. Every firearms safety rule says be sure of your target and what is beyond it: a bullet that misses or passes through keeps going, far past any yard or rural lot, and can ricochet off water, rock or frozen ground. In town, what is beyond is a neighbour's house. Shots also tell everyone nearby that the house is armed and occupied, and damage hearing. What helps most: no live fire at home, dry practice and traps instead (removes it); only into a solid earth backstop, never toward houses or roads, never at a target above the horizon, nobody downrange, neighbours told (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-12. Defensive use of force: our household rule

options.label: Write our own rule
options.summary: The adults read this page together and write the household's use-of-force rule in their own words on the worksheet, sign and date it, and rehearse it.

cards.settings_summary: This card has no multiple choice. Every household that keeps any means of defence, firearm or not, needs a rule written in calm advance about when force may be used against another person. Without courts or police, nobody else will draw that line. The traditional tests are: the threat is happening now; nothing less will stop it; the force matches the threat; and a calm person would see it the same way. Mistakes cannot be undone: a bullet passes through walls into neighbours' homes, people are shot by family members who misidentified them in the dark, and with no surgeon any wound may be fatal. The neighbourhood remembers. Read the page, then write the rule in your own words on the worksheet.

cards.title: DC-13. Drinking water from a pool, hot tub or untreated surface source

options.label: Distil before drinking
options.summary: Water from a pool, hot tub or untreated stream, pond or lake is drunk only after distilling (boil it and collect the steam). Undistilled, it is used for flushing, washing and cleaning only.

options.label: Fresh pools: filter and chlorinate
options.summary: A freshwater (not salt) pool known to hold no algaecide or other additive may be drunk after settling, filtering and disinfecting by the published method. Salt pools and hot tubs still need distilling; surface water still needs distilling.

options.label: Surface water through the treatment ladder
options.summary: Streams, ponds and lakes away from obvious fuel, chemical or farm runoff are drunk after the full ladder: settle, filter, then boil or disinfect by the published method. Pools follow the two options above.

cards.settings_summary: A swimming pool or a nearby stream can look like a large water supply. Germs in water (bacteria, viruses, parasites) are killed by boiling or by chlorine used as CDC and EPA describe. Chemicals are not. Pool water holds chlorine, stabilizer, often algaecide, and in a salt pool, salt that no boiling or filter removes. Hot tubs hold bromine and body oils. Streams and ponds can carry fuel, farm or industrial runoff. CDC says water that may contain fuel or toxic chemicals cannot be made safe by boiling or disinfecting. Only distillation (boil and catch the steam) removes salt and most chemicals, and it is slow and uses fuel. What helps most: use pool and hot-tub water for flushing and washing, saving stored water for drinking (removes most of it); distil what you drink from them (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-14. Food past its date, dented or rusted cans, or food from a failed freezer

options.label: Follow the label and the published rules strictly
options.summary: Food past its date is discarded; dented, rusted or swollen cans are discarded; anything from the fridge or freezer above 40 °F for 2 hours or more is discarded, as USDA advises.

options.label: Inspect and eat, with the rules for each case
options.summary: Shelf-stable food past its quality date is eaten if the package is intact and it looks and smells normal; lightly dented cans with sound seams are eaten; thawed food still holding ice crystals is cooked or refrozen; the floor lines still apply.

cards.settings_summary: In a long emergency a household will have food past its printed date, dented or rusty cans, and fridges and freezers that have warmed. Most dates on food mark best quality, not safety; infant formula is the exception. Canned food stays safe for years if the can is sound and was not frozen or overheated. The dangers are a can whose seal has failed, which can carry botulism, a toxin that paralyses and looks, smells and tastes normal, and perishable food held warm, which grows bacteria that cause severe vomiting and diarrhoea. USDA says discard perishables above 40 °F for 2 hours. What helps most: rotate stock and check freezers with a thermometer (removes much of it); inspect every can and package, discard any bulging, leaking or spurting can (floor), and cook thoroughly (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-15. Giving someone else's prescription medication

options.label: Never
options.summary: Each prescription medicine is taken only by the person it was prescribed for. If someone runs out, the household looks for a clinician, pharmacy or the same prescription elsewhere.

options.label: Same drug and strength, already prescribed to them
options.summary: Only when the person was already prescribed the same drug at the same strength and has run out: they take it as their own label said, after checking allergies and their other medicines. Never a new drug for a new problem; never to a child from an adult's supply.

cards.settings_summary: When pharmacies close, one person may run out of a medicine that someone else in the house or the neighbourhood still has. Prescriptions are written for one person because the right drug and dose depend on the illness, allergies, other medicines, kidney and liver function, weight and age. Shared medicine can cause an allergic reaction, a dangerous interaction, a dose far too strong (for example a painkiller or sleeping medicine that stops the breathing of someone not used to it), or the wrong insulin causing severe low blood sugar. What helps most: get each person's own supply and a written plan from their clinician now (removes most of it); share only the same drug at the same strength the person already takes, after an allergy and interaction check (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-16. Antibiotics without a prescription (stockpiled or veterinary)

options.label: Never without a clinician
options.summary: Antibiotics are taken only when a clinician prescribed them for that person and that illness, or wrote a plan in advance. No stockpiled, shared, veterinary or aquarium antibiotics are used on a guess.

options.label: Last resort for adults, with the infection page
options.summary: Only for an adult showing the signs of a spreading or serious bacterial infection on the infection page, with no clinician reachable: a human antibiotic, with the drug and dose taken from a clinician's written plan or a published adult table printed as published. Never for children.

cards.settings_summary: Before antibiotics, ordinary wounds and infections killed healthy adults, so many preppers stockpile them, sometimes as fish or farm-animal products. Antibiotics are prescription drugs because the right one depends on the infection, the person's allergies and other medicines, and the dose depends on weight and kidney function. Most coughs, colds and stomach bugs are viral, and antibiotics do nothing for them. The wrong antibiotic can cause a severe allergic reaction or severe diarrhoea, hide a worsening infection, and breed resistant bacteria. Products sold for animals are not made or checked for human use. What helps most: ask a clinician now for a written plan and supply (removes most of it); use only for adults with clear signs of a serious bacterial infection, by a written or published adult table, never for children (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-17. Old kerosene, diesel or gasoline in a heater or engine

options.label: Fresh fuel only, on a rotation schedule
options.summary: Every can is dated. Gasoline is stabilised when bought and rotated into vehicles on a schedule; kerosene and diesel are used and replaced on a schedule. Fuel past the household's age limit is not burned in heaters or the generator.

options.label: Jar-test old fuel and use it if it passes
options.summary: Old fuel may be used if a sample in a clear jar, left to stand, is clear and bright with no water layer, cloudiness, sludge or colour change, and it smells like the right fuel. Any doubt, or an unlabelled can, and it is not used.

cards.settings_summary: Fuel ages. Gasoline loses the parts that help it start, can absorb water and leaves gum that blocks small-engine carburettors. Kerosene and diesel take up water from the air in part-full cans and can grow sludge. One common wick-heater maker says never use kerosene stored from one season to the next. The real danger is in heaters: old or wet kerosene fouls the wick, so the flame burns badly and makes more smoke and carbon monoxide (CO) indoors. Old gasoline in a generator mostly means it will not start when needed. What helps most: date, stabilise and rotate (removes most of it); store full, sealed, cool and dark, and jar-test before every fill (reduces it a lot). An unlabelled or unknown can is never poured.

cards.title: DC-18. Feeding a food-allergic person unlabeled, traded or scavenged food

options.label: Never: only food with a full, readable label
options.summary: The allergic person eats only food whose full ingredient label has been read, or food the household made itself from labelled ingredients in a clean kitchen. No traded, donated, scavenged or foraged food, ever.

options.label: Single-ingredient foods only
options.summary: Unlabelled or traded food is allowed only if it is one plain, recognisable ingredient (whole rice, dry beans, a whole vegetable or fruit, a whole cut of meat) that is not on the person's allergen list, washed and cooked in the household's own clean pots.

options.label: With epinephrine in hand, by our own line
options.summary: Unlabelled food may be tried by the household's own written line, only with in-date epinephrine in hand, an adult who knows the plan watching, the first taste small, and never alone or at night.

cards.settings_summary: When stores close, food arrives without labels: bartered, donated, scavenged, repackaged or foraged. For a person with a food allergy, a label is how you find the hidden egg, peanut, milk, sesame or soy. US law requires the nine major allergens to be declared on packaged food, but only while labels exist. Without one, a trace of the allergen, or a pot or spoon that touched it, can cause anaphylaxis: throat swelling, trouble breathing, collapse, death within minutes to hours without epinephrine. With no ambulance, epinephrine is the only treatment, and a reaction can need more than one dose. What helps most: a deep stock of verified safe food and kept labels (removes most of it); single-ingredient foods cooked in the household's own pots (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-19. When to leave home: our triggers

options.label: Write our own rule
options.summary: The adults fill in the trigger table on this page with their own thresholds and destinations, agree it, sign and date it, and review it each year.

cards.settings_summary: This card has no multiple choice. Leaving home is the highest-stakes decision a household makes in a long emergency, and the one most often made badly: too late, in a panic, in bad weather, with children. Staying in a stocked, known home is usually safer than moving. Leaving into a storm or extreme cold kills people every winter, and the Red Cross and National Weather Service both say avoid travel in winter storms unless you must. But staying past the point where medicine, heat, water or safety runs out forces a move in the worst condition. The answer is thresholds written now, while calm, that turn a 3 a.m. judgement into a checklist. Fill in the trigger table on the page.

cards.title: DC-20. Open-flame cooking, candles or oil lamps indoors

options.label: No open flame indoors
options.summary: Light comes from flashlights, headlamps and battery lanterns; cooking happens outdoors or on electric appliances run from stored power. No candles, oil lamps or flame cooking inside.

options.label: Indoors with extinguisher, alarms and rules
options.summary: Candles, oil lamps or stove-top flame cooking are allowed only with working smoke and CO alarms, an extinguisher within reach, 12 inches clear all round, an adult in the room, never where anyone sleeps, out when the room is left.

cards.settings_summary: In an outage, candles, oil lamps and cooking on a match-lit gas stove are the oldest answers to dark and cold food. US Fire Administration advice is to use flashlights, not candles, in a power outage, because candles cause many home fires, often when they are left burning, placed too close to something that burns, or reached by children or pets. Any flame indoors also adds carbon monoxide and uses oxygen, and CDC says never use a gas stove or oven to heat a home. Lamp oil and kerosene are poisonous if a child swallows them. What helps most: battery lights and outdoor cooking (removes it); working smoke and CO alarms, an extinguisher in reach, an adult present, nothing within 12 inches, never in sleeping areas (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-21. Using a fireplace or wood stove that has not been inspected this year

options.label: Inspect first, using the chimney page
options.summary: No fire until the household has done the inspection on the chimney page (cold flue, light and mirror, scrape test, cap and blockages) or a professional has. A flue with glaze, cracks or a blockage is not used until fixed.

options.label: Use it with small hot fires and a watch
options.summary: If it cannot be inspected now: small, hot fires of dry wood only, never smouldering overnight, CO and smoke alarms in the room, an extinguisher in reach, someone checking the chimney and attic, and an inspection at the first chance.

cards.settings_summary: A fireplace or wood stove can heat a house with no power, but the chimney is part of the appliance. Wood smoke leaves a tar called creosote on the inside of the chimney; it builds up faster with damp wood and slow, smoky fires, and it burns. A chimney fire can crack the chimney and set the house alight. A chimney blocked by a nest, leaves or fallen brick sends smoke and carbon monoxide back into the room. The national fire code for chimneys (NFPA 211) and chimney safety groups say inspect at least once a year. What helps most: inspect first, by a professional or with the household's own light-and-mirror check (removes most of it); dry wood, small hot fires, alarms, an extinguisher and a watch on the chimney (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-22. Potassium iodide for adults over 40

options.label: Follow FDA: over 40 only at very large exposure
options.summary: Adults over 40 take potassium iodide only if officials say a very large dose of radioactive iodine is expected, as FDA advises. Everyone younger follows the FDA table on the potassium iodide page, on official direction.

options.label: Adults over 40 take it whenever others do
options.summary: When officials direct potassium iodide for the area, adults over 40 in the household take the FDA adult dose too, after checking the FDA list of people who should not take it, accepting a higher chance of side effects.

cards.settings_summary: Potassium iodide (KI) is a tablet that fills the thyroid gland with ordinary iodine so it does not absorb radioactive iodine released by a nuclear accident or bomb. It protects only the thyroid, only from radioactive iodine, and only when taken on official direction. FDA's guidance says adults over 40 have the lowest risk of thyroid cancer from radioactive iodine and a higher chance of side effects from KI (thyroid problems and allergic reactions), so they should take it only if a very large exposure is expected. Sheltering indoors protects far more than KI does. What helps most: shelter first; know who should not take it; decide now with a clinician; take it only when officials say so.

cards.title: DC-23. Chlorinating very dirty water beyond the published dose

options.label: Clear it first, then the published dose
options.summary: Very dirty water is settled and filtered until it is as clear as possible, then disinfected at the published dose (doubled only if it is still cloudy, coloured or very cold, as CDC and EPA say), with the full wait.

options.label: Heavy dose and a longer wait when it cannot be cleared
options.summary: When the water cannot be settled or filtered, it gets the doubled published dose, a longer wait, and a smell check; if no chlorine smell, dose again and wait again. The household accepts strong taste and that some germs may survive.

cards.settings_summary: Household bleach and dissolved pool shock kill most germs in water at the dose CDC and EPA publish, and they say to double that dose for cloudy, coloured or very cold water. Very dirty water is the problem: mud and plant matter use up the chlorine and hide germs inside particles, so even a big dose may not disinfect it, and a parasite called Cryptosporidium survives ordinary chlorine anyway. Pouring in much more chlorine than published mostly makes water taste and smell harsh and can upset stomachs; mistakes with concentrated pool shock are dangerous. What helps most: settle and filter first, then the published dose (reduces it a lot); boiling clear water instead (removes most germ risk). Never mix chlorine with other cleaners (floor).

cards.title: DC-24. Children doing dangerous jobs because hands are short

options.label: Write our own rule
options.summary: The adults fill in the job table on this page with the age, training and supervision each child needs for each dangerous job, agree it, sign and date it, and review it on each child's birthday.

cards.settings_summary: This card has no multiple choice. In a long emergency there is more work than adults to do it, and children want and need real jobs. But fire, fuel, cutting tools, chainsaws, large animals and open water injure and kill children every year on farms, where the same jobs are done. The US farm-safety programme at NIOSH matches each job to a child's age, size, strength and judgement, and stresses training and adult supervision. The answer is a rule written in advance: for each job, the age to start learning, the training, the supervision, and the habit a child must show before doing it alone. Fill in the table on the page. Locked storage of firearms, fuel, medicines and chlorine stays a floor.

destination-honest-read.text:
# ai block: destination-honest-read - **Used on:** `01-05-choosing-a-destination` (household layer), under "The honest read", after the destinations table and the status definitions.
- **Written by:** C01, 2026-11-16. ## Purpose One short, honest paragraph per destination that pulls together what the template can only print
in separate cells: how its status, distance, climate and hazards, the people there, and this
household's needs fit together, and what remains to be done to make it real. The owner household's
binder had such a paragraph per destination ("the distance is the whole problem: a one-shot early
trip, never a reactive winter one"); this block writes the equivalent for any household from its
own answers and the region data. ## Inputs (exact context paths; nothing else) - For each `destinations[]` entry, in profile order: `name`, `state_name`, `county`, `status_text` (agreed / unannounced / property only / undecided), `who_is_there`, `how_to_reach_them`, `route_notes`, `approximate_miles`, and from its `region`: `jan_low_f`, `jul_high_f`, `snow_in`, `zone`, `hazards` (name, rating, rating_text).
- Household: `household.size`, `home.county`, `home.state_name`, `region.home.hazards`.
- Flags: `has.refrigerated_meds`, `has.oxygen`, `has.cpap`, `has.mobility_aid`, `has.anaphylaxis`, `has.infant`, `has.young_child`, `has.elder`, `has.pregnant`, `has.pets`, `has.vehicle`, `has.trailer`, `has.condition.CL-NN`. ## Output - Markdown. For each destination, one paragraph starting with the destination name in bold and its status in bold, e.g. `**Name** (**agreed**): ...`. Paragraphs in profile order.
- Each paragraph covers, in this order and only where the inputs support it: 1. What the status means for this place in practice (expected or not; can supplies be cached). 2. Distance in the household's own miles, and what that implies for timing: a long trip suits only an early, seen-it-coming departure in good weather; a short one can be a later move. Say "the fuel worksheet on → 01-03" rather than computing fuel. 3. Winter and climate from the region values (state the values as given, with units), and the destination hazards rated 2 or 3 by name, compared with home's in words ("more", "fewer", "different"). 4. The household's needs that make this place harder or easier, in words (for example refrigerated medicine and an unknown power source; a wheelchair and an unknown house; a small child and a working farm), pointing to → 01-07 for medical needs. 5. The one or two most important open items, chosen from: ask them; visit; place a cache; settle water, heat, storm shelter or medical distance; drive the route.
- If `destinations[]` is empty: output exactly: "No destination is entered. Until one is agreed, staying is strongly preferred, and the realistic move is toward town, family or medical help. Add destinations in settings and regenerate." ## Constraints - **Never introduce** a number, distance, drive time, road, town, facility, phone number, law or procedure that is not in the inputs. Use `approximate_miles` exactly as given; do not convert it to hours or fuel. Do not name highways, hospitals or pharmacies unless they appear verbatim in `route_notes` or `who_is_there`.
- Do not change or soften the status. An unannounced or undecided destination is never described as safe, expected or reliable. Property only is never described as having anyone there.
- Do not recommend one destination over another, and do not make the go/no-go decision; the household does that on → 01-02.
- Quote the household's free text (`who_is_there`, `route_notes`) only briefly and only as fact about what they wrote; never invent relationships or agreements.
- Plain words, short sentences, calm. No headings, no tables, no bullet lists. ## Length Each paragraph 50 to 110 words. At most three paragraphs (the profile allows three destinations). ## Example shape (illustrative only; never copy) **The cabin** (**property only**): nobody lives there, so nothing has been kept warm or stocked
unless you did it, and someone may be there before you. At about 140 miles it is within reach of a
later departure, but check → 01-03's fuel worksheet. January lows of 4 °F and 60 inches of snow a
year make it a hard winter arrival. With refrigerated medicine in the household and no known power
source there, the cold chain has to ride with you (→ 01-07). Next: visit, and decide what can be
cached there safely.

roles-must-know.text:
# ai block: roles-must-know - **Used on:** `00-07-household-roles` (household layer), directly under "The one that is not optional".
- **Written by:** C01, 2026-11-16. ## Purpose Name, for this household, the life-sustaining routines that every adult must be able to run, and
whose routine each one is, so the generic paragraph above it becomes concrete. The template cannot
do this because it needs to pick out, from members, conditions, allergies, medicines and devices,
only the items that are life-sustaining, and group them by person. ## Inputs (exact context paths; nothing else) - `members[]`: `label`, `role`, `age_text`, `conditions` (condition-library ids and titles, plus the free-text "other" condition if present)
- `allergies[]`: `member`, `allergen`, `severity`, `carries_epinephrine`
- `meds[]`: `member`, `name`, `refrigerated` (do **not** use `strength`, `schedule` or `if_missed`)
- flags: `has.anaphylaxis`, `has.epinephrine`, `has.refrigerated_meds`, `has.oxygen`, `has.cpap`, `has.mobility_aid`, `has.infant`, `has.pregnant`, `has.nursing`, `has.condition.CL-NN`
- the titles and kit page ids of the selected condition-library modules (Section 02 page ids, `02-NN`, where `NN` is the CL number) ## Output - A Markdown bullet list, one bullet per person who has at least one life-sustaining routine, in the order of `members[]`. Each bullet: the person's label in bold, then the routine(s) in plain words, each followed by the page reference in the form `→ 02-NN` (the condition module) or `→ 02-03` (anaphylaxis), `→ 29-07` (refrigerated medicines), `→ 09-06` (powered devices).
- What counts as a routine: giving or backing up a refrigerated or daily medicine; recognising and treating that condition's emergency as the module describes it (name it only, e.g. "a severe low", "anaphylaxis", "a seizure"; do not describe treatment steps); keeping a powered device running (oxygen, CPAP); moving someone who uses a wheelchair or walker; infant feeding.
- After the list, one sentence: "Each of these has its own page; every adult reads it and practises the emergency part with a trainer or the prescriber (→ 24-01)."
- If no member has any such routine: output exactly one sentence: "No one in this household has a condition, allergy, medicine or device marked life-sustaining in settings. If that changes, regenerate the binder, and the routine will be listed here." ## Constraints - **Never introduce** a number, dose, timing, phone number, product name, law or procedure that is not in the inputs. Do not restate strengths or schedules. Do not explain how to treat anything: the condition pages do that.
- Do not infer a condition from a medicine name, or a medicine from a condition. Use only what is typed.
- Do not rank people or judge the household. No reassurance, no alarm.
- Plain words, short sentences, the binder's voice (calm, direct). No headings, no tables.
- Medicine names exactly as typed. ## Length At most 8 bullets, each at most 30 words; total at most 220 words. ## Example shape (illustrative only; never copy) - **Alex**: daily refrigerated medicine and its cold chain (→ 29-07); recognising a severe low (→ 02-01).
- **Sam**: anaphylaxis to a food; epinephrine first (→ 02-03). Each of these has its own page; every adult reads it and practises the emergency part with a
trainer or the prescriber (→ 24-01).

notice_md:
# Notice shown inside every generated binder

This text appears (1) on the settings page while the household fills it in, (2) on the download
screen, and (3) as the second page of the generated binder, after the safety disclaimer. It is
written for someone who has never thought about any of this before.

---

## Your answers are never stored

Nothing you type on this page is saved by us. There is no account, no database and no log of your
answers. Your answers live only in this browser tab. If you close the tab before you download your
binder, they are gone and you start over. You may choose to save a copy of your answers as a file
on your own device so you can come back and regenerate later; that file stays with you.

When you press **Generate**, your answers are sent once to the AI service that writes your binder
(Anthropic's Claude API), through a small relay program whose only jobs are to check your access
key and pass the request along. The relay keeps a count of requests and nothing else. Its source
code is shown on the settings page's privacy section so you can check this. Cloudflare, which
hosts the page and the relay, keeps its own standard request metrics (times, sizes, rough location)
like any web host; it does not see your answers' meaning unless it inspected the request, and we
have not asked it to keep anything. The AI provider's own data-handling terms apply to the
request; we do not control those and we say so here rather than promise more than we can.

## This file is your private copy. Do not share it.

Your binder contains the full text of documents written by other people and organisations:
appliance manuals, first-aid guides, fire-safety standards, medical-society fact sheets, university
publications. They were fetched for **your personal use** when you downloaded this file, because
in an emergency you need the whole document in your hand, not a web address that no longer works.

Those documents are copyrighted by their publishers. Giving your binder file to someone else copies
their work without permission and breaks copyright. **Keep this file to your own household.** If a
friend wants a binder, send them to the settings page and they can make their own.

## What this binder is, and is not

This binder was assembled and checked by an AI from a verified core text, public datasets and the
answers you gave. **No doctor, engineer, electrician or other professional has reviewed your copy.**
It is a reference for a time when the normal references, services and professionals are not
available. While they are available, use them. Where this binder and a professional disagree, the
professional is right.

Several pages ask you to choose between options that carry real risk. Those pages explain the
hazard, what the manufacturer or agency says and why, what reduces the risk, and the choices. The
choice is yours and so is the responsibility for it.
